  release commit (not the runner's wall clock), and stages `alp.lock` under
  a real `alp-sdk-<TAG>/` directory instead of a `tar --transform` sed
  expression -- both needed to keep the tarball byte-reproducible per
  CHANGELOG.md's #610 §7 promise; a bare `tar --append` stamped the runner's
  mtime/uid/gid and a `,`-delimited `--transform` broke on a tag containing
  a literal `,`.
- `scripts/bump_version.py` no longer regenerates `alp.lock` on a version
  bump (`regenerate_alp_lock` removed) -- nothing to keep in sync in a
  tracked file that no longer exists.
- `scripts/resolve_generated_conflicts.py`'s `REGENERATORS` no longer carries
  an `alp.lock` entry -- an untracked file can't appear in a merge conflict.
- `docs/getting-started.md` "Reproducing a build with alp.lock" no longer
  says to commit it or re-run-and-commit on a metadata change; it now
  documents the generate-and-validate model and that the release tarball
  carries one.

Unverified: `signex` and `alp-studio` are not checked out in this workspace
and could not be swept for `alp.lock` references. Checked and clear:
`alp-sdk-internal` (0 refs), `alp-sdk-vscode` (0 refs), `tan-cli` (one prose
comment in a fixture explaining what `alp.lock` is NOT -- not a consumer).

### Fixed — CC3501E OTA never completed: a misaligned staging buffer hung `psa_fwu_start`, and the polled bridge desynced on an 8-byte RX FIFO (Closes #1610)

Streaming a firmware image to the CC3501E over the inter-chip SPI bridge never
finished. Two independent defects, both now proven on silicon:

**1. `ota.window` was misaligned, and `psa_fwu_start` hung on it.** The OTA
staging buffer is the last member of the OTA state struct in
`cc3501e-bridge-firmware:hal/ti/cc3501e_hw_ti_ota.c`, and the members ahead of it summed
to an odd offset (41), so `window[]` sat at an address ≡ 1 (mod 4). `ota_flush()`
passes that pointer straight to `psa_fwu_start()` for manifest verification — a
crypto/DMA path — where a misaligned buffer does not fail, it **hangs**, and the
device is never heard from again. The buffer is now
`__attribute__((aligned(32)))` (32 rather than 4, because the same buffer also
feeds `psa_fwu_write()`'s DMA path).

Note for future debugging: an earlier bisect appeared to clear everything
downstream of `psa_fwu_start`, because skipping it made the flush "complete in
1 ms with the link alive". With the slot never opened, `psa_fwu_write()` was only
returning early — it never demonstrated the buffer was usable. When a
crypto/flash/DMA call hangs rather than returning an error, check pointer
alignment before interrupts, XIP, bus contention, or task priorities.

**2. The polled bridge desynced because the RX FIFO is 8 frames deep.**
`SPIWFF3DMA`'s polling path counts `dataGet` reads rather than SCLK edges and
runs with `RETURN_PARTIAL` disabled, so a chip-select deassert is invisible to
it; any byte clocked while the slave is between transfers is not lost data but a
permanent phase shift, and the RX-overrun interrupt is enabled only on the DMA
path, so it is silent and never self-heals. `bridge_transport_spi_poll_service()`
now resets the RX+TX FIFOs at the start of every frame, so each frame begins from
a known-empty state.

**3. Four host-side costs made the transfer far slower than the link.**
`OTA_BEGIN` treated the device's BUSY reply (the op was queued) as a lost reply
and blind-slept a flat 180 s on *every* OTA; the per-chunk poll slept 50 ms per
iteration; the polled inter-phase settle was sized at 5000 us against the desync
fixed above; and the example streamed 256 B chunks while
`ALP_CC3501E_OTA_MAX_CHUNK` is 508.

**4. `cc3501e_ota_update_mode()` was declared in no header.** It was defined in
`chips/cc3501e/cc3501e_ota.c` and called by `cc3501e_ota_update()`, but invisible
to any caller outside that translation unit and absent from the ABI snapshot. It
is now declared in `include/alp/chips/cc3501e/ota.h` with the update-mode
contract, and the v0.16 ABI snapshot regenerated.

**5. A socket receive stalled the whole bridge worker.**
`CC3501E_SOCK_RCVTIMEO_MS` was 4000, and the receive runs on the worker, which
has a single job slot — so a blocking `lwip_recv` held it for the full window and
no other job, and therefore no bridge frame, was served while it waited. It is
now 50 ms; the wire contract is already poll-based (EWOULDBLOCK maps to OK with
0 bytes and the host re-issues `CMD_SOCK_RECV`), so a long block was never needed
for correctness. **This did not move measured socket RX throughput** — a TCP
drain still delivers roughly one 487 B frame and then stalls for tens of seconds
(`NET first-miss rc=-4 after 0 B` / `after 487 B` / `after 974 B` across a 135 s
capture). The 4 s worker stall was a real defect on its own terms; the socket RX
limit is a separate, still-open one.

Measured on an E1M-AEN801 with a CC3501E, full 1095276 B signed image, radio
live, CC35 vendor image `0.149.42.0`: **1373 s -> 123 s** end to end (`BEGIN`
180035 ms -> 1067 ms on a clean slot; streaming ~936 B/s -> ~9.2 kB/s), reaching
`OTA all 1095276 B accepted -- FINISH`, `OTA finish -> 0` and `STAGED`. `BEGIN`
now varies with real slot state instead of reporting a constant.

Throughput is still bounded by per-frame overhead rather than by the wire, and
that is tracked separately: the bridge already runs at 14 MHz against a ~15 MHz
CC35 slave maximum, so a 516-byte maximum frame is 295 us of wire time against
four 200 us inter-phase settles. Raising it materially needs large payloads, DMA
and no per-chunk round trip — a redesign, not tuning.

### Fixed — `aen-cc3501e-bringup` never associated to Wi-Fi, and did not build in its default configuration

Wi-Fi association had never actually run from this example: an earlier refactor
left `cc3501e_wifi_probe()` as a bare `(void)` cast, so the whole CONNECT / RSSI
/ IP path was dead code the compiler stripped. It is now called from the liveness
soak once the SCAN has landed, gated on credentials supplied at build time (never
hardcoded here), and bounded to 5 attempts — `WIFI_CONNECT` is intermittent on
this silicon (`ALP_OK` and `ALP_ERR_IO` alternate across runs) but the bridge
survives a failed attempt, so a retry is safe.

The example also failed to compile in its DEFAULT configuration — the one twister
builds — because `CC3501E_BENCH_RADIO_BEFORE_OTA` is defined inside the OTA-demo
block but referenced unconditionally by the soak, and every `CC3501E_OTA_*`
option is off by default.

Adds a build-time-gated network probe (inert unless `CC3501E_SPEEDTEST_IP0` is
set, so no address is baked into the public example) that proves the associated
link carries IP traffic and measures end-to-end throughput over Wi-Fi plus the
SPI bridge. Verified on silicon: `soak WIFI_SCAN ok -> 4 AP(s)`,
`soak BLE_ENABLE ok`, `WIFI_CONNECT -> 0`, `RSSI -> -43 dBm`,
`IP -> 192.168.1.14`, and the HTTP GET reaching the server
(`192.168.1.14 - - "GET /speed.bin HTTP/1.0" 200`). The probe is what makes the
socket RX stall measurable rather than invisible.

### Fixed — scaffolded `board.yaml` and the `multicore-rpmsg` catalog entry disagreed on the RPMsg carve-out default (#1613)

`metadata/templates/board.yaml`'s commented `ipc:` stanza said `carve_out_kb:
512`; `metadata/templates/catalog-v1.json`'s `rpmsg_carve_out_kb` parameter
said `"default": 256`. Nothing in the tree derived either number, so a reader
could not tell which was intended.

512 is not merely the larger, safer-looking choice: `resolve_carve_outs()`
(`scripts/alp_orchestrate/carveout.py`) prefers the non-cacheable region,
smaller-first, and on RZ/V2N/V2M the only non-cacheable region an
`[a55_cluster, m33_sm]` pair can both reach is `ocram_low`
(`metadata/socs/renesas/rzv2n/n44.json`), which is exactly 512 KiB. A default
of 512 there consumes the *entire* region, leaving nothing for a second IPC
entry.

`metadata/templates/catalog-v1.json`'s existing `256` default is already
proven in tree — `examples/multicore/rpmsg-aen/board.yaml` ships it as-is,
using under 5% of E1M-AEN801's 5632 KiB `mram_main` — and 256 KiB is half of
`ocram_low`, not all of it. `metadata/templates/board.yaml`'s scaffolded
comment now matches at `256`, and both files carry a comment/description
pointing at the SoC facts and allocator behaviour the number is derived
from, so the next reader is not left to guess again.

`alp.lock` regenerated (metadata digest moved).

Note: `examples/multicore/rpmsg-v2n/board.yaml` and
`examples/multicore/heterogeneous-offload/board.yaml` both still declare
`carve_out_kb: 512` against this same `ocram_low` region — out of scope
here (this fix only touches the two scaffolding/catalog defaults), but the
same exhaustion applies to them and is worth a follow-up.

### Fixed — `alp_i2s_write()` copied a caller-supplied length into a fixed-size slab block (#1619)

`src/backends/i2s/zephyr_drv.c:228` ran `memcpy(slab_block, block, bytes)` with
the caller's `bytes` into a `k_mem_slab` block whose size was computed at
`open()` and then discarded — the sidecar stored `slab_buf_bytes` but never the
per-block size, so `z_write()` had nothing to compare against. An oversize write
corrupted the neighbouring slab block and the `k_malloc` heap behind it.

Zephyr's own `i2s_write()` rejects an oversize length with `-EINVAL`, but it is
called on the line *after* the `memcpy`, so it never saw the write that mattered.

The path is reachable from portable code with no I2S knowledge at all:
`src/backends/audio/zephyr_drv.c:516` derives `bytes = frames *
bytes_per_frame(&state->cfg)` from an unclamped `frames` and hands it to
`alp_i2s_write()`, while `src/audio_dispatch.c:184` validates only
`buf == NULL || frames == 0` and `src/i2s_dispatch.c:132` only
`block == NULL || bytes == 0u`.

Fixed in two places, so the oversize request is both refused and never generated:

- `src/backends/i2s/zephyr_drv.c:161` records the negotiated block size on the
  sidecar, and `:221` rejects `bytes > s->block_bytes` with
  `ALP_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` *before* claiming a slab block.
- `src/backends/audio/zephyr_drv.c:514` refuses `frames` beyond the
  `frames_per_block` negotiated at open, before the byte count is derived.

`alp_i2s_write()` and `alp_audio_out_write()` now document
`ALP_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` in their `@return` lists, and their length parameters say
the bound is enforced rather than merely expected.

**Verified on `native_sim`.** The regression test moved to
`tests/unit/i2s_write_bounds/` and now runs against a test-local `alp,test-i2s`
DT fake (`src/fake_i2s.c`, aliased as `alp-i2s0`) whose `configure`/`trigger`
always succeed, so `alp_i2s_open()` resolves a real device instead of the NULL
that made the old in-place ztest (`tests/zephyr/peripheral/src/i2s.c`) always
skip. `zephyr_drv` (priority 100) wins backend selection over `sw_fallback`
(priority 0) once a real device is present, so an exact-block write reaching
`ALP_OK` — not `ALP_ERR_NOSUPPORT` — confirms the test exercised the fixed
`z_write()` path, not the fallback. The selector fall-through gap this
originally hit (`i2s_dispatch.c` has no `alp_backend_select_next()`) is
unrelated to the fix itself and stays filed on #1642.

### Fixed — a timed-out GATT read/write left the BT host holding a dead stack frame (#1620)

`z_gatt_read()` / `z_gatt_write()` handed Zephyr's BT host an **automatic**
`ble_read_ctx` / `ble_write_ctx` and, on the `k_sem` timeout path, returned
without cancelling the outstanding ATT procedure. When the peer's response
eventually arrived on the BT RX thread, the completion callback cast `params`
back to that dead stack frame and wrote through it — a use-after-return into
another thread's stack, from a path the caller had no way to see.

Zephyr offers no general "cancel this ATT procedure" call, so the fix is an
ownership change rather than a cancel: the contexts move into
`_read_ctx_pool` / `_write_ctx_pool`, claimed with the existing
`alp_slot_try_claim()` and released by whichever side wins a one-byte
`alp_lifecycle_cas()`. A timeout marks its slot `ABANDONED` and returns; the
late callback loses the CAS, touches nothing, and frees the slot itself. The
issue's own suggestion — putting the context inside `struct ble_conn_be` — was
rejected on inspection, because `_conn_be_free()`'s memset would then clear a
context a live registration still points at.

Three caller-visible consequences, all now documented on the public
declarations in `include/alp/ble.h` rather than left for someone to discover:

- **`ALP_ERR_BUSY` is a new return code** for both functions, returned when
  every concurrent-procedure slot is held. It was previously impossible.
- **A timeout does not cancel anything.** `ALP_ERR_TIMEOUT` now means "not
  answered in time", not "abandoned", and the slot stays held until the peer
  answers or the link drops. `timeout_ms == 0` is the pathological case: each
  such call burns a slot, and the default
  `CONFIG_ALP_SDK_BLE_MAX_GATT_PROCS` is 4.
- **A procedure completing just after the deadline now returns its real
  result** instead of `ALP_ERR_TIMEOUT`.

`alp_ble_gatt_write()` additionally documents that the host may re-read the
caller's `data` buffer after the call returns. In upstream Zephyr's BT host, a
long write goes out as a prepare-write sequence (`gatt_prepare_write()`), and
`att_req_retry()` re-encodes the request on an encryption-change retry under
`CONFIG_BT_SMP` even for a **short** write — wider than the long-write case the
issue named. Both re-read `params->data`, which the caller owns.

**Not closed by this change:** the issue's regression test for the abandon path
is still owed. `native_sim` has no BLE controller, so the late-callback race
cannot be driven by a real peer; it needs a test seam in the backend, and the
existing `tests/zephyr/ble_gatt_server` cases only ever exercise the
`LIVE -> DONE` win. The abandon path, the CAS loss, and the `ALP_ERR_BUSY`
branch are unexecuted code.

### Fixed — 34 chip-driver call sites busy-waited >= 1ms through `alp_delay_us()` (#1621)

`alp_delay_us()` is documented (`include/alp/peripheral.h`) as a non-yielding
busy-wait — Zephyr's backend routes it straight to `k_busy_wait()`, which
never releases the CPU to other threads. It is scoped to sub-millisecond
hardware-timing sequences only; `alp_delay_ms()` (-> `k_msleep()`, which
yields) is the contract for anything a millisecond or longer.

34 fixed-literal call sites across 16 chip drivers passed >= 1000us through
`alp_delay_us()` — up to a 1.5s spin in `ublox_sara_r5_power_on()` — stalling
every equal-or-lower-priority thread on that core for the whole window, long
enough to starve a watchdog-feed thread. Every such site is now
`alp_delay_ms()`, with an in-file comment on the caller side explaining why
sleeping instead of spinning is safe there.

One site is deliberately left as an `alp_delay_us()` spin, with an in-file
comment explaining why: `chips/gd32g553/gd32g553.c`'s SPI reply-retry ladder
(`gd32g553_reply_retry_us`) includes a 1600us tail rung, indexed off the
array by a variable rather than a fixed literal — the whole ladder is
bench-tuned to bound a live SPI slave-reply race at ~3.2ms total, and
`alp_delay_ms()` rounding up to a whole system tick would blow past that
bound.

Added `scripts/check_delay_us_literal.py`: a grep-grade CI gate under
`chips/**` that rejects a new fixed-literal `alp_delay_us(N>=1000)`, with unit
tests in `tests/scripts/test_check_delay_us_literal.py`. Wired into the
`validate` job of `pr-metadata-validate.yml` (`metadata/quality-tasks-v1.json`),
whose `paths:` filter now also covers `chips/**` and the gate script itself —
a PR that only touches a chip driver, or only the gate, now retriggers it; the
filter previously listed `include/alp/chips/**` but not `chips/**`, so the
regression lock was unreachable on exactly the change class it exists to
catch (same defect class as #1487/#1528/#1585). Regression-locked by
`tests/scripts/test_delay_us_literal_gate_paths_cover_input.py`.

By design the gate only catches a fixed *integer literal* argument — a
variable, macro, or expression argument (e.g.
`chips/eeprom_24c128/eeprom_24c128.c`'s `#define`d `EEPROM_WRITE_POLL_STEP_US`)
is caller/config-controlled and is out of scope for this bulk sweep; it is
reviewed case by case instead.

### Fixed — three E1M-EVK `adc:` entries described nets that don't exist on the board (#1622)

Issue #1622's premise was inverted: the hand-authored `EVK_ARD_A0` / `EVK_MB_ANA`
macros in `include/alp/boards/alp_e1m_evk.h` (both `ALP_E1M_ADC0`, with a comment
that mounting an Arduino shield and a mikroBUS click together contends the
channel) were already correct. It was the **generated** `metadata/boards/e1m-evk.yaml`
`adc:` block that was wrong, traced against the authoritative netlist
(`E1M-EVK-2626-R2_pinmap.csv` in `alp-sdk-internal`):

- **`EVK_ADC_BOARD_ID` (`E1M_ADC0`)** claimed a carrier-side BOARD_ID resistor
  divider. No `BOARD_ID` net exists anywhere in the pinmap — the only `*_ID`
  nets are the three USB ID pins. `ANA_S0` is net `ARD.A0`, reached from
  mikroBUS `CK_ANA` through `R52` (series), `R63` (pulldown) and `C60`
  (filter) — the genuinely shared Arduino-A0/mikroBUS-ANA input the
  hand-written header already documents. Renamed to `EVK_ADC_ARDUINO_A0`,
  matching the `EVK_ADC_ARDUINO_A1..A5` convention.
- **`EVK_ADC_MB_AN` (`E1M_ADC6`)** claimed the mikroBUS click AN pin — but
  mikroBUS ANA is `E1M_ADC0` (above); no Click net touches `ANA_S6`. `ANA_S6`
  is net `A6`, a DAC0 output loopback sense: `R88` from `DAC0_OUT`, `R89`
  pulldown, `C107` filter. Renamed to `EVK_ADC_DAC0_LOOPBACK`.
- **`EVK_ADC_VBAT_SENSE` (`E1M_ADC7`)** claimed a 4:1 battery-voltage divider.
  There is no `VBAT` net in the pinmap at all. `ANA_S7` is net `A7`, a DAC1
  output loopback sense: `R90` from `DAC1_OUT`, `R91` pulldown, `C108`
  filter. Renamed to `EVK_ADC_DAC1_LOOPBACK`. No example used the old macro
  to read a battery — `examples/` has no consumer of any of the three old
  names — so nothing was silently measuring a DAC loopback and calling it
  VBAT.

No legacy compat: the three old macro names are gone, not aliased.
`include/alp/boards/alp_e1m_evk_routes.h` regenerated via
`scripts/gen_board_header.py`; `tests/scripts/test_gen_board_header.py`'s
"not generated" list (previously listing `EVK_ARD_A0` / `EVK_MB_ANA` next to a
stale comment naming the old macros) updated to reference the corrected names.
`alp.lock`'s `digests.metadata` and `docs/abi/v0.16-snapshot.json` regenerated
to match, along with the two affected `tests/fixtures/emit-snapshots/proj-aen.*`
goldens.

Not touched, deliberately: `hw_revisions.r1.board_id.adc_channel: TBD` a few
lines below the `adc:` block is a separate, still-accurate placeholder for a
BOARD_ID path the EVK schematic hasn't assigned a net for yet — it was already
`TBD`, consistent with "no BOARD_ID net exists today". `docs/board-id.md`
documents that unrelated EEPROM-authoritative SoM `board_id` concept and
doesn't reference these ADC macros.

### Added — a reusable record for INTENTIONAL public-symbol removals (#1622)

Renaming the three macros above is a real, deliberate ABI removal against
whatever last shipped (`EVK_ADC_VBAT_SENSE` in particular is actively
dangerous to keep — it invites reading a battery voltage off a DAC output
loopback), and the ABI freeze gate had no way to record "removed on purpose,
here's what to use instead" — only "removed" full stop.

`docs/abi/removed-symbols.json` is the new record: one entry per removed
symbol, carrying its header, category, the release it left in, the issue
number, a one-sentence customer-actionable reason, and the replacement symbol
(or an explicit `null` when none exists). `scripts/abi_snapshot.py`'s
`diff()` now loads it (`load_removed_allowlist`, hard-erroring on a malformed
entry) and reports a matching removal as `ALLOWED macro
alp/boards/alp_e1m_evk_routes.h::EVK_ADC_BOARD_ID (intentional removal, #1622
-> EVK_ADC_ARDUINO_A0)` instead of a bare `REMOVED` — still visible in the
diff for review, just no longer unexplained, and never matching the freeze
gate's `grep -q '^  REMOVED '` or the exit-code check that gates the PR. A
removal with no allowlist entry still fails exactly as before. See
`docs/abi/README.md`'s "Recording an INTENTIONAL removal" for the full
mechanism, and `docs/abi/removed-symbols.json` for the three entries this
issue adds.

Upgrading past this release: if your code referenced `EVK_ADC_BOARD_ID`,
`EVK_ADC_MB_AN`, or `EVK_ADC_VBAT_SENSE`, switch to `EVK_ADC_ARDUINO_A0`,
`EVK_ADC_DAC0_LOOPBACK`, or `EVK_ADC_DAC1_LOOPBACK` respectively — there is
no compat alias for any of the three.

### Fixed — `rv3028c7_dispatch_irq()` could silently swallow a one-shot RTC event that fired mid-dispatch (#1623)

`rv3028c7_dispatch_irq()` read `STATUS`, ran the registered handlers, then wrote
`STATUS = 0x00` unconditionally to acknowledge -- clearing every write-0-to-clear
flag, including any one-shot source (`RV3028C7_SRC_ALARM`, `RV3028C7_SRC_EXT_EVENT`,
`RV3028C7_SRC_BSF`) that latched during the handlers' own I2C work. A one-shot
source has no "next event" to re-latch it, so the flag -- and its handler
invocation -- was lost with no error returned and no trace in `status_seen`.

The acknowledge is now a write-0x00-then-re-read step
(`rv3028_status_ack()`, `chips/rv3028c7/rv3028c7.c`) shared by
`rv3028c7_init()`, `rv3028c7_alarm_check_and_clear()` and
`rv3028c7_dispatch_irq()`: a bit that races the acknowledge comes back on the
re-read instead of being silently dropped. `rv3028c7_dispatch_irq()` loops
(bounded to 3 passes) re-dispatching anything that races its own acknowledge;
`rv3028c7_alarm_check_and_clear()` folds a raced `AF` into `*fired` without
looping -- a raced bit it can't fully drain self-heals on the next call
instead of being lost.

This intentionally does **not** assume anything about what writing a `1` to a
`STATUS` bit that reads `0` does on real silicon (no cited RV-3028-C7
Application Manual table settles that); it relies only on the driver's
existing "write 0 clears" contract. Writing back `~status & 0x7F` (setting
unobserved bits to `1` to "preserve" them) would need that unverified fact,
so the fix does not do that.

Regression test: `tests/unit/rv3028c7_dispatch_ack/`. It links the real
`chips/rv3028c7/rv3028c7.c` against a small in-TU fake I2C register file
(the driver's only bus dependency is `alp_i2c_write()` /
`alp_i2c_write_read()`) so it exercises the actual dispatch/ack code path,
including the exact race from this issue.

### Fixed — GD32 bridge PWM backend never resolved the "use DT default" period, so every non-zero duty on V2N/V2M failed `ALP_ERR_INVAL` (#1624)

`src/backends/pwm/gd32_bridge.c`'s `br_open()` wrote `cfg->period_ns`
verbatim into both its private channel state and the dispatcher-owned
`struct alp_pwm::period_ns` field that `alp_pwm_set_duty()` bounds-checks
`pulse_ns` against. `include/alp/pwm.h` documents `period_ns == 0` as "use DT
default" — the value `ALP_PWM_CONFIG_DEFAULT()` produces — but the bridge has
no devicetree to resolve it against, so a caller using the canonical default
config still ended up with `period_ns == 0` and every non-zero duty request
on E1M-V2N101/102 and E1M-V2M101/102 was rejected as out of range.

`br_open()` now resolves `period_ns == 0` to 1 kHz before writing it to
either field, matching the fallback the `sw_fallback` and `yocto_drv` PWM
backends already use.

Regression test: `tests/unit/pwm_gd32_bridge_period/`.

### Fixed — `alp_update_log_open()`'s election loop could livelock under cross-priority contention (#1625)

The OPENING/CLOSING wait loop in `alp_update_log_open()` looped straight back
on itself with no yield, reintroducing the #1114 priority-inversion hang: a
higher-priority caller that observed the elected-but-not-finished OPENING
state (or lost the UNOPENED->OPENING race) never yielded the core, so a
lower-priority initializer stuck inside `_elect_backend()`'s `ops->ready()`
call (a TF-M round trip on the HW_ENFORCED tier) could never run again on a
single-core preemptive-priority scheduler. That is a livelock, not a slow
path: the higher-priority spinner never blocks, so the lower-priority holder
of the singleton's OPENING lock never gets scheduled, and `alp_update_log_open()`
never returns for either caller.

`src/update_log_dispatch.c` now calls `alp_slot_sleep_tick()` on both
non-terminal branches of the loop, matching the sleep-poll shape #1114 already
applied to the generic close drain (`alp_handle_begin_close_blocking()`) and to
`ble_dispatch.c`'s open-time join scan.

Regression test: `tests/unit/update_log/src/test_update_log.c`'s
`test_open_election_unequal_priority_no_livelock`. A low-priority thread wins
the open election and parks, via a controllable gate, inside the HW backend's
`ready()` call; a higher-priority contender is proven — by a semaphore
rendezvous, not a timing guess — to have observed OPENING before the gate
releases.

### Fixed — `alp_power_profile_set()` accepted any `rail_mv` and forwarded it straight to the Alif SE DC-DC mailbox (#1626)

The Alif SE aiPM DC-DC rail (`run_profile_t.dcdc_voltage` / `off_profile_t.dcdc_voltage`,
`modules/hal/alif/se_services/include/aipm.h`) only accepts 750-850 mV. `alif_profile_set()`
in `src/backends/power/alif_se_profile.c` copied a caller's `rail_mv` into that field
unchecked for both `ALP_POWER_PROFILE_RUN` and `ALP_POWER_PROFILE_STANDBY`, so a caller
typo such as `8000` (an mV/uV slip) or any other out-of-window value reached the SE mailbox
verbatim instead of being rejected.

`alif_profile_set()` now validates `rail_mv` against the 750-850 mV window before writing
either profile and returns `ALP_ERR_INVAL` on an out-of-range value, on both the RUN and
STANDBY call sites — the SE mailbox setter is never invoked for a bad value.
`include/alp/power.h` documents the per-SoM window on the `rail_mv` field and the new
refusal on `alp_power_profile_set()`'s `@return`.

Regression test: `tests/unit/power_alif_dcdc_bounds/`. It compiles the real
`src/backends/power/alif_se_profile.c` translation unit against a fake `<se_service.h>`
(the same technique `tests/unit/se_cryptocell_hash_bounds/` uses for the same
Alif-SE-gated situation) and calls the shipped `alif_profile_set()` through the backend's
own vtable, asserting both that an out-of-range `rail_mv` returns `ALP_ERR_INVAL` on RUN
and STANDBY *and* that the fake `se_service_set_run_cfg()` / `se_service_set_off_cfg()`
were never called for those inputs — proving the SE mailbox itself was never written, not
just that an error code came back.

### Fixed — `zephyr_drv`'s counter `close()` could leave a stale channel alarm armed (#1627)

`z_close()` stopped the counter but never cancelled the channel-0 alarm
`counter_stop()` does not guarantee cancellation of, so a still-armed alarm
from a closed handle could deliver into a recycled handle, or make a freshly
reopened handle's `alp_counter_set_alarm()` fail `ALP_ERR_BUSY` on the
native-sim counter driver.

`z_close()` now cancels the channel-0 alarm before releasing the slot. On the
canonical `alp_counter_stop()` + `alp_counter_close()` teardown order the
counter is already stopped by the time `close()` runs, and at least the
native-sim backend's `cancel_channel_alarm()` refuses (`-ENOTSUP`) on a
stopped counter without clearing the pending alarm — so if the first cancel
attempt fails, `z_close()` now briefly restarts the counter to let the cancel
take effect, then leaves it stopped as the caller left it.

`alp_counter_dispatch.c`'s `close()` also clears `alarm_cb`/`alarm_user` on
the handle independent of backend behaviour, and `alp_counter_set_alarm()`
now rolls those fields back to NULL when the backend rejects the arm request
(e.g. `ALP_ERR_BUSY`) instead of leaving a callback installed that a leaked
driver-side alarm could still reach.

`include/alp/counter.h` now documents that `alp_counter_close()` cancels any
armed alarm as part of teardown, and softens `alp_counter_set_alarm()`'s
replace-semantics claim to note it is backend-dependent.

Regression tests: `tests/unit/counter_registry/` gained
`test_zephyr_drv_close_cancels_channel_alarm` (close while still running) and
`test_zephyr_drv_close_cancels_channel_alarm_after_stop` (the
`alp_counter_stop()` + `alp_counter_close()` ordering) — both exercise the
real `zephyr_drv` backend against a `counter0` alias newly wired into the
`native_sim`/`native_sim/native/64` overlays.

### Fixed — two camera backends still called the pre-v4.4 Zephyr video API (#1628)

`src/backends/camera/zephyr_video.c` (the portable backend, registered at
`silicon_ref="*"`) and `src/backends/camera/v2n_n44_isp.c` used the endpoint-id
video API that Zephyr removed in v4.4, while `west.yml` pins **v4.4.1**: the
`VIDEO_EP_OUT` argument was replaced by an `enum video_buf_type` carried on the
caps/format structs, and `video_buffer_alloc()` gained a `k_timeout_t`.

Both are ported to the upstream API, mirroring
`src/backends/camera/alif_isp_pico.c`, which already talked it — the port copies
that file rather than reconstructing an API shape from memory. Buffer sizing
stops assuming a flat 2 B/px, which is only correct for the packed 16-bit
formats and under-allocates for the rest.

`alif_isp_pico.c`'s own header comment described itself as the only backend on
the new API and named the other two as "still using the pre-v4.4 endpoint-id
helpers". That is now false in both directions, so it is rewritten rather than
left to mislead the next reader into porting work that is already done.

### Fixed — portable-C FIR read its own output as the delay line (#1629)

The portable-C `fir_apply()` in `src/backends/dsp/sw_fallback.c` read
`in[n-k]` for `k >= 1` as the FIR delay line, but every real call site runs
it in-place (`out == in`), so for `n >= k` that index is `out[n-k]` — a
sample this same loop had already overwritten on an earlier iteration. The
filter ran over its own output, a recursive and potentially unstable
response, instead of the caller's FIR, and the tail-state save at the end of
the call inherited the same aliasing bug.

`fir_apply()` now tracks the `M-1` delay-line samples from a copy of each
input sample taken before its output is written, so the kernel never reads
back through `out[]`. Every real `alp_dsp_chain_apply_samples()` /
`alp_dsp_chain_apply_samples_f32()` caller through the portable-C path was
affected — any FIR with more than one tap running in-place on a SoM without
CMSIS-DSP.

Regression test: `tests/zephyr/dsp` — a 3-tap moving-average FIR checked
against its closed form, both in one call and split across two calls to
confirm the saved delay-line state stays correct at a chunk boundary.

### Fixed — nine handle pools still claimed a slot with an unlocked check-then-set, and nothing stopped a tenth (#1630)

`if (!in_use) { in_use = true; }` is two operations. Two callers opening
concurrently can both read the flag false, both take the slot, and alias their
handles — so one caller's `close()` frees state the other is still using. #1115
converted the pools it knew about onto `alp_slot_try_claim()`'s atomic
compare-exchange (`src/common/alp_slot_claim.h`) and nine survived, because that
remediation worked from a hand-written site list rather than from a grep. #629
had the same shape. Each issue closed and the class kept shipping.

Converted, alloc and free path both, to `alp_slot_try_claim()` /
`alp_slot_release()`:

- `src/backends/storage/zephyr_littlefs.c` — the worst of the nine. Two aliased
  handles onto one littlefs mount is two `lfs_t` states over one flash area:
  filesystem corruption on a persistent store, not a lost handle.
- `src/backends/inference/tflm.cpp` — the single shared default tensor arena.
  Two interpreters both won it and ran inference over each other's activations
  instead of one getting a clean `ALP_ERR_NOMEM`. This one is a bare scalar with
  no loop and no array subscript, which is precisely why every array-shaped grep
  in #1115's remediation walked past it.
- `src/backends/mproc/zephyr_drv.c` — all three pools (shmem, mbox, hwsem), which
  are verbatim copies of each other.
- `src/backends/ble/zephyr_drv.c` (connection pool),
  `src/backends/usb/zephyr_drv.c`, `src/backends/dac/zephyr_drv.c`,
  `src/backends/power/zephyr_pm_policy.c`.

All eight array-shaped pools keep `in_use` in a parallel `bool[]` rather than
inside the slot struct, so the winner may `memset` the whole slot after claiming
it; the `offsetof` form used by the in-struct pools is neither needed nor
compilable here.

**The sweep is the precondition; the gate is the deliverable.** New
`scripts/check_slot_claim_atomic.py` rejects the antipattern anywhere under
`src/`. It matches the *set* half — any plain assignment of an `in_use` flag to
`true` — rather than the `if (!in_use)` test half, for two reasons:
`alp_slot_try_claim()` never assigns the flag, so its absence is a complete
signal; and the test half is not always a negation — the TFLM site guarded a
singleton with `if (g_default_arena_in_use) { fail; }`, which no
array-shaped-negation grep can see. Comments are stripped before scanning, since
`src/` carries a dozen lines that quote the antipattern while explaining why the
code below no longer does it.

Four sites are allowlisted because their claim is already serialised by a held
lock, and each entry has to name that lock so the list cannot grow by assertion:
`src/zephyr/handles.c` (`k_mutex_lock(&kind##_lock, K_FOREVER)`),
`src/yocto/peripheral_gpio.c` (`pthread_mutex_lock(&g_irq.mu)`),
`src/backends/can/yocto_drv.c` (`pthread_mutex_lock(&d->lock)`), and
`src/backends/can/testing_drv.c` (a per-handle filter table reached through one
handle, not a shared static pool).

`.github/workflows/pr-metadata-validate.yml` now triggers on `src/**`. It did
not before, listing only `src/common/stub_backend.c` and `src/common/stub/**`,
so a PR adding a tenth unlocked claim would never have run the new gate — and,
already today, would never have run `check_stub_issues.py` (which sweeps
`src/backends/**/*_stub.c`) or `check_sw_fallback_tags.py` (which sweeps
`src/backends/**/sw_fallback.c`) either. Same trigger hole, three gates.

`src/zephyr/handles.c` carries a *different* defect that is deliberately not
touched here: `kind##_slots[i] = (struct type){ 0 };` re-owns a slot while an
operation may still be in flight. That is the close-versus-op class tracked by
#1644.

### Fixed — an fd-flagged frame on a classic-mode CAN handle could overflow the Zephyr backend's on-stack frame (#1631)

`alp_can_send()`'s `payload_len` bound check let a frame with `fd = true`,
`payload_len = 64` through even on a handle opened `ALP_CAN_MODE_CLASSIC` — 64
is not greater than the CAN-FD max, and the classic-only bound check is
skipped because `frame->fd` is true. On a Zephyr build without
`CONFIG_CAN_FD_MODE`, the backend's on-stack `struct can_frame.data[]` is only
8 bytes (Zephyr's `CAN_MAX_DLEN`), so `src/backends/can/zephyr_drv.c`'s
`z_send()` copied up to 56 bytes past it.

`src/can_dispatch.c`'s `alp_can_send()` now rejects an fd-flagged frame on a
handle not opened `ALP_CAN_MODE_FD` with `ALP_ERR_NOSUPPORT`, once, for every
CAN backend — `<alp/can.h>`'s `alp_can_send()` doc now lists this case.
`z_send()` keeps its own bound check as defense-in-depth regardless of what
the dispatcher already validated.

Two related gaps closed in the same backend:

- `_rx_trampoline()`'s RX decode clamped the copy length only against the
  destination (the alp frame's 64-byte `data[]`), not the source (Zephyr's
  `struct can_frame.data[]`, 8 bytes without `CONFIG_CAN_FD_MODE`) — a classic
  frame reporting a wire DLC of 9–15 (`can_dlc_to_bytes()` maps that to
  12–64 bytes) could read past the source buffer. The copy is now bounded by
  both.
- `z_open()` only rejected `ALP_CAN_MODE_FD` on a `CONFIG_CAN_FD_MODE=n` build
  when `cfg->bitrate_data_hz > 0`; a caller passing `bitrate_data_hz == 0`
  fell through and opened successfully in normal mode while the handle's
  `cfg.mode` stayed `ALP_CAN_MODE_FD`, contradicting `alp_can_open()`'s
  documented contract. It now rejects unconditionally.

### Fixed — the Zephyr RPC backend's async dispatch read the subscribe table with no lock while subscribe/unsubscribe wrote it with none either (#1632)

`src/backends/rpc/zephyr_drv.c`'s `rpc_ept_recv()` runs on the ipc_service
worker thread; its async dispatch block read `sub->cb`/`sub->user` straight off
the per-channel subscribe table and called `sub->cb(...)` with no lock held.
`z_subscribe()` and `z_unsubscribe()` mutate the same table from the
application thread, also lock-free. A subscribe/unsubscribe racing an in-flight
dispatch could hand the callback a torn `(cb, user)` pair, or a concurrent
unsubscribe could clear the entry out from under the dispatch mid-read and
silently drop the callback entirely -- worse than an error, since nothing
observed it.

The channel already has `be->lock` (a `k_spinlock`, used by the close protocol
for GHSA-xhm8-7f87-93q5): holding it across the callback call itself would
deadlock, since the callback may call `alp_rpc_close()` on its own channel
(self-close), and `alp_rpc_close()` -> `z_shutdown()` also takes `be->lock`.
The fix is snapshot-under-lock, invoke-outside: `rpc_ept_recv()` takes the
lock, finds the subscribe-table entry, copies `cb`+`user` into locals, releases
the lock, then invokes through the locals. `z_subscribe()`/`z_unsubscribe()`
now take the same lock around every table read/write.

This closes the write/write and write/read races on the table itself. It does
**not** close every race a caller might assume: once the snapshot is taken and
the lock released, a concurrent `alp_rpc_unsubscribe()` can still complete
before the callback actually runs -- the callback fires once more for a
message that was already in flight, exactly as if the unsubscribe had landed a
moment later. This residual window is documented at the call site; a caller
needing a hard "no callback after unsubscribe returns" guarantee must
serialise on its own.

Regression test: `tests/unit/rpc_zephyr_backend/` scenario 5
(`test_1632_dispatch_vs_unsubscribe_snapshot_is_coherent`), added alongside the
four existing GHSA-xhm8-7f87-93q5 scenarios in the same file. It drives a
genuinely concurrent, higher-priority `z_unsubscribe()` against an in-flight
`rpc_ept_recv()` dispatch, timed via a new test-only hook
(`g_rpc_dispatch_test_sync_hook`) fired from inside the fix's `be->lock`
critical section -- mirroring the file's existing
`test_defect1_recv_vs_timed_out_call_race` technique. Reverting only the lock
(keeping the hook call site at the equivalent unlocked position) reproduces the
defect exactly: the higher-priority unsubscribe preempts before the dispatch
reads `sub->cb`, clears the entry, and the callback is silently never invoked.

### Fixed — streaming ADC and UART RX ring-buffer handles could recycle a pool slot while a read was still in flight (#1634)

`alp_adc_stream_t`/`alp_adc_filter_t`/`alp_adc_spectrum_t` and
`struct alp_uart_rx_ringbuf` carried only a bare `in_use` bool with no
active-op tracking. `alp_adc_stream_close()` (and its filter/spectrum
wrappers) and `alp_uart_rx_ringbuf_detach()` could recycle a pool slot
while `alp_adc_stream_read_mv()` / `alp_uart_rx_ringbuf_pop()` was still
reading it — a concurrent open/attach then reused the same struct
address and the still-running read delivered one caller's data (ADC
channel samples, UART ring bytes) into another caller's buffer.

The ADC half of this landed on `dev` already via #1803 (adding
`lifecycle`/`active_ops` to `alp_adc_stream`/`filter`/`spectrum` and
routing every read through `alp_handle_op_enter`/`alp_handle_op_leave`
and every close through `alp_handle_begin_close_blocking`); that
change is kept as-is here rather than duplicated, with only the
test-only synchronisation hook (`alp_adc_stream_read_test_sync_hook`,
see below) layered on top of it. The UART half — `alp_uart_rx_ringbuf`
gaining the same `lifecycle`/`active_ops` fields and guard, mirroring
`i2c_regfile.c` and `counter_dispatch.c` — is new in this change. The
sleep-poll close variant is required (not busy-spin) because the ADC
guarded op can block for a long time inside
`alp_z_v2n_supervisor_acquire()`.

Adds `tests/zephyr/adc_stream_close_race` and
`tests/zephyr/uart_rx_ringbuf_close_race`, deterministic two-thread
regression tests proving each close/detach-vs-op race against the real
struct, pool, and close/detach function — closing out the committed
regression test #1803's own changelog fragment recorded as still owed
for the ADC side. Both drive the fix through the real public read
entry point (`alp_adc_stream_read_mv()` / `alp_uart_rx_ringbuf_pop()`)
via a test-only synchronisation hook
(`alp_adc_stream_read_test_sync_hook` / `alp_uart_rx_ringbuf_pop_test_sync_hook`,
default no-op in production, mirroring
`src/backends/rpc/zephyr_drv.c`'s `g_rpc_recv_test_sync_hook`) rather
than hand-rolling the `alp_handle_op_enter`/`_leave` calls in the test
body — an earlier draft of the ADC test counted the op in by calling
`alp_handle_op_enter` directly instead of the fixed function, so it
stayed green even with the op-counting half of the fix reverted.
Mutation-tested: both suites fail with their respective close/detach
drain guard reverted, and the ADC suite additionally fails with
`alp_adc_stream_read_mv()`'s op-counting reverted to a bare lifecycle
check.

`tests/zephyr/peripheral/prj_v2n_supervisor.conf` now also sets
`CONFIG_ALP_SDK_DSP=y`: `ALP_ADC_HAS_FILTER_PATH` (the
`alp_adc_filter_*`/`alp_adc_spectrum_*` bodies in
`src/zephyr/peripheral_adc.c`) needs both that and the V2N bridge
path, and no config in the tree set both before this, so roughly 100
of the changed lines in that file were never compile-tested by any
gate.

### Fixed — eight backend-parity guards from the #1635 audit: an unbounded GD32-bridge qenc instance id, three missing vendor-ext NULL guards, a missing MQTT timeout clamp, a UART sw_fallback empty-read contract violation, an unaligned storage erase-size, a PWM out-of-range-vs-invalid status split, a storage read-only status split, and a DRP-AI tensor-shape gap (#1635)

`src/backends/qenc/gd32_bridge.c`'s `br_open()` stored `cfg->encoder_id` with
no bound of its own, then narrowed it to `uint8_t` before handing it to the
chip driver's own `GD32G553_BRIDGE_QENC_CHANNELS` check — so `encoder_id ==
256` aliased to channel 0 and opened fine, unlike every sibling GD32-bridge
backend (`counter`, `adc`, `dac`, `pwm`), which all bound the instance id at
open before any narrowing. `br_open()` now rejects an out-of-range
`encoder_id` with `ALP_ERR_INVAL` (matching the qenc `zephyr_drv.c` sibling's
convention) before the id is ever narrowed.

`src/backends/adc/alif_e8.c` and `alif_e7.c`'s
`alp_alif_adc_set_trigger_source()` checked `h == NULL` but then dereferenced
`h->backend->vendor` unchecked; `src/backends/ext/renesas/power.c`'s
`alp_renesas_power_supervisor_mode_set()` checked `handle->backend == NULL`
but not `handle->backend->vendor == NULL`. Six of the seven other vendor-ext
gates already carry the full three-part guard (`h != NULL && h->backend !=
NULL && h->backend->vendor != NULL`); these three now do too.

`src/backends/mqtt/yocto_drv.c`'s `y_connect()` passed `(int)timeout_ms`
straight to `mosquitto_loop()`, unlike `y_loop()` 65 lines below it, which
clamps at `INT_MAX` so a `UINT32_MAX`-as-forever caller doesn't roll over
into a negative timeout. `y_connect()` now applies the same clamp.

`src/backends/uart/sw_fallback.c`'s `sw_read()` ignored `timeout_ms`
entirely and returned `ALP_OK` on an empty ring with the destination buffer
untouched — a silent-failure violation of the documented contract
(`include/alp/peripheral.h`: "If the deadline is reached with zero bytes
collected, the call returns `ALP_ERR_TIMEOUT`", and for `timeout_ms == 0`,
"return immediately with `ALP_ERR_TIMEOUT` if no byte is already
available"). `sw_read()` now returns `ALP_ERR_TIMEOUT` whenever it drains
zero bytes, matching the `zephyr_drv.c` sibling.

`src/backends/storage/zephyr_flash.c`'s `z_get_info()` hardcoded
`erase_size = 1u` with a comment claiming the device API is opaque — false,
`flash_area_get_device(fa)` is already called two lines below and supports
`flash_get_page_info_by_offs()`. This contradicted `include/alp/storage.h`
("Both bounds MUST align to the device's erase_size"). `z_get_info()` now
reads the real page/sector size via `flash_get_page_info_by_offs()` when
`CONFIG_FLASH_PAGE_LAYOUT` is enabled, falling back to `1u` only if that
lookup is unavailable or fails.

Considered and reverted: a `wdt_disable(dev)` call on `zephyr_drv.c`'s
`z_open()` failure path, meant to undo the channel `wdt_install_timeout()`
installs before `wdt_setup()` can fail. It is not the right undo —
`wdt_disable()` is documented as device-wide ("automatically uninstalls all
timeouts", `zephyr/drivers/watchdog.h`), never per-channel, and in the state
this path runs in (setup just failed, instance not enabled) it returns
`-EFAULT` on `wdt_nrfx.c`, `wdt_renesas_rz.c`, and `wdt_fwdgt_gd32.c` — a
no-op on exactly the drivers where the leak is real. On `wdt_counter.c` it
*does* succeed, but as a bare `counter_stop()` with no enabled-check: it
stops the shared counter backing every installed channel and clears no
bookkeeping, disarming a running watchdog while still leaking. The channel
leak on a failed `wdt_setup()` is real but needs a per-driver-class fix, not
a device-wide disable; left open.

Left for a deliberate decision, not fixed here: `src/backends/counter/gd32_bridge.c`'s
`ALP_ERR_NOSUPPORT` for an out-of-range `counter_id`, a fourth status
alongside the `ALP_ERR_INVAL` `adc`/`dac`/`pwm`/`qenc` siblings use,
well-argued in place (E1M-X connector identities are a form-factor bound,
not a per-SoM promise) but part of the same convention split — see the
dedicated note at the end of this fragment; and the wdt
channel-leak-on-failed-`wdt_setup()` noted above, which needs a
per-driver-class fix, not a device-wide `wdt_disable()`. (The PWM
out-of-range-channel status split, `storage_dispatch.c`'s `read_only`
status split, and `inference_drpai.cpp`'s tensor-rank gap were originally
flagged alongside these two in an earlier draft of this fragment; all
three are resolved below, not left open.)

Not open bugs: `allow_unsafe_write` (`include/alp/storage.h`) and
`allow_modeset` (`include/alp/display.h`) are documented Yocto-only /
DRM-master-path-only by design and are ignored elsewhere on purpose — not
missing guards. The audio/i2s `timeout_ms`-forever handling
(`audio/zephyr_drv.c`'s `(int32_t)timeout_ms` cast, `i2s/zephyr_drv.c`'s
missing `UINT32_MAX` case) is a real inconsistency worth a closer look, but
narrower than previously stated here: `(int32_t)UINT32_MAX == -1 ==
SYS_FOREVER_MS`, so the exact `UINT32_MAX`-as-forever case already works.
The gap is the range `(INT32_MAX, UINT32_MAX-1]`, which casts to a negative
value other than `-1` and the underlying drivers treat as no-wait — a
~25-day timeout returns immediately instead of waiting. Neither
`alp_audio_in_read` nor `alp_i2s_write` currently promises
`UINT32_MAX`-as-forever the way `camera.h`, `mproc.h`, `peripheral.h`, and
`rpc.h` do, so this is a consistency gap against those siblings rather than
a documented-contract violation; outside this patch's assigned scope.

A `tests/zephyr/peripheral` regression
(`test_v2n_supervisor_qenc_open_out_of_range_id_rejected`) covers the
GD32-bridge qenc bound check without needing real V2N hardware — the check
now runs before the supervisor acquire, so it fires the same way whether or
not a bus is configured. A `tests/unit/uart_registry` regression
(`test_sw_fallback_empty_read_returns_timeout`) covers the UART empty-read
fix directly against the `sw_fallback` ops.

**PWM channel-id status.** `alp_pwm_open()`'s channel-id validation collapsed a real two-tier distinction into a single
status on two of the three PWM backends. `src/backends/pwm/zephyr_drv.c` already got this right
(and `src/backends/wdt/zephyr_drv.c` mirrors the same shape): `ALP_ERR_INVAL` for a channel index
outside the alp_pwm ABI's 0..7 space at all (a malformed argument, not a hardware limit), versus
`ALP_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` for a well-formed index the active SoC doesn't populate that many instances
of. On a board.yaml that runs the same portable app across different silicon, collapsing these to
one code destroys information a caller acts on — "fix your argument" versus "this part can't reach
that channel."

`src/backends/pwm/yocto_drv.c` returned `ALP_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` for every out-of-range channel_id,
including ones that aren't even in the ABI's 0..7 space. It now returns `ALP_ERR_INVAL` for those,
and reads the target pwmchip's own `npwm` sysfs attribute (`Documentation/ABI/testing/sysfs-class-pwm`)
to return `ALP_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` for a well-formed channel_id the running kernel's PWM controller
doesn't actually expose — the dynamic equivalent of `zephyr_drv.c`'s `ALP_SOC_PWM_COUNT`, since this
backend's `silicon_ref = "*"` gives it no static per-SoC ceiling to check at compile time. A failed
`npwm` read (chip not present yet) is not itself treated as out-of-range; that case already surfaces
as `ALP_ERR_NOT_READY` from the subsequent export write.

`src/backends/pwm/gd32_bridge.c` returned `ALP_ERR_INVAL` unconditionally. Its channel_id genuinely
has no second tier to split: `metadata/chips/gd32g553.yaml`'s `pwm_routing:` table wires all eight
E1M PWM channels to a real GD32 TIMER0/TIMER7 channel on V2N, with no partial-population case — so
`ALP_ERR_INVAL` was already the complete answer, not a collapsed one, and stays unchanged. The
backend's real hardware floor (a period the GD32 timer's 1 us prescaled tick can't represent —
`period_us == 0`, i.e. under 1 us, under 2 us center-aligned) already surfaces as
`ALP_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` from `br_set_duty()` / `br_set_period()` via the bridge firmware's own
`STATUS_OUT_OF_RANGE` (wire `0x08`); the comment at `br_open()` now says so instead of citing a
since-superseded "mirror the adc bridge" rationale, and instead of an earlier draft's ~303 us
"longest period" figure, which was wrong on two counts: it was the *unprescaled* 4.63 ns-core-clock
ceiling, not the firmware's actual 216:1-prescaled 1 MHz tick (real ceiling 65.536 ms, the 16-bit
ARR's full count), and an over-long period is currently silently clamped and returns `OK` rather
than surfacing `ALP_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` at all — filed separately as #1730, not fixed here.
`docs/gd32-bridge-protocol.md` and `metadata/chips/gd32g553.yaml` carried the same stale ~303 us
figure and are corrected too.

`include/alp/pwm.h`'s `alp_pwm_open()` Doxygen previously lumped both codes under one vague
"channel_id out of range or alias unset" bullet; it now states the `ALP_ERR_INVAL` /
`ALP_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` split explicitly, per `alp_last_error()`'s documented convention in
`include/alp/peripheral.h`.

**storage read-only status.** `src/storage_dispatch.c` split on `state.read_only`: `alp_storage_write()` returned
`ALP_ERR_NOT_READY`, `alp_storage_erase()` returned `ALP_ERR_INVAL` — same attribute, same
handle, same cause, two contracts. A read-only handle is a *state*, not a malformed argument:
the call is well-formed and would succeed on a writable handle. `alp_storage_erase()` now
returns `ALP_ERR_NOT_READY` too, matching `alp_storage_write()` and the convention the #1646
cluster (merged as PR #1713) settled for `alp_handle_op_enter()` failure — itself a state
problem, and already `ALP_ERR_NOT_READY` at 110 of 122 sites. ADR-0002 frames `ALP_ERR_INVAL`
as "programmer error" and a case could be made for that reading instead, but that rule is
already unimplemented at ~104 of 110 fused `op_enter` sites, so aligning storage with the real
convention beats aligning it with the aspirational one.

`include/alp/storage.h`'s `@return` docs for both `alp_storage_write()` and
`alp_storage_erase()` are updated to describe the unified behaviour — this was a documented
contract, not just an internal code path. A new `tests/unit/storage_registry` case
(`test_read_only_handle_write_and_erase_agree`) opens a read-only handle through the real
`alp_storage_open()`/`alp_storage_write()`/`alp_storage_erase()` public API and asserts both
calls surface `ALP_ERR_NOT_READY`, guarding against a regression back to `ALP_ERR_INVAL` on the
erase path.

**littlefs erase-size.** `src/backends/storage/zephyr_littlefs.c`'s `z_get_info()` hardcodes
`erase_size = 1u`, reviewed against this same #1635 sweep and confirmed as a deliberate
difference from its `zephyr_flash.c` sibling, not drift: this backend only ever touches its
mount by path (`fs_open`/`fs_stat`), never obtains a `struct device` or `flash_area` to query,
and littlefs's own logical block is a wear-levelling unit the filesystem chooses, not the
underlying physical erase geometry — unlike `zephyr_flash.c`, which derives a real page size via
`flash_get_page_info_by_offs()` because it holds a `flash_area` handle. A comment at
`src/backends/storage/zephyr_littlefs.c:169-179` ("Deliberately 1u, not derived like the raw-flash sibling") now says so explicitly, so a future reader does not "fix" it to
match `zephyr_flash.c`.

**DRP-AI tensor shape.** `alp_inference_drpai_get_input()`/`get_output()` set `rank = 0` with an empty
`shape[]`, because `MeraDrpRuntimeWrapper::GetInputInfo()`/`GetOutputInfo()`
only report `(name, size_bytes, dtype)` — no shape. That comment was true but
irrelevant: the shape is on disk the whole time. `deploy.json`, the TVM
graph-runtime JSON `scripts/alp_model/adapters/drpai.py` tars into every
`drpai_dir` blob alongside `drp_desc.bin`/`weight.bin`, carries every graph
input's and output's shape, and lands flat in `st->model_dir` before
`open()` returns.

Both hooks now resolve real rank/shape from that file. `open()` parses
`deploy.json` once via a new, dependency-free JSON scanner — alp-sdk
carries no JSON library, so this understands only the narrow TVM graph-JSON
subset it needs: nodes, `node_row_ptr`, `arg_nodes`, `heads`, and the
`attrs.shape` "list_shape" table — and correlates each entry to the
existing `in_info`/`out_info` vectors via `correlate_input_shapes()`:
inputs by node name, outputs positionally (`deploy.json`'s `heads` order
already matches `GetOutput(idx)` order). The positional (graph-input
order) fallback fires ONLY when *no* input matched by name and the counts
agree — a mixed match (some names hit, some don't) never falls back
per-tensor, since an unmatched slot would otherwise take another tensor's
already-claimed shape by position, which is a wrong shape, not an honest
rank 0. Anything that doesn't resolve cleanly — the file missing or
unreadable, a schema that doesn't match, a corrupt dim — leaves that
tensor's `rank` at 0, identical to the prior behaviour; a wrong shape is
worse than no shape, so the parser bails (or, for a single unmatched
input, `correlate_input_shapes()` simply leaves it unresolved) rather
than guessing.

The parser itself (`JsonValue`/`JsonParser`/`DeployShapes`/
`_drpai_parse_deploy_shapes`/`correlate_input_shapes`) now lives in its own
header, `src/yocto/drpai_deploy_shapes.h`, split out of
`inference_drpai.cpp` specifically because it has zero dependency on
`MeraDrpRuntimeWrapper.h`/`<linux/drpai.h>`/the RUHMI TVM sysroot that the
rest of that file needs to compile — see "Verified" below.

A tensor whose real rank exceeds 4 also keeps `rank = 0`, deliberately.
`alp_inference_tensor_t.shape` is a frozen `uint16_t[4]`
(`[ABI-STABLE]`, `include/alp/inference.h`), and the sibling ORT/DEEPX
backends silently truncate a rank > 4 tensor to its first 4 dims — now
filed as #1729. DRP-AI does not add a third behaviour to that question.

Verified via a standalone unit test —
`tests/yocto/inference_drpai_deploy_shapes.cpp`, registered in
`tests/yocto/CMakeLists.txt` as `alp_test_inference_drpai_deploy_shapes`
alongside its `alp_test_inference_*` siblings (not linked against
`alp::sdk`; the header pulls in nothing from the SDK). It builds and
runs as a first-class `ctest` target with a plain host C++ compiler —
no Zephyr, no RUHMI/DRP-AI TVM sysroot, no DRP-AI hardware:
`cmake -B build -DALP_OS=yocto -DALP_BUILD_TESTS=ON && cmake --build
build --target alp_test_inference_drpai_deploy_shapes && ctest
--test-dir build -R alp_test_inference_drpai_deploy_shapes`. It
exercises the real parser against a fixture whose node/row_ptr/heads
shape and every dimension were checked byte-for-byte against a real
compiled `yolox-s-voc` DRP-AI model's `deploy.json` on a RUHMI-equipped
host (input `images` → `[1,3,640,640]`; three detection-head outputs →
`[1,25,80,80]`/`[1,25,40,40]`/`[1,25,20,20]`), plus a rank-5 tensor
(must yield `rank = 0`, not a #1729-style truncation), a
truncated/malformed file, a missing file, and
`correlate_input_shapes()`'s mixed-match case (the fix two paragraphs
up) proven both ways: the pre-fix per-tensor fallback assigns a wrong
shape on a mixed match, the fixed version leaves it unresolved instead.
The rest of `inference_drpai.cpp` — the parts that DO need
`MeraDrpRuntimeWrapper.h`/`<linux/drpai.h>`/the RUHMI TVM sysroot — is
syntax-checked against a minimal local stub of that vendor surface, same
as before. **Code-complete and bench-unverified**: the DRP-AI runtime
only executes on V2N silicon under the MERA2/DRP-AI TVM sysroot, which
does not exist on this dev host — this change has not run on real
hardware.

**Left unchanged, deliberately: `src/backends/counter/gd32_bridge.c`'s `ALP_ERR_NOSUPPORT`.** An earlier pass changed it to `ALP_ERR_INVAL` for consistency with its adc/dac/pwm siblings, and that was reverted. `include/alp/e1m_x_pinout.h` publishes COUNTER0..3 as E1M-X *connector identities* -- a form-factor bound, not a per-SoM promise (#1242) -- and the V2N/V2M bridge populates only id 0. Asking for COUNTER2 is a valid form-factor id this SoM does not serve, which is what `ALP_ERR_NOSUPPORT` means; it is not a malformed argument. `docs/portability.md` (4.5) and `e1m_x_pinout.h` both state that a published id never reports `ALP_ERR_INVAL`, and `tests/zephyr/peripheral/src/counter.c` pins it. The sibling backends returning `ALP_ERR_INVAL` for their own out-of-range ids may themselves be the drift; that is left open on #1635.

### Fixed — hardware facts had drifted back out of `metadata/` into hand-written board headers (#1636)

Every hardware fact in this SDK is supposed to have one source under `metadata/`,
with headers generated from it. Two blocks had drifted back the other way.

**The five E1M-X EVK INA236 current-shunt monitors** — addresses, shunt
resistances and max currents — existed **only** in the hand-written
`include/alp/boards/alp_e1m_x_evk.h`. `grep -n "i2c_devices"
metadata/boards/e1m-x-evk.yaml` returned nothing, while the sibling E1M carrier's
identical data was already generated into
`include/alp/boards/alp_e1m_evk_routes.h` by `scripts/gen_board_header.py`. They
now live in `metadata/boards/e1m-x-evk.yaml` and are generated the same way, along
with the five remaining on-board sensor addresses (`BMI323`, `ICM42670`,
`BMP581`, `TCAL9538`, `EEPROM`) — leaving that header carrying prose only.

This is the shape of drift that does not announce itself. `XEVK_INA236_SHUNT_3V3_OHMS`
is `0.020f`: a **scaling factor** consumed by `ina236_init()`, not an identifier.
A board respin that changes a shunt desynchronises it into plausible-but-wrong
current readings rather than a build break.

**The eleven E1M EVK `EVK_PIN_OVERLAY_BASE + N` pad indices** were hand-maintained
in `include/alp/boards/alp_e1m_evk.h`, absent from the YAML that generates the
rest of that header. The audit did not distinguish whether these are independent
hardware facts or derivations, and the right fix differs — putting a derived
value in metadata creates two sources of truth for one fact, which is the same
defect in different clothes.

**They are derivations.** `zephyr/dts/bindings/alp,pin-array.yaml` states that
`pin_id` is the index into the `gpios` property, and no in-tree `alp,pin-array`
node comes near 52 entries — the largest is 44, then 42 — so `N` has no external
hardware anchor at all. The real per-entry hardware fact, which E1M/Alif pad was
repurposed, was already captured in prose. So the **generator** computes `N` by
position and the YAML stores ordering only; that ordering is pinned by a test
which goes red if two entries are swapped.

**A comment is a second source of truth exactly like a `#define` is.** The first
cut of this change moved the duplication rather than removing it — the X-EVK
header still listed the whole INA236 table in prose (`U21 INA236A 3V3 rail
A0 = GND -> 0x40 (20 mOhm)` and so on), and the E1M header still carried all
eleven per-pad paragraphs verbatim. Nothing syncs prose and no gate checks it.
Both are now deleted, and the per-device A0 strap facts moved into the YAML
`doc:` strings where the sibling carrier already kept them.

**Byte-identity was the acceptance test, not a green suite.** A metadata lift that
silently changes a hardware value is worse than not doing the lift, so the proof
is that every macro survives unchanged: verified with `abi_snapshot.build_snapshot`
across both trees (1025 macros each side, 27 `MOVED`, **zero** `VALUE-DIFF`) and
independently with `gcc -E -dM`, which diffs the 45 affected macro lines
identically — including `0.020f`, `0.050f`, `1.6f`, `4.0f` and two values that had
been written with line continuations.

`metadata/schemas/board-preset.schema.json`'s `overlay_pin_entry` pattern is
`^EVK_PIN_`, deliberately not `^X?EVK_PIN_`: `scripts/gen_board_header.py`
hard-codes `EVK_PIN_OVERLAY_BASE ALP_E1M_GPIO_COUNT` with no E1M-X branch, so
admitting an `XEVK_PIN_*` entry emitted a reference to `ALP_E1M_GPIO_COUNT` (52u)
into a header that only includes `alp/e1m_x_pinout.h`, where that symbol does not
exist — the E1M-X count is `ALP_E1M_X_GPIO_COUNT` (99u). A schema must not promise
what the generator cannot deliver; a test now reproduces that case and asserts the
schema rejects it.

`tests/scripts/test_abi_snapshot.py`'s #794 line-continuation guard was re-pointed
at `TPS628640_CTRL_DEFAULT`, because it had been anchored to
`XEVK_I2C_ADDR_INA236_VCAM2`/`_VCAM3` in the now-deleted hand-written location.
That is a **stronger** case, not a weaker one — a two-continuation-line macro
where the old anchors were single-continuation — and it still fails with #794's
exact symptom if the continuation joining is removed.

**Not in scope, deliberately.** Task 3 (the NPU arena envelope, zero on all nine
SoCs) is deferred: the generator gate it wants would reject every shipped SoC JSON
until real arena sizes are supplied, which is a per-SoC hardware fact. So
`src/backends/inference/alp_model_select.c` still reads a zero arena as
accept-anything and `ALP_ERR_NO_FIT` remains dead on every shipped SoM. Task 4 is
**refuted** — `include/alp/cap.h:58` is `ALP_CAP_ID_NPU_DRPAI`, an enum member that
`gen_soc_caps.py`'s `_emit_cap_h()` emits from `CAP_ALIASES`; generator and header
agree and there was no drift there.

This change transcribes `XEVK_I2C_ADDR_INA236_VCAM2` as `0x48u` **unchanged**,
which collides with `TAS2563_I2C_ADDR_BROADCAST` (`0x48u`) on the same bus
`E1M_X_I2C0`. That is a real hardware finding surfaced by this work and filed
separately as #1659; a metadata lift is not the place to silently change a
strapping.

### Fixed — one subsystem's `alp_wdt_close()` silently removed another subsystem's watchdog protection (#1637)

`alp_wdt_open()` validated `timeout_ms` and picked a backend but never compared
`cfg->wdt_id` against a live handle, so two subsystems could each open
`ALP_E1M_WDT0` and both believe they were protected. They were not: the backend
close path used to disable the whole watchdog **device**, not the handle's
channel — `src/backends/wdt/zephyr_drv.c`'s `z_close()` called
`wdt_disable(dev)` and cast the result to `(void)` — so the first close
disarmed the second owner's deadline. No error surfaced on any path, in either
caller's return value or `alp_last_error()`. A device that believes it is
watchdog-protected and is not is worse than one with no watchdog at all,
because nobody is looking.

A watchdog instance is now **exclusive**. The dispatcher's handle pool is
indexed by `wdt_id` rather than being a free list, which makes the existing
atomic slot claim (`alp_slot_try_claim`, #1115) *be* the exclusivity check: one
compare-exchange, no scan of the pool, and no TOCTOU window between "is this
instance taken?" and "take it". A second `alp_wdt_open()` on a live `wdt_id`
returns NULL with `ALP_ERR_BUSY` until the owner calls `alp_wdt_close()`, after
which the instance is claimable again.

Two consequences worth knowing:

- `cfg->wdt_id` is now bounded by the dispatcher (`ALP_ERR_INVAL` above the
  portable instance count) instead of only by whichever backend was selected.
  `src/backends/wdt/yocto_drv.c` previously passed any id straight into
  `/dev/watchdog%u`. The portable ID space is exactly `{0, 1}` —
  `ALP_E1M_WDT0..1` / `ALP_E1M_X_WDT0..1` are `0u` and `1u`.
- Two subsystems that both need a deadline must use two instances or share one
  handle. `include/alp/wdt.h` documents the rule on `alp_wdt_open()`.

Regression test: `tests/unit/wdt_exclusivity/`. It deliberately builds with
`CONFIG_WATCHDOG=n` so the `sw_fallback` backend is selected and
`alp_wdt_open()` actually succeeds under `native_sim` — with `CONFIG_WATCHDOG=y`
the priority-100 `zephyr_drv` wins selection, finds a NULL device (`native_sim`
has no `alp-wdt0` DT alias) and fails every open, so the test could only skip
and would prove nothing. The rule under test is pure dispatcher code, so
exercising it over `sw_fallback` is faithful.

Exclusivity closed the *concurrent*-owner half of this defect but not the
close-time one: `z_close()` still called `wdt_disable(dev)` on the way out, so
while another `alp_wdt_t` handle can no longer coexist on the same `wdt_id`, a
non-SDK Zephyr consumer sharing the same underlying device (e.g.
`CONFIG_TASK_WDT`) still had its channel silently pulled out from under it by
every alp-owned close. `z_close()` no longer calls `wdt_disable()` at all — it
only releases the handle. Zephyr's `wdt_*` driver class has no per-channel
disable or uninstall, so there was no way to scope the call to just this
handle's channel; removing it entirely is the only way to stop it reaching
outside this handle's own state. `alp_wdt_close()`'s Doxygen now spells out,
per backend, what close does and does not disarm; `alp_wdt_disable()` is the
explicit, documented way to get a best-effort SoC-wide disable before closing.

One consequence of dropping the automatic disable: Zephyr's
`wdt_install_timeout()` refuses a second install on a device that is already
`wdt_setup()` and was never disabled, so a bare `alp_wdt_open()` right after a
`close()` that didn't call `alp_wdt_disable()` first would otherwise never
succeed again on the Zephyr backend. `z_open()` now detects exactly that case
— an `-EBUSY` from `wdt_install_timeout()` on a `wdt_id` the dispatcher's own
exclusivity check just confirmed has no live SDK owner — and reclaims the
device with one `wdt_disable()` + retry before giving up, so a `wdt_id` is
no longer permanently stranded by an ordinary close on hardware whose
`wdt_disable()` actually succeeds. A watchdog that refuses to disable once
armed (some are write-once; Zephyr's own `watchdog.h`: "not all watchdogs can
be restarted after they are disabled") surfaces that refusal from the reclaim
instead of retrying blindly, and stays genuinely un-reopenable — a hardware
limit, not something this fix can paper over.

`ALP_WDT_INTERRUPT_ONLY` had the same "protection nobody can see" shape as the
close-time bug above: the Zephyr backend selected `WDT_FLAG_RESET_NONE` with a
hardcoded `.callback = NULL`, so a missed deadline notified nobody — no
callback ever ran, strictly worse than not offering the mode. (Whether the
requested `WDT_FLAG_RESET_NONE` itself also suppresses the hardware reset is
separately driver-dependent, not something this fix changes — see
`include/alp/wdt.h`'s `alp_wdt_close()` doc.)
`alp_wdt_config_t` gains `on_expire` + `user`; `alp_wdt_open()` rejects
INTERRUPT_ONLY with `ALP_ERR_INVAL` when `on_expire` is NULL, and the Zephyr
backend wires a real ISR trampoline (Zephyr's `wdt_callback_t` carries no
user-data cookie of its own, unlike `counter_alarm_cfg`'s, so `open()`
registers `(dev, channel_id) -> owner` in a small backend-local table and
`close()` clears it — a deadline that fires after `close()` finds no owner and
delivers nothing, by design, rather than touching a freed handle). The Yocto
backend now returns `ALP_ERR_NOSUPPORT` for INTERRUPT_ONLY instead of silently
accepting a mode the Linux watchdog ABI has no ioctl to deliver.

**Needs-silicon, not verified on a bench.** `native_sim` has no `alp-wdt0` DT
alias, so `zephyr_drv`'s `z_open()` always returns `ALP_ERR_NOT_READY` before
reaching `wdt_install_timeout()` -- the `-EBUSY` reclaim path and the ISR
trampoline are compiled and linked, and covered by 8 wdt cases (7 in
`tests/zephyr/peripheral/src/wdt.c` plus `test_wdt_config_default` in
`config_defaults.c`), `alp.unit.wdt_exclusivity` (3 cases), and the `wdt-feed`
example, all exercised under the required `twister · native_sim/native/64` CI
gate -- but none of that runs the reclaim or the trampoline at runtime. Whether
the reclaim actually reopens a still-armed device, whether the ISR trampoline
actually fires, and how wide the close-vs-latched-interrupt race window is,
all need an E1M-AEN801 or E1M-V2N101 bench run.

### Added — windowed watchdog feed and sleep/debug pause in `<alp/wdt.h>` (#1637)

`alp_wdt_config_t` gains two fields, both zero by default, so existing configs are unchanged:

- **`window_min_ms`.** A feed earlier than this many milliseconds after the previous one counts as a violation. It must be below `timeout_ms`.
- **`flags`.** `ALP_WDT_PAUSE_IN_SLEEP` and `ALP_WDT_PAUSE_HALTED_BY_DEBUG`.

On Zephyr they map to `wdt_timeout_cfg.window.min` and to the `WDT_OPT_PAUSE_IN_SLEEP` / `WDT_OPT_PAUSE_HALTED_BY_DBG` options of `wdt_setup()`. A driver that cannot do a window or a pause makes `alp_wdt_open()` fail with `ALP_ERR_NOSUPPORT`; the request is never silently dropped. The Linux `/dev/watchdog` backend has no such controls, and the software fallback has no timer, so both refuse a non-zero value the same way.

The dispatcher rejects `window_min_ms >= timeout_ms` and unknown `flags` bits with `ALP_ERR_INVAL`, before any backend runs. This completes #1637. The close-disarms-the-whole-device defect and `ALP_WDT_INTERRUPT_ONLY` landed earlier in #1928.

### Fixed — 27 Zephyr backends hand-rolled the same errno switch and drifted; a timed-out transfer surfaced as `ALP_ERR_IO` at 11 of them (#1638)

`src/common/alp_errno.h` has documented since #630 that its baseline takes a
**positive** POSIX errno and that a Zephyr mapper for the **negative** values the
Zephyr driver APIs return was "future work". In the absence of one, every Zephyr
backend wrote its own `static alp_status_t _errno_to_alp(int err)` switch — 27 of
them — and they drifted exactly as the 31 POSIX copies #630 consolidated had:

| errno | what the 27 did |
|---|---|
| `-EBUSY` | all 27 agree — the only consistent arm |
| `-EAGAIN` | 16 → `ALP_ERR_TIMEOUT`, 11 had no arm → `ALP_ERR_IO` |
| `-ETIMEDOUT` | 19 mapped it, 8 had no arm → `ALP_ERR_IO` |
| `-ENXIO`, `-EPERM`, `-EACCES`, `-EOVERFLOW` | appeared in no Zephyr switch at all |

`alp_status_from_zephyr_errno()` and `alp_status_from_zephyr_errno_ex()` are the
negative-domain twins. They negate and delegate to the POSIX baseline rather than
restating the table, so the two cannot drift apart arm by arm. A **positive**
value handed to the Zephyr mapper is the wrong domain and yields `ALP_ERR_IO`
rather than accidentally matching a case arm.

Three arms are answered locally rather than delegated:

- **`-EAGAIN` → `ALP_ERR_TIMEOUT`, a deliberate divergence** from the POSIX
  baseline's `ALP_ERR_BUSY`. In Zephyr driver APIs `-EAGAIN` signals an expired
  deadline (`i2s_read`, `spi_transceive`, `k_sem_take`-backed paths); in POSIX
  socket/file APIs it means "would block, retry now". Sixteen of the 27 already
  answered TIMEOUT, and `src/backends/can/yocto_drv.c` overrides the POSIX
  baseline the same way for the same reason. Delegating naively would have
  silently rewritten 16 drivers.
- **`-ENOSPC` → `ALP_ERR_NOMEM`** and **`-ERANGE` → `ALP_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE`**,
  neither of which the POSIX baseline maps at all. Both are live arms in
  `src/backends/storage/zephyr_littlefs.c`, `src/backends/storage/zephyr_flash.c`
  and `src/backends/jpeg/alif_hantro.c`, so delegating them would have demoted a
  full filesystem and an out-of-range offset to a generic I/O error.

**This is not a pure refactor.** All 26 delegating sites widen what a caller can
receive — every arm they lacked previously fell to `ALP_ERR_IO`. Eleven widen on
the axis that matters most: `src/backends/{counter,dac,gpio,pwm,qenc,rtc,spi,uart,wdt}/zephyr_drv.c`
and both storage backends had no `-EAGAIN` and/or no `-ETIMEDOUT` arm, so a
driver-reported deadline was indistinguishable from an I/O error. No site's
existing arm *conflicted* with the twin — verified arm-by-arm across all 27
before deleting a switch — so nothing narrows and nothing changes answer.

`src/backends/storage/zephyr_littlefs.c` closes a real documented-contract
violation: `include/alp/storage.h` promises `alp_storage_open()` can return
`ALP_ERR_TIMEOUT` "translated from the underlying flash-area / littlefs error",
and that mapper had no arm that could produce one. Its `zephyr_flash.c` sibling
could. One header, one of two backends, contradicting itself.

`src/backends/jpeg/alif_hantro.c` keeps `-ENOBUFS → ALP_ERR_NOMEM` through an
override table rather than losing the arm: from the Hantro encoder it means the
caller's **output** buffer was too small, which is not a general allocation
failure and has no business in the shared baseline. Note its key is **negative**,
unlike the CAN table's positive POSIX keys — each `_ex` form matches in its own
domain, so a positively-keyed table there would compile and silently never match.

No ABI impact: `src/common/alp_errno.h` is internal-only. `CMakeLists.txt`
installs only `include/alp`, no public header includes it, and `docs/abi/` carries
no `alp_errno` reference.

Regression test: `tests/unit/errno_mapping/`, covering every baseline arm, the two
locally-answered arms the POSIX baseline lacks, the `-EAGAIN` divergence
(asserting both that the twin says TIMEOUT and that the POSIX baseline still says
BUSY), wrong-domain rejection of positive values, and the override form.

Out of scope, noted so the next reader does not think they were missed:
`se_rc_to_alp` exists as four byte-identical copies
(`src/backends/soc_info/alif_se.c`, `src/backends/security/se_cryptocell.c`,
`src/backends/mproc/alif_se_boot.c`, `src/backends/power/alif_se_profile.c`),
which map `-EAGAIN` to a **third** answer, `ALP_ERR_NOT_READY`. That is the same
disease in a mixed negative-errno / positive-SE-firmware-code domain and wants its
own shared helper. `src/yocto/inference_drpai.cpp`'s `_drpai_errno_to_status` is
positive-POSIX and belongs to that baseline's migration;
`src/yocto/inference_ort.cpp`'s `_ort_errorcode_to_status` maps `OrtErrorCode`,
not errno.

### Added — `alp_uart_config_t` gains hardware/software flow control (#1639)

`alp_uart_config_t` carried baud rate, data bits, stop bits and parity but no
flow-control field, so RTS/CTS was unreachable through the portable UART API
even though the Zephyr and Linux backends both sit on top of a real
mechanism (`uart_config.flow_ctrl`, termios `CRTSCTS`) that neither one wired
up. Anyone attaching a UART radio, modem or GNSS receiver above roughly
230400 baud, or against any peer with a shallow FIFO, had no way to prevent
the peer overrunning and silently dropping bytes -- `alp_uart_write()`
returned `ALP_OK` for data the far end never saw.

- **New `alp_uart_flow_t` enum** (`include/alp/peripheral.h`):
  `ALP_UART_FLOW_NONE` (default) / `ALP_UART_FLOW_RTS_CTS` (4-wire hardware
  flow control) / `ALP_UART_FLOW_XON_XOFF` (in-band software framing). New
  `flow_control` field on `alp_uart_config_t`, appended after `parity` so
  every existing designated-initialiser call site in the tree (examples,
  tests) keeps compiling unchanged and defaults to `ALP_UART_FLOW_NONE`.
  `ALP_UART_CONFIG_DEFAULT(id)` now also sets `.flow_control =
  ALP_UART_FLOW_NONE`.
- **The field cannot be silently dropped -- three in-tree backends fixed.**
  `src/backends/uart/zephyr_drv.c` used to hardcode `.flow_ctrl =
  UART_CFG_FLOW_CTRL_NONE` regardless of the caller's request, and its
  `uart_configure()` call tolerated `-ENOSYS`/`-ENOTSUP` unconditionally on
  the theory that the devicetree-provided params were good enough;
  `vendors/alif/uart.c` (the bare-metal Ensemble CMSIS-Driver wrapper) had
  the identical `ARM_USART_FLOW_CONTROL_NONE` hardcode. Both now map
  `flow_control` onto the real backend field, and `alp_uart_open()` returns
  `ALP_ERR_NOSUPPORT` -- instead of a silent `ALP_OK` with no flow control
  -- when the caller asked for `ALP_UART_FLOW_RTS_CTS` and the controller
  can't attempt `uart_configure()` at all (`-ENOSYS`/`-ENOTSUP`); a driver
  that rejects the request outright surfaces whatever status it actually
  returned (e.g. `ALP_ERR_INVAL` for `-EINVAL`), not necessarily
  `ALP_ERR_NOSUPPORT`.
- **Accepted-but-ignored is also closed, on both backends.** A driver can
  report success from `uart_configure()`/`tcsetattr()` without having
  acted on the flow-control bits at all -- nothing in the Zephyr UART API
  requires a driver to reject a `flow_ctrl` it merely stores (`uart_emul`
  does exactly this), and POSIX `tcsetattr()` returns success as soon as
  ANY requested change lands, even when the specific tty driver clears
  `CRTSCTS` inside `set_termios()`. Both backends now read the
  configuration back after a reported success (`uart_config_get()` /
  `tcgetattr()`) and turn a mismatch on the requested bits into
  `ALP_ERR_NOSUPPORT`.
- **`ALP_UART_FLOW_XON_XOFF` has no Zephyr or CMSIS-Driver USART
  equivalent.** `enum uart_config_flow_control` carries only `NONE` /
  `RTS_CTS` / `DTR_DSR` / `RS485`; CMSIS-Driver USART has no in-band
  software framing mode either. The Zephyr backend refuses it before
  calling `uart_configure()` at all; the CMSIS backend still has to run
  `Initialize()`/`PowerControl(ARM_POWER_FULL)` first (CMSIS-Driver
  requires that before any `Control()` call), then refuses it -- both
  return `ALP_ERR_NOSUPPORT`/`NULL` without ever handing the request to
  `Control()`.
- **The Linux/Yocto backend** (`src/yocto/peripheral_uart.c`) gets a real
  mapping for *both* enumerators, since termios has no such gap: `CRTSCTS`
  in `c_cflag` for `ALP_UART_FLOW_RTS_CTS`, `IXON|IXOFF` in `c_iflag` for
  `ALP_UART_FLOW_XON_XOFF`. The mapping lives in a new pure helper,
  `apply_flow_control()`, unit-tested directly against a scratch `struct
  termios` (`tests/yocto/peripheral_uart_flow_control.c`) without needing a
  real `/dev/tty*`.
- **The sw_fallback and testing (`alp_testing`) UART backends stay
  unchanged, deliberately.** Neither drives a real line: `sw_open` is a
  64-byte in-process ring buffer and `t_open` is a test double documented
  to always succeed regardless of config, so the flow-control
  refusal/readback guarantee in `<alp/peripheral.h>` -- scoped to backends
  that drive actual hardware -- does not cover them; both already ignore
  every line-config field in `alp_uart_config_t` (`sw_open`/`t_open` never
