  That line is how the raw wire integer leaked into customer-facing threads.
- `scripts/check_protocol_version_policy.py` fails a MAJOR bump with no justified
  row in ADR 0033's machine-readable ledger. The failure it prevents is social:
  a MAJOR bump is never technically *wrong*, costs the person shipping it
  nothing, and spends a customer's reflash.

**Breaking:** this is one final bump by construction — a v9 host and a `3.1`
firmware do not interoperate even though their frames are identical. Taken now,
at one customer on the protocol, rather than later at ten.

It also repaired two gates that would have gone quietly green: the firmware
repo's "protocol version parity" job greps for digits after
`ALP_CC3501E_PROTOCOL_VERSION`, which now matches nothing (the macro is a
composed expression) and would have compared empty to empty; and this repo's own
version-mismatch test used `PROTOCOL_VERSION + 1`, which under the composed
encoding only bumps MINOR — an accepted case — so it would have kept passing
while testing nothing.

Paired firmware change: `cc3501e-bridge-firmware` (`protocol-version.txt` → `3.1`,
`CMD_GET_CAPABILITIES` handler, honest stub-build bitmap via a new
`CC3501E_HAL_STUB` define).

### Fixed — `aen-wdt-feed` watchdog clock is 160 MHz, not a 100 MHz placeholder (#1937)

The example's `rtss_he_clk` fixed-clock carried a 100 MHz placeholder. The
upstream CMSDK watchdog driver computes its reload as `timeout_ms * freq_khz`,
so every requested timeout ran at 0.625x its length. Measured on E1M-AEN803
serial 2026W36-0001, the watchdog counts at 160009 kHz, which matches the Alif
fork's `ensemble_rtss_he.dtsi` (160000000). Both board overlays now say 160 MHz.

### Fixed — CAST CAN-FD driver delivers a classic DLC 9..15 frame as 12..64 bytes (#1937)

On a `CONFIG_CAN_FD_MODE` build, `can_cast_receive()` reported a received
classic frame (FDF=0) with wire DLC 9..15 as `can_dlc_to_bytes(dlc)` =
12/24/64 bytes, copying stale receive-buffer words beyond the 8 data bytes
classic CAN carries (measured on E1M-AEN803 in internal loopback: DLC 9 gave
`payload_len` 12 with `data[8..11]` stale). Per ISO 11898-1 such a frame
carries 8 bytes.

Changes:
- `zephyr/drivers/can/can_cast.c`: a classic frame with DLC > 8 is reported
  with `dlc = 8` and only 8 bytes are copied, on FD and non-FD builds alike.
  An FD frame on a non-FD build is still dropped (no room in `can_frame`).
- `src/backends/can/zephyr_drv.c`: the RX trampoline caps a classic frame's
  `payload_len` at 8 so drivers that pass the raw DLC through agree.

### Fixed — `cc3501e_reset()` could return `ALP_OK` without ever negotiating the wire MAJOR (#1937, #1927)

Found on E1M-AEN803 silicon (1 of 5 matched cold boots): the reset-time `GET_VERSION` missed, the transport-miss branch of `cc3501e_reset()` (`chips/cc3501e/cc3501e_core.c`) restored the "previous" MAJOR — `0` on a fresh context — and returned `ALP_OK` with `initialised=1`. Every later request was framed CRC-less against a MAJOR-4 firmware, so `GET_CAPABILITIES` and every `PING` failed `-5` for the whole run while a bare `GET_VERSION` kept answering.

`cc3501e_reset()` now retries the version query (3 attempts, 200 ms apart) and, if a fresh context still negotiates nothing, returns `ALP_ERR_TIMEOUT` with `initialised=0`, so later calls fail `ALP_ERR_NOT_READY` instead of `-5`. A context that already negotiated a MAJOR keeps it, as before. `aen-cc3501e-bringup` now compares only the MAJOR when printing the `GET_VERSION` verdict (MINOR skew is compatible, ADR 0033).

### Fixed — the PUBLISH-payload drain now resumes across `alp_mqtt_loop()` calls instead of silently wedging the connection when a payload spans TCP segments (#1938)

`mqtt_drain_remaining()` (added by #1645 to stop an oversized PUBLISH from
wedging the connection) drained the leftover payload in a single
non-blocking pass: it kept reading only while `mqtt_read_publish_payload()`
returned a positive count, and gave up the instant that call answered
anything else -- including a plain `-EAGAIN` because the rest of the
payload simply hadn't arrived on the wire yet. A payload split across TCP
segments therefore reproduced the exact wedge #1645 set out to close:
Zephyr's `mqtt_client::internal.remaining_payload` stayed non-zero, and
every later `mqtt_input()` answered `-EBUSY` forever, with nothing in
`alp_mqtt_loop()`'s return value ever saying so. There was no deadline, no
`zsock_poll()`, and no `mqtt_abort()` anywhere in this path -- the drain
just gave up in silence and left the connection dead.

The drain is now resumable across calls instead of one blind pass.
`struct mqtt_be` carries the pending drain's progress (bytes still owed, how
much has already landed in `rx_buf`, the QoS/msg-id needed to finish
delivery) plus a spanning lifetime deadline stamped once when the drain
first becomes pending. Each `alp_mqtt_loop()`/`alp_mqtt_connect()` call
resumes the drain, spending only what the socket has ready within its OWN
`timeout_ms` (via `zsock_poll()`) before returning -- never aborting a
healthy connection just because that one call's budget ran out. Only the
drain's own spanning lifetime (`ALP_MQTT_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS`, 5 s, measured
from when the drain started rather than reset on every call) tears the
connection down with `mqtt_abort()`, so a peer that goes permanently silent
mid-payload still can't wedge the client forever -- the gap #1645's fix
left open.

Also fixed while replacing the drain:

- Neither `alp_mqtt_loop()` nor `z_connect()` surfaced the drain's own
  `mqtt_abort()` (or a peer-initiated `MQTT_EVT_DISCONNECT`) as anything
  but `ALP_OK`: `mqtt_input()` still answers 0 and `mqtt_live()` answers
  `-EAGAIN` whenever no keepalive is due, so nothing told the caller their
  connection was gone. `docs/tutorials/11-mqtt-tls-publish.md` already
  documents the intended contract -- a broker disconnect surfaces as
  `ALP_ERR_IO`, since there is no separate is-connected query -- so
  `z_loop()` (and `z_connect()`'s drain-resume path) now compare the
  connected flag before and after and return `ALP_ERR_IO` the moment it
  flips, whether the loss was graceful (`MQTT_EVT_DISCONNECT`) or the
  drain's own `mqtt_abort()`.
- The drain's new `zsock_poll()` call inspects `revents` for
  `POLLNVAL`/`POLLERR` rather than trusting a bare `rc < 0`: Zephyr reports
  a torn-down/invalid fd as `POLLNVAL`/`POLLERR` with a POSITIVE return,
  never `-1`; missing that would have `mqtt_read_publish_payload()` answer
  `-EAGAIN` forever while `zsock_poll()` kept returning immediately --
  hot-spinning at 100% CPU for the rest of the deadline.
- `timeout_ms` is now clamped to `INT32_MAX` before
  `k_uptime_get_32() + timeout_ms`, so the `(int32_t)(deadline - now)`
  comparisons this file uses throughout can't be fooled by a caller passing
  a timeout near `UINT32_MAX`.

`examples/connectivity/iot-connected-camera/src/main.c`'s
`alp_mqtt_loop(g_mqtt, 10)` teaching comment and
`docs/tutorials/11-mqtt-tls-publish.md`'s `ALP_ERR_IO`-on-disconnect contract
both already documented the intended behaviour; this change makes the code
honor it rather than needing either updated.

**Bench-gated:** the resumable drain is logic-reviewed and confirmed against
a host harness (a synthetic 300 B PUBLISH split into a 100 B then a 200 B
segment 150 ms apart, drained across two `alp_mqtt_loop()` calls with the
connection surviving), not against a real broker. `tests/zephyr/iot`'s new
`alp_sdk.iot.mqtt_build` scenario compiles this file's
`CONFIG_ALP_SDK_IOT_MQTT` arm under `native_sim` -- closing the compile-only
gap `changelog.d/1645.md` recorded for this same file -- but it is
build-only: `native_sim` has no MQTT-capable network stack to run a live
client against, so a real-broker round trip still needs the AEN-Zephyr bench
(`docs/ci/HW-IN-LOOP.md`).

### Added — real coverage for the GATT context pool's CAS loss and `ALP_ERR_BUSY` refusal; the abandon path is bench-owed (#1939)

`changelog.d/1620.md` shipped the `_read_ctx_pool`/`_write_ctx_pool` +
`alp_slot_try_claim()`/`alp_lifecycle_cas()` fix for the GATT read/write
context-lifetime bug with its regression test still owed: three branches of
the pool state machine in `src/backends/ble/zephyr_drv.c` -- the abandon path
(a caller's timeout winning the `LIVE -> ABANDONED` CAS), the CAS loss (a
late `ble_read_cb()`/`ble_write_cb()` losing that same CAS because the
caller already won it), and the `ALP_ERR_BUSY` refusal (`z_gatt_read()`/
`z_gatt_write()` refusing once `_read_ctx_alloc()`/`_write_ctx_alloc()`
return `NULL` against an exhausted pool) -- had zero execution anywhere, CI
or bench. `native_sim` ships no BLE controller, so no real peer can drive
`z_gatt_read()`/`z_gatt_write()` end-to-end offline to reach them.

New `CONFIG_ZTEST`-only seams in `src/backends/ble/zephyr_drv.c`, in the same
style as the existing `alp_ble_test_read_cb()` (issue #480):

- **CAS loss** (genuinely covered): `alp_ble_test_read_cb_loses_cas_after_abandon()`
  / `alp_ble_test_write_cb_loses_cas_after_abandon()` pre-abandon a synthetic
  ctx via the real `alp_lifecycle_cas()` call, then feed it into the real
  `ble_read_cb()`/`ble_write_cb()` so its own CAS genuinely loses -- against
  the actual production callbacks, not a reimplementation.
- **`ALP_ERR_BUSY` refusal** (genuinely covered, driven through the production
  entry point): `alp_ble_test_gatt_read_busy()` / `alp_ble_test_gatt_write_busy()`
  exhaust the real pool through `_read_ctx_alloc()`/`_write_ctx_alloc()`, then
  call the real (`static`) `z_gatt_read()`/`z_gatt_write()` with a non-NULL
  `bt` sentinel that the pool-exhaustion check refuses before ever
  dereferencing it. Both seams require their own claiming loop to have
  actually reached the pool's real capacity before calling into
  `z_gatt_read()`/`z_gatt_write()` -- otherwise they return `ALP_ERR_NOT_READY`
  instead, distinct from the `ALP_ERR_BUSY` the test asserts, so a broken
  allocator (one that refuses every claim, or a pool already exhausted on
  entry) fails the test loudly instead of answering `ALP_ERR_BUSY` for the
  wrong reason.
- **Pool-exhaustion tautology avoided**: `alp_ble_test_read_ctx_pool_exhausts()`
  / `alp_ble_test_write_ctx_pool_exhausts()` report the claim count rather
  than re-reading the same `_read_ctx_alloc() == NULL` condition the loop
  already exited on, and only probe for a spare slot once every real slot is
  confirmed held -- freeing that probe immediately rather than leaking it if
  a bug ever lets it succeed.
- **Abandon path: declared bench-owed, not seamed.** `z_gatt_read()`'s /
  `z_gatt_write()`'s own timeout-driven `alp_lifecycle_cas(LIVE ->
  ABANDONED)` stays zero-executed -- no offline seam reaches it without
  reimplementing the timeout race itself. Tracked as bench-owed in
  `docs/test-plan.md` instead of claimed.

All seams are `#if defined(CONFIG_ZTEST)`-gated, the same guard the file's
existing `alp_ble_test_read_cb()` seam already used -- a release build never
sees these symbols at all, so this changes no production behaviour.

**Still not closed by this change:** the abandon branches above, plus
`z_gatt_read()`/`z_gatt_write()`'s own calls into `bt_gatt_read()`/
`bt_gatt_write()`, stay `BENCH-UNVERIFIED` and need a real two-device bench
proof. `src/backends/**` is bench-held per #1937; this change is authored
only, not merge-eligible on its own.

### Fixed — `changelog.d/` fragment names had no way to disambiguate a second fragment for one issue, so the collision got named after the PR instead (#1941)

`scripts/check_changelog_fragments.py` (via `scripts/assemble_changelog.py`'s
`FRAGMENT_NAME_RE`) required every fragment filename to be exactly
`<digits>.md`. Since the digits are the issue number, that made the filename
a unique key on issue number, and two unmerged fragments for the same issue
could not coexist — an issue legitimately closed by more than one PR (a
tiered fix, a split, two independent defects under one number) had no legal
suffixed name to fall back on. Hit for real on 2026-09-04: `changelog.d/1909.md`
was already taken by an unrelated fragment for #1700, so the #1909 fix landed
as `changelog.d/1932.md` — named after the PR that closed it instead of the
issue it describes, silently breaking the convention the number exists to
encode.

`FRAGMENT_NAME_RE` now accepts `<issue>.md` or `<issue>-<slug>.md`
(`^\d+(-[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*)?\.md$`), so `1909-diagnostic-format-uri.md`
is legal and still sorts and greps under `1909`. `assemble_changelog.py`'s
`_fragment_sort_key()` was updated in lockstep: it now orders by the
*leading* issue number (matched with a regex, not `str.isdigit()`) so a
suffixed fragment folds into `CHANGELOG.md` next to its plain-numbered
sibling by issue order, not lexicographically by slug. The gate's error text
changed to name both accepted shapes
(`expected \`<issue>.md\` or \`<issue>-<slug>.md\`, issue digits first`).
`changelog.d/README.md` now states the collision rule explicitly, which it
did not before.

`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py` and `scripts/bump_version.py` glob
`changelog.d/*.md` without parsing the filename for structure beyond the
`README.md` exemption, so neither needed a change.

### Fixed — `scripts/validate_metadata.py` no longer imports `alp_model` (#1943)

`resolve_targets()` / `npu_backend()` / `accel_config()` moved from
`scripts/alp_model/targets.py` into `scripts/alp_project_loader.py`. The
model-perf-v1 semantic cross-check that `validate_metadata.py` runs on every
PR had grown a load-bearing, module-scope
`from alp_model.targets import resolve_targets, _npu_backend, _accel_config`,
which meant `scripts/alp_model/` (12 files) — due for deletion now that the
host-side model engine lives in tan-cli's `tan.model` — could not be removed
without breaking that gate on every PR (#1470, #1884, #1896).

Per the just-recorded ADR-0026 §C/§D decision that alp-sdk stays canonical
for rendered bytes and tan consumes rather than re-implements, the
resolution logic moved to an in-repo home (`alp_project_loader.py`) rather
than repointing the gate at tan-cli. `scripts/alp_model/targets.py` is
deleted outright rather than kept as a re-export shim: its only remaining
caller, `scripts/alp_model/build.py`, now imports `resolve_targets` from
`alp_project_loader` directly (this repo has no legacy customers to shield,
so the shim was worth zero once its one caller could be repointed).
`tests/scripts/test_alp_model_targets.py` — coverage of this resolution
logic, not of anything else in the package — is renamed to
`test_alp_project_loader_targets.py` so it survives Task 6 instead of
matching a `git rm tests/scripts/test_alp_model_*.py` glob.
`tests/scripts/test_validate_metadata_no_alp_model_import.py` no longer
AST-walks `validate_metadata.py`'s imports (a proxy a transitive or
in-function `import alp_model` would pass); it copies the real `scripts/`,
`metadata/`, and `zephyr/boards/alp` trees, deletes `scripts/alp_model/`
from the copy, and actually runs `validate_metadata.py` against it.

`alp_model` is **not** deleted by this change — Task 6 remains its own PR —
and the earlier claim that "nothing PR-blocking depends on it" once that
happens was wrong. Two things still block a clean Task 6, named here so the
next PR isn't surprised by either:

* `scripts/alp_model/`'s own test suite is not touched by this fix:
  `tests/scripts/test_alp_model_{adapters,build,manifest,package,tensorio}.py`,
  `test_deepx_yolo_internal.py`, and `test_vela_yolo_internal.py` all import
  the package directly and must be deleted in the **same** PR as
  `scripts/alp_model/` itself, or `pytest tests/scripts/` aborts collection
  the moment the package is gone.
* `docs/bring-up-drpai-v2n.md` documents `ALP_DRPAI_TVM_HOME`, whose only
  in-tree definition is `scripts/alp_model/adapters/drpai.py`. `check_doc_drift.py`
  harvests `scripts/**/*.py` as one of its "does this identifier exist
  somewhere real" sources; deleting the adapter without giving that doc a
  new home for the identifier fails `check_doc_drift.py` on the Task-6 PR.

Cross-repo note: this fix's edits to `scripts/alp_project_loader.py` change
its sha256, and tan-cli pins that exact file's content hash verbatim in
`python/tests/gates/test_planner_relocation_freshness.py`'s
`HAND_PORT_HASHES` table (the file is hand-ported into tan's own planner
modules). Not red in alp-sdk today, but tan-cli's freshness gate will flag
the pin as stale the next time someone re-audits that table against an
alp-sdk commit at or past this one.

### Decided — `new-som`'s `alif:ensemble` `ospi_memories`/`hyperram` scaffold stays out of alp-sdk (#1944)

PR #1470 carried an enhancement to the `new-som` scaffold that emitted
`ospi_memories:`/`hyperram:` skeletons for `alif:ensemble` parts, plus two
dedicated tests. It was dropped mid-rebase because `210e9fedc` had already
retired the whole `scripts/alp_cli/` CLI surface on `dev` — `new-som` now
lives only in tan-cli, and there is no alp-sdk file left for that hunk to
land in. Confirmed on this pass: `scripts/alp_cli/` keeps only its
non-CLI library modules (`_workspace.py`, `diagnostic.py`,
`diagnostic_format.py`, `validator.py`, `yaml_pos.py`, `__init__.py`); no
`new_som.py`/`main.py` and no other alp-sdk file emits either field.

**Decision: do not port the hunk into alp-sdk. `new-som` scaffolding is a
tan-cli concern.** Filed as
[tan-cli#1220](https://github.com/alplabai/tan-cli/issues/1220) for a native
port — not merely asserted as "tracked", since no such issue existed before
this pass (`gh issue list --repo alplabai/tan-cli --search "new-som ospi
hyperram scaffold"` returned none).

**Engaging ADR-0026, not just citing it.** §D's own words are "the producer
of hardware truth and the renderer of hardware truth belong in the same
repo" — read broadly, a scaffold that writes an `ospi_memories:`/`hyperram:`
skeleton into `metadata/e1m_modules/*.yaml` looks like a hardware-truth
*producer*, which clause 2 keeps in alp-sdk. That reading does not survive
contact with what §D is actually scoped to: its "producer" is the
already-authored metadata `clause 2` protects (`metadata/`,
`metadata/schemas/`) and what a *renderer* derives from it at
configure/build time (`alp.conf`, sysbuild, kconfig, headers, secure bytes)
— both are read-then-emit pipelines over metadata that already carries
schema-validated facts. `new-som`'s scaffold is neither: it writes
`TBD`/placeholder text a human still has to replace with a real MPN, CS
index and population state, and the result is not "hardware truth" until
`validate_metadata.py` (which *does* stay in alp-sdk, unmoved by any of
this) accepts it. It is authoring tooling, not a truth pipeline — the same
category as the `new-som` SoC/SoM-YAML skeleton generation that already
moved to tan-cli in full (`210e9fedc`, 2026-08-27), eight days before
ADR-0026 §C/§D was decided (2026-09-04). §C/§D discuss the configure-time
CMake call and the renderer axis by name and do not mention scaffolding at
all; reopening an already-shipped, working placement on an ADR that does
not address it would be the drift, not honoring it.

The metadata *schema* already has correct homes for both fields
(`ospi_memory`/`hyperram` in `som-preset-v2.schema.json`), and every shipped
AEN preset now *declares* population explicitly, per
`changelog.d/1990-aen-ospi-chip-select.md`: `assembled: true` where a real
per-SKU source backs it (`E1M-AEN803.yaml`'s own header states both
external memories are its SKU contract), `assembled: optional` where
population is genuinely unconfirmed (the five E3–E7 family SKUs — round-2
review found the first pass's `true` there rested on a boilerplate comment
`E1M-AEN801.yaml` itself falsifies), and marked DNI where not
(`E1M-AEN801.yaml`'s `assembled: false`) — so the scaffold gap is a
generation-time convenience, not a validation gap.
`docs/porting-new-som.md` now carries the gap + the tan-cli#1220 pointer
inline, so the next person filling in a new Ensemble SoM's
`ospi_memories:`/`hyperram:` by hand does not rediscover this in PR history.

### Changed — E1M-V2M101's CM33 board carries the OpenAMP/MHU-B carve-out (#1948)

`topology.m33_sm.openamp_ipc` was set only on E1M-V2N101, which left the
generated `alp_e1m_v2m101_m33_sm` devicetree without the OpenAMP
reserved-memory block, the `mbox1` MHU-B node and the CAN-FD analysis,
as if the V2M101 hardware differed. It doesn't: both SoMs carry the same
RZ/V2N die, the same MHU-B and the same CM33-NS DDR alias. E1M-V2M101 now
sets the flag and its board `.dts` is regenerated to match.

The A55 half of this link (the `4f70xxxx` UIO and reserved-memory nodes)
is not in any shipped Linux devicetree for either SoM. Board #1
(E1M-V2M103, 2026-09-28) shows `48000000-13fffffff : System RAM` with no
hole at the A55 view `0x4f700000`, and no `/sys/class/uio`. So OpenAMP
between the cores still needs that overlay on both families. BENCH:
the V2M101 CM33 image with the carve-out has not been booted yet.

### Fixed — `metadata/chips/gd32g553.yaml` cited three closed issues as the reason it is still `partial`

The manifest's `driver_status: partial` comment named #495, #494 and #496 as
open. All three closed months ago -- #494 and #495 via #730, #496 via #764 --
so the file was telling a reader to go and check work that was already
finished, and giving the wrong reasons for a status that is nonetheless
correct.

The chip really is still `partial`. The comment now records why, taken from
each issue's own closing comment rather than restated:

- PWM dead-time and break stay `NOSUPPORT` because the V2N connector routes
  neither the complementary CHxN pad nor a BRK pad. That is a carrier-routing
  limit needing a future carrier revision, not firmware work.
- ADC 14/16-bit is unsupported (DRES tops out at 12, UM Rev1.2 p.434
  section 17.4.16).
- End-to-end DSP-chain analog measurement is deferred because the bench ADC
  pins float.
- `PWM_CAPTURE` edges remain pending a V2N pad-routing rework.

No status word, symbol or schema changed -- `driver_status` stays `partial`,
so `check_driver_status_backing.py` and `check_chip_header_status.py` are
unaffected. Comment text only.

Found by a whole-repo stub/partial triage pass against #500. The gate gap that
let it drift -- no check validates an issue number cited in metadata prose
against that issue's state -- is filed separately.

### Added — a gate flags a closed issue cited as an open driver-status blocker (#1950)

`metadata/chips/gd32g553.yaml`'s `driver_status: partial` comment named #495,
#494 and #496 as the open reasons the driver wasn't `complete`. All three had
closed months earlier -- #494/#495 via #730, #496 via #764 (#1949) -- and the
six chip-status gates (`check_stub_issues.py`, `check_stub_symbol_matrix.py`,
`check_driver_status_backing.py`, `check_chip_header_status.py`,
`check_sw_fallback_tags.py`, `check_vendor_ext_tags.py`) all stayed green
throughout: every one of them binds a status *word* to a source artefact,
never the free prose explaining it. A reader who follows a citation like
that into a closed issue either wrongly concludes the entry is done, or
re-does analysis the closing comment already has.

New `scripts/check_issue_citations.py` harvests `#NNNN` citations out of two
narrow, by-construction-a-claim-about-what-remains locations -- a
`<...>driver_status:` field's trailing YAML comment block
(`metadata/**/*.yaml`) and an `@par Driver status:` Doxygen paragraph
(`include/alp/chips/*.h`) -- and fails when a cited number resolves to a
closed/merged state while its own `.`/`;`-delimited clause reads as a
blocker claim. A citation whose clause carries a historical marker (`via`,
`closed`, `closing`, `landed`/`lands`, `fixed`, `resolved`, `merged`,
`shipped`, `done`, `already`) is skipped, not flagged -- "#494, #495 and #496
all closed (#494/#495 via #730, #496 via #764)" must not trip the gate the
day #1949 lands. Everywhere else (`changelog.d/`, `CHANGELOG.md`, ADR prose,
a `notes:` block, any other field's comment) is deliberately out of scope for
this first cut: those are full of legitimate historical references, and a
blanket `#NNNN` harvest over them is noise from day one. Widening there is
filed as a follow-up, #1958, if it turns out to be cheap.

The gate is offline by design -- a live `gh` call inside every PR run would
make it a network-flake gate on every metadata/** PR. It reads a committed
snapshot, `metadata/issue-state-snapshot.json`, refreshed by a human running
`python3 scripts/refresh_issue_state_snapshot.py`. There is no scheduled
workflow -- refresh is manual, so an ageing snapshot is the normal
case, not a rare cron miss: a stale-but-present snapshot still enforces every
citation it has a record for and prints one loud warning naming the refresh
command; only an entirely missing/unparsable snapshot, or a cited number the
snapshot has never seen, degrades that citation to a non-blocking warning
instead.

A `driver_status`-family field with no comment attached to it at all
(`nor_flash_driver_status`/`emmc_driver_status`/`driver_status` with nothing
after the value -- the common shape, 52 of 97 such fields on this tree) gets
the same indentation-drift WARN as a field that does have a comment: a
comment-only line right after it, indented deeper than the field itself, is
flagged as a slipped continuation that was NOT read into the block, instead
of being silently skipped with zero diagnostic.

`scripts/refresh_issue_state_snapshot.py` refuses to write and exits
non-zero, rather than silently degrading enforcement, in two cases: every
cited number failing to resolve via `gh` (a total auth/network outage would
otherwise overwrite the snapshot with `{}`), and any number that has a
record on disk and is still cited but did not resolve this run (a partial
outage dropping citations from enforcement one at a time). The second check
is keyed on the dropped numbers themselves, not a size ratio, so it catches
a drop of any size and does not fire when a citation is legitimately
removed from the source entirely; `--allow-shrink` overrides it for the
rare case where the drop is deliberate (e.g. the GitHub issue was deleted).

Registered in `metadata/quality-tasks-v1.json` (`issue-citations`, `pr` /
`full` / `release` profiles) and wired into
`pr-metadata-validate.yml:validate`, per the four-site rule in
`adding-a-ci-gate`.

Run against the real tree, the gate found three pre-existing instances of the
exact defect it exists to catch, not just the `gd32g553.yaml` case described
above: `metadata/chips/dp83825.yaml:4` citing the now-closed #1241/#1244, and
`include/alp/chips/pca9451a.h:10` citing the now-closed #474. Both files'
prose is fixed in this same change -- a new gate that ships pointing at
findings it doesn't itself resolve would land red. `gd32g553.yaml`'s own
citations are fixed by #1949, which landed on `dev` first and gets the
14/16-bit-resolution cause right (a GD32G553 RM effective-resolution
question needing its own bench proof); this change defers to #1949 for that
file rather than carrying a competing rewrite.

With those three fixed, every remaining driver-status citation on the tree
classifies as historical, so this gate's live enforcement is zero known
citations today (`harvested N, N historical, 0 evaluated`) -- expected, not
a gap: it activates the moment a future citation is phrased as a live
blocker against an issue that has since closed.

### Added — a scheduled alarm for silent `dev` merge-queue ejections (#1952)

PR #1887 was enqueued on `dev`, sat at `AWAITING_CHECKS`, and was ejected
without merging while every one of its own checks stayed green -- its four
`merge_group` runs were still `queued` past the ruleset's
`check_response_timeout_minutes` when a starved runner pool never started
them. The ejected PR kept reading `OPEN` / `MERGEABLE` / `CLEAN`, so nothing
in the PR view distinguished "dropped an hour ago and will not merge on its
own" from "still waiting". A human had to notice `dev` had stopped moving
while the queue looked healthy.

`.github/workflows/merge-queue-ejection-alarm.yml` runs
`scripts/merge_queue_ejection_alarm.py` on a 30-minute schedule (also
`workflow_dispatch`-able) to surface exactly that state. It never fails or
blocks CI -- it is an alarm, not a gate.

Detection: a PR targeting `dev` that is `MERGEABLE` / `CLEAN` (which already
encodes every required check passing), is not currently in the merge queue
(live `repository { mergeQueue { entries { pullRequest { number } } } }`
GraphQL query -- verified against the real API before relying on it), and
whose issue timeline's *last* queue-related event is a
`removed_from_merge_queue` with actor `github-merge-queue[bot]` more than 15
minutes ago. That actor check is load-bearing: a human clicking "Remove from
queue" produces the same event type but with *their own* login as actor, and
must not alarm. Validated against this repo's real data, both directions:
PR #1887's three `removed_from_merge_queue` events (the recorded incident)
all carry actor `github-merge-queue[bot]`, and replaying the detector
against its timeline truncated to just after the first (2026-09-04
09:44:43Z) ejection fires true; PRs #1673 and #1670 (`needs-silicon`, held
open on purpose, currently `MERGEABLE`/`CLEAN`) were removed from the queue
with actor `alpCaner` during the incident's manual mitigation and correctly
do not fire. Alarms once per ejection via a PR comment carrying the
timeline event's id as a dedup marker; a second ejection of the same PR
carries a different event id and alarms again.

Known scope limit, stated rather than hidden: the actor field cannot tell a
genuine ejection apart from the queue removing an entry to complete its own
merge -- but that case is excluded for free, since a merged PR's state is
`MERGED`, not `OPEN`, so it never reaches this detector's candidate list.

This is the detection half only. It is not a `check_*.py` gate (nothing in
it validates a diff or blocks a merge, so the four-site quality-registry
lockstep does not apply) and it does not touch the ruleset itself.

Correcting this issue's own now-stale premise: it was filed citing
`check_response_timeout_minutes: 60`. That value was already `180` before
this work started (`repos/alplabai/alp-sdk/rulesets/20781492`), and
`max_entries_to_build` was separately raised `1` -> `2` on 2026-09-06.
Neither is touched by this change, which only adds detection.

The forensics that settle WHY an entry is dropped are worth recording here,
because the issue's own account has the clock wrong. #1887's first ejection:

    07:18:15Z  added_to_merge_queue
    08:40:47Z  merge_group runs CREATED   <- 82 min waiting for a build slot
    09:14:15Z    pr-static-analysis            success
    09:35:45Z    pr-bootstrap-distro-install   success
    09:44:43Z  removed_from_merge_queue by github-merge-queue[bot]
    09:52:49Z    pr-twister                    success
    09:56:14Z    cross-platform-zephyr         success

Build start to ejection is 63.9 minutes -- the 60-minute timeout of the
day, measured from when the entry began BUILDING, not from when it was
enqueued. Enqueue-relative arithmetic (146 minutes) fits nothing, which is
why the mechanism looked unexplained. And every one of the four checks
passed; the last finished 11.5 minutes after the entry was thrown out.

So the timeout is the executioner and contention is what puts an entry in
front of it: neither raising the timeout nor raising `max_entries_to_build`
shortens that 82-minute wait to start. What measurably helped was reducing
competing `pull_request` CI load.

### Added — `alp_uptime_ms()`: a portable monotonic clock, and `poll_by_repeat()` now bounds by wall time instead of flooring it (#1953)

`chips/cc3501e/cc3501e_core.c`'s `poll_by_repeat()` — the retry wrapper every
worker-routed CC3501E op goes through (Wi-Fi, BLE, sockets, the GPIO proxy,
OTA) — charged only its own back-off sleeps against `timeout_ms`. The time
spent inside `cc3501e_request_locked()` on each attempt (up to four SPI
transfers, plus whatever the transport waits on a stalled link) was free, so
`timeout_ms` was a **floor** on wall time, not a bound, and the skew grew
with the number of attempts: gaps ramp 1 ms to 50 ms, so a 30 s budget is
roughly 610 attempts, and every millisecond an attempt costs became another
~610 ms of overrun.

A correct fix needs a monotonic millisecond clock read at entry and a loop
bound to a deadline — and `chips/cc3501e/*.c` has none available: it is
deliberately OS-agnostic (builds into both the Zephyr module and the plain-
CMake / Yocto `libalp_chips.a`; per `CMakeLists.txt`, none of the
`chips/<id>/<id>.c` cores include a Zephyr/vendor header), and
`<alp/peripheral.h>` exposed `alp_delay_ms()` but no clock.

**New portable API:** `alp_uptime_ms()` in `<alp/peripheral.h>` —
milliseconds since an arbitrary fixed epoch (usually boot), monotonic and
unaffected by wall-clock/RTC changes. Returns `uint64_t`; a millisecond
count at that width wraps after roughly 584 million years, so callers
compare two readings directly instead of needing wraparound-safe unsigned
subtraction. Three backends:

- Zephyr (`src/zephyr/delay_zephyr.c`): `k_uptime_get()`.
- Yocto (`src/common/stub/stub_core.c`, `__linux__` branch, also covers the
  plain-CMake baremetal build on the CI host): `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)`.
- The clockless baremetal fallback (`src/common/stub/stub_core.c`,
  non-`__linux__` branch — dormant today; no non-Linux target builds this
  file yet): a running total of every `alp_delay_us`/`alp_delay_ms` wait
  this backend itself performed. Monotonic and internally consistent, but
  cannot see time spent outside those calls — a real vendor HAL bring-up
  should replace it with a cycle-counter read (SysTick / DWT->CYCCNT / core
  timer), same upgrade path the delay spin already notes.

`alp_delay_ms()`'s own contract is unchanged.

**`poll_by_repeat()` now loops on a deadline** (`alp_uptime_ms() +
timeout_ms`, computed once at entry) instead of decrementing a sleep-only
budget: each attempt is followed by a real elapsed-time check, and the
final back-off gap is clamped to whatever's left before the deadline. Still
always makes at least one attempt, including for `timeout_ms == 0`, since
the first attempt runs unconditionally before the deadline is ever checked.
The remaining, unavoidable slack is bounded by one attempt's own cost (SPI
transfers + any transport wait), not by the number of attempts made — a
world apart from the old unbounded-with-attempt-count overrun.

**Behaviour change at `timeout_ms == 0`:** the old sleep-budget form set
`remaining = (timeout_ms > 0) ? timeout_ms : 1u`, so a still-busy first
attempt always bought one more 1 ms back-off gap before `remaining` hit
zero — i.e. exactly two attempts. The deadline form's `deadline_ms ==
alp_uptime_ms()` at entry means the post-attempt check `now_ms >=
deadline_ms` is true as soon as any wall time has elapsed, so a still-busy
first attempt returns `ALP_ERR_TIMEOUT` immediately — exactly one attempt.
Both honour "`timeout_ms == 0` still tries once"; only the retry count for
an immediately-busy peer changes.

**Round-18 correction:** the paragraph above previously claimed "no caller in
this tree passes `timeout_ms == 0` today". That was false, and was flagged
false in round 16 without being corrected in round 17.
`examples/aen/aen-cc3501e-bringup/src/main.c` calls
`cc3501e_ota_status(fw, &bs/&ps, 0u)` at two sites in `cc3501e_demo_ota()`
(the BEGIN-attempt diagnostic probe, and the per-chunk window-flush hold-off
poll), and `chips/cc3501e/cc3501e_ota.c:436`'s `cc3501e_ota_status()`
forwards `timeout_ms` straight into `poll_by_repeat()` — so this example DID
observe the difference: reproduced on a host harness, a still-busy peer got
two attempts (6 `alp_spi_transceive` calls) under the old sleep-budget form
and exactly one (3 calls) under the deadline form, a silently dropped retry
in a shipped example.

**Decision:** keep the deadline form's one-attempt-at-zero as the correct,
now regression-locked behaviour of `poll_by_repeat()` itself (an honest
"instant, no-budget poll", not the old form's accidental one-more-attempt
floor — re-adding that floor would reintroduce a version of the exact
unbounded-slack problem this issue exists to fix, just narrowed to the
`timeout_ms == 0` case). Instead, fixed the two call sites: both now pass
`CC3501E_OTA_BENCH_FLUSH_POLL_TIMEOUT_MS` (200 ms) instead of a bare `0u`.
That constant already existed in the example, already documented as "cap
each STATUS frame so the hold-off budget above is REAL", and mirrors
`chips/cc3501e/cc3501e_ota.c`'s own `CC3501E_OTA_BLACKOUT_POLL_TIMEOUT_MS`
(also 200 ms) — it was simply never wired into the two call sites that
needed it, leaving them to rely on `poll_by_repeat()`'s old zero-timeout
floor by accident. A real, intentional per-poll budget restores retry room
for a transient BUSY/IO without reintroducing an unbounded wait.

Regression-locked by a new native_sim suite,
`tests/zephyr/cc3501e_poll_deadline`, with a stub clock that advances only
on demand (via the test's own `alp_delay_ms`/`alp_spi_transceive` seams) so
the deadline logic is exercised without any real sleeping or hardware.

**Round-18 correction:** `test_zero_timeout_still_makes_one_attempt_1953`
asserted `g_transceive_calls >= 3u`, which the pre-fix sleep-only budget
also satisfies (6 calls), so it locked nothing. Changed to
`zassert_equal(g_transceive_calls, 3u, ...)`. Mutation-proven twice, in
both directions. First with a standalone host harness linking the
production `chips/cc3501e/cc3501e_*.c` sources against this suite's own
fake-clock model: the fixed code gives exactly 3 calls; reverting
`poll_by_repeat()` to the pre-#1953 sleep-only form
(`git show 9efc3f033^:chips/cc3501e/cc3501e_core.c`) gives 6 and reddens
the `== 3u` assertion. Then on real `native_sim/native/64` twister against
a mutant module tree built from `git archive HEAD` with only
`cc3501e_core.c` replaced:

    MUTANT_TWISTER_RC=1
    Assertion failed at src/test_poll_deadline.c:187: ...
      test_zero_timeout_still_makes_one_attempt_1953:
      (g_transceive_calls not equal to 3u)
      "zero timeout_ms must make exactly one attempt, no more
       (got 6 transceive calls)"
    SUITE FAIL - 0.00% [cc3501e_poll_deadline]: pass = 0, fail = 2

At HEAD the same suite is rc=0, 2 of 2 passed. The sibling
`test_timeout_bounds_wall_time_1953` was already genuinely mutation-proven
(500 ms observed under the same revert, against a 200 ms budget plus 60 ms
headroom) — round-18 only found the second assertion under-specified.

**Bench-owed:** this touches `chips/**`, which is bench-held per #1937.
No HIL run backs this fix;
`docs/test-plan.md` records it `⏳ untested` pending a bench pass confirming
a worker-routed op against a genuinely wedged/stalled companion still
returns within its declared `timeout_ms` on real silicon.

**Coverage caveat:** `check_test_coverage.py` counts `alp_uptime_ms` as
covered, but every one of `tests/zephyr/cc3501e_*`'s eight suites defines
its OWN fake `alp_uptime_ms()` for link purposes (`cc3501e_poll_deadline`'s
on-demand stub clock, six sibling suites' shared fake-clock counter, and
`cc3501e_transport_lock`'s direct `k_uptime_get()` call) — under `tests/`,
that is the only place the symbol is ever CALLED, and it is always a test
double, never one of the three PRODUCTION backends.

COMPILED and EXECUTED are different questions, though, and neither real
backend is absent from a build: `src/common/stub/stub_core.c` (the Yocto
`clock_gettime` wrapper, `#if defined(__linux__)`-gated — true on the Linux
CI host regardless of `ALP_OS`) is unconditionally part of `alp::sdk` for
the Yocto and baremetal backends (`src/yocto/CMakeLists.txt:141`,
`src/baremetal/CMakeLists.txt:30`), so it is compiled into every Yocto host
test that links `alp::sdk`, plus 13 further `tests/yocto/CMakeLists.txt`
targets that `#include` a production `.c` file directly (dispatcher or
backend, to avoid a duplicate-definition link against `alp::sdk`) and add
`stub_core.c` alongside it for the same reason (e.g. `:171`
`alp_test_inference_latency`, `:1288` `alp_test_peripheral_gpio_self_close`).
`src/zephyr/delay_zephyr.c`'s `k_uptime_get()` wrapper is compiled into the
alp Zephyr module, and hence into every native_sim suite whose `prj.conf`
sets `CONFIG_ALP_SDK=y` (23 `*.conf` files today). What's actually true is
narrower than "not compiled": no test source under `tests/` CALLS `alp_uptime_ms()`
directly except the eight cc3501e_* fakes above, and none of those eight
sets `CONFIG_ALP_SDK=y` or links a Yocto build of `alp::sdk` — they
override the symbol rather than exercise it, so the real Zephyr and Yocto
backends sit in the linked binary unexercised. Only the clockless baremetal
accumulator (the non-`__linux__` branch) is genuinely uncompiled anywhere
today, per its own header comment: no non-Linux target builds this file
yet. The green coverage signal says nothing about whether the Zephyr or
Yocto backend is correct.

**Known-incomplete bug class (#1985, milestoned Backlog):**
`chips/cc3501e/cc3501e_wifi.c`'s `cc3501e_wifi_connect()` (`:393`, `:400`) and
`cc3501e_wifi_ap_start()`'s AP role-up confirm wait (`:551`, `:558`) still run
the pre-fix
`remaining -=`/estimated-`attempt_cost` pattern this issue fixed in
`poll_by_repeat()`, including the same false "a successful read costs
nothing" premise. Deferred to #1985 rather than folded in here: converting
either to an `alp_uptime_ms()` deadline changes the exact retry-attempt
counts `tests/zephyr/cc3501e_host_driver`'s `..._bounds_status_attempts_
on_wedged_transport_1382` and `..._healthy_poll_not_over_debited_1481`
assert, which needs re-deriving against the new model, not just re-running
— and both call sites are the same bench-held, bench-down `chips/**` this
fix itself cannot validate on silicon right now.

### Added — a gate enforcing that a changelog.d/ fragment's leading digits match the issue its own heading cites (#1957)

`changelog.d/README.md` documented a fragment filename's leading digits as the join key back to its GitHub issue, but nothing checked that a fragment's own `### ... (#N)` heading actually agreed with it. Four fragments on `dev` already disagreed: `changelog.d/1909.md`'s heading cited `(#1700)`, `changelog.d/1917.md`'s cited `(#1648)`, `changelog.d/1932.md`'s cited `(#1909)`, and `changelog.d/1940.md`'s cited `(#1848, #1814)` — the first of those is exactly what *caused* the collision #1941 exists to fix: the `1909.md` slot was occupied by the misfiled `#1700` fragment, so the real `#1909` fix had nowhere to go and was filed under the PR number instead.

`scripts/check_changelog_fragment_issue.py` now fails a PR the moment a fragment's heading cites exactly one issue number that disagrees with the filename's leading digits, or cites more than one and the filename's number is outside both the cited set and the span between the smallest and largest cited number. It deliberately under-flags: a heading with no `(#N)` at all (`changelog.d/813.md`, `changelog.d/853.md`, `changelog.d/1652.md`, `changelog.d/1949.md`) or citing more than one distinct issue where the filename falls inside that span (a genuine range, e.g. `changelog.d/1761.md`'s `(#1757-#1783)`, or a list) is left to hand review rather than guessed at — only the heading is scoped, never the body, where a fragment legitimately cites other issues in prose.

The four disagreeing fragments are renamed to their true issue numbers: `changelog.d/1909.md` -> `changelog.d/1700-seram-floor-diagnostic.md` (a disambiguating slug, legal since #1941's suffix rule, because `1700.md` is already taken), `changelog.d/1917.md` -> `changelog.d/1648-i2s-negotiated-rate.md` (same reason, `1648.md` is already taken), `changelog.d/1932.md` -> `changelog.d/1909.md` (no slug needed -- renaming the misfiled `#1700` fragment out of that slot frees it), and `changelog.d/1940.md` -> `changelog.d/1848-brd-i2c-housekeeping-documented.md` (`1848.md` is already taken by the other #1848 fragment, which this one withdraws the verdict of). `scripts/assemble_changelog.py --dry-run`'s output changes by more than the reordering these renames justify: `changelog.d/1909.md`'s old body carried a 9-line "Filed as `1932.md` (the PR number) rather than `1909.md`..." provenance paragraph that is now self-contradictory once the rename frees the plain `1909.md` slot, so that paragraph is dropped along with the rename. `changelog.d/README.md`'s leading-digit rule, previously documented as "convention, not enforced" pending this gate, now says the join key is enforced.

### Investigated — widening the issue-citation harvester past driver-status blocks was measured and declined (#1958)

`scripts/check_issue_citations.py` (#1950) harvests `#NNNN` citations only
out of a `driver_status:` field's trailing YAML comment and an `@par Driver
status:` Doxygen paragraph, by design. #1958 asked whether widening it to
`changelog.d/`, `CHANGELOG.md`, ADR prose and `notes:` blocks was cheap
enough to do, and said to check the same historical-marker heuristic against
the noise floor there first.

Measured, not guessed: applying the (#1963-tightened) historical/futurity
classifier to a naive `#NNNN` harvest over all four locations on the real
tree found 1627 citations, of which 17 would have hard-failed the gate. All
17 were read by hand; every one is a false positive. Changelog/ADR prose
narrates history in vocabulary the driver-status word list was never tuned
for -- `### Added — GD32 bridge ADC/PWM/DSP\n\nADC oversample + resolution
control (#494), ...` and `**Settled (#1244):** ...` and "#495, #494 and #496
... wasn't complete" all carry none of `_HISTORICAL_RE`'s marker words near
the citation, so each reads as a live blocker though every cited issue
closed long ago. Worse, `CHANGELOG.md`'s released sections describe a past
tree on purpose (the same carve-out `check_changelog_citations.py` already
makes for `path:line` citations there): a "the order code stays TBD
(#1241)" note that was accurate the day it shipped becomes an unfixable
false positive the moment #1241 later closes, with no way to "correct"
already-published history short of rewriting it.

Re-derivability: the decision-relevant column is the 17-total split across
the four locations -- 4 in `changelog.d/`, 7 in `CHANGELOG.md`, 5 in
`docs/adr/`, 1 in a `notes:` block -- which is re-derivable by anyone: grep
`#\d+` over those four locations, drop every hit whose clause is
`_HISTORICAL_RE`-historical, and hand-read what is left against the
snapshot. The 1627 intermediate total is a one-time observation from an
ad-hoc harvester script that was not committed; it is not independently
re-derivable without rewriting that script, and no claim in this fragment
depends on its exact value -- only the 17-total column drove the decision
to decline widening.

Widening would also have MISSED the one real drift already sitting in the
measured corpus:
`docs/adr/0023-ethernet-out-of-the-alp-surface.md:221` says "#1241, still
open" and #1241 is in fact closed -- exactly the defect class this gate
exists to catch. It is missed because the neighbouring clause's "#1244, now
fixed" trips `_HISTORICAL_RE` for the whole compound sentence, clearing
#1241's flag too. Widening would ship 17-for-17 false positives against a
`gate: true` merge-queue blocker to buy back one still-missed catch -- the
wrong trade for a gate whose stated bias is to under-flag.

Declined. Not widened; closing #1958 with this measurement rather than
leaving it open or landing the widening unmeasured. The ADR-0023 drift
found above is real and is fixed directly in this change: "#1241, still
open" became "#1241, now closed"
(`docs/adr/0023-ethernet-out-of-the-alp-surface.md:221` ("now closed (every AEN"))
since the repo's rule is docs change with
the code, not left for a mechanical gate that cannot make this call given
the false-positive rate above.

### Fixed — `_emit_extra_library_profile` could raise instead of returning its diagnostic, and a same-shaped crash sat ahead of it on the same path (#1961)

`scripts/alp_orchestrate/kconfig.py`'s `_emit_extra_library_profile` is
contracted to return a `#`-prefixed diagnostic line, never raise, when the
`extra_libraries[].profile:` file it walks is missing, unreadable, or
malformed. Its `try`/`except (OSError, yaml.YAMLError)` was narrower than
the failure modes of the I/O it wraps: `.resolve()` sat outside the `try`
entirely and raised `RuntimeError("Symlink loop from ...")` on a symlink
loop (`ELOOP`), and `read_text(encoding="utf-8")` raises
`UnicodeDecodeError` -- a `ValueError` subclass, not an `OSError` -- on
non-UTF-8 bytes, before the YAML parser ever runs.

The fix drops `.resolve()` entirely -- nothing downstream of it needs a
canonicalized path, only `read_text` does -- rather than widening the
`except` tuple to catch its `RuntimeError`. A real symlink loop still
fails, but via `read_text`'s own `OSError` (`[Errno 40] Too many levels of
symbolic links`), which the original `except (OSError, yaml.YAMLError)`
already caught; the `except` tuple only needed to grow by
`UnicodeDecodeError`. This is the same shape as tan-cli's relocated copy
(`python/tan/planner/kconfig.py`, tan-cli#1122), so the two now match.

The `kconfig.py` fix reconverges; `validate.py`'s does not. tan-cli's
`python/tan/planner/validate.py:180-181` carries the identical
unguarded `prof_path = (REPO / prof).resolve()` / `if not
prof_path.is_file():` this fragment's `validate.py` fix wraps, with no
`try`/`except` at all -- filed as tan-cli#1217 rather than folded into
this alp-sdk-only PR.

Separately, and load-bearing for reachability: `scripts/alp_orchestrate/
validate.py`'s `_validate_consistency` -- run by *every* `load_board_yaml`
call, i.e. every `--emit` mode including `--emit build-plan` (tan-cli's
documented planner fallback, `PYTHONPATH=<sdk>/scripts python -m
alp_orchestrate --emit build-plan`) -- does its own `(REPO /
prof).resolve()` + `.is_file()` on the identical user-supplied
`profile:` path, and runs strictly *before* the kconfig emitter above is
ever reached. Left unguarded, a symlink-loop or permission-denied
`profile:` still crashed `load_board_yaml` with an unhandled
`RuntimeError` / `PermissionError` regardless of the kconfig.py fix, so
the defect stayed reachable on tan-cli's own documented fallback command.

That guard's first cut (`except (RuntimeError, PermissionError)`) was
itself POSIX-shaped and still crashed on Windows: a real symlink loop
built with `ln -s` from WSL on an NTFS drive, driven through the real
CLI with Windows CPython 3.11.3, showed `.resolve()` returning
*without* raising at all, and `.is_file()` raising a plain `OSError`
(`WinError 1920`, "The file cannot be accessed by the system") -- not
a `RuntimeError` and not a `PermissionError`. The `except` tuple is now
`(OSError, RuntimeError)` (`PermissionError` is already an `OSError`
subclass), which covers both the POSIX shape (`RuntimeError` from
`.resolve()`) and the Windows shape (`OSError` from `.is_file()`) --
verified by re-driving the real CLI against a real symlink loop on
both platforms, not by widening the catch and trusting it. Both calls
are now wrapped and raise a normal `OrchestratorError` (the CLI's
usual clean exit-1 path) instead, on both platforms.

New `tests/scripts/test_kconfig_extra_library_profile_never_raises.py`
table-drives the eight shapes issue #1961's acceptance list + tan-cli's
sibling gate exercise (non-UTF-8 bytes, a symlink loop, a
permission-denied path, a directory where a file is expected, a parent
that is a file, malformed YAML, a missing file, a valid profile), a
mutation-proof regression guard against the pre-fix shape (monkeypatches
`pathlib.Path.resolve` to raise the `RuntimeError` CPython's own ELOOP
detection raises; against the SHIPPED `kconfig.py`, which drops
`.resolve()` entirely, the patch is inert and the assertions pass via
`read_text()`'s own already-caught `OSError` instead -- it proves
nothing about today's code by itself, only that reverting `kconfig.py`
to the pre-#1961 `.resolve()`-outside-`try` shape turns it red), and an
end-to-end check (`load_board_yaml` -> `_slice_alp_conf`) for the one
shape that survives board.yaml load-time validation. `tests/scripts/
test_orchestrate_libraries.py` covers `validate.py`'s half with three
tests, not one: `test_extra_libraries_profile_symlink_loop_clean_error`
monkeypatches `pathlib.Path.resolve` to the POSIX `RuntimeError` shape,
`test_extra_libraries_profile_permission_denied_clean_error` monkeypatches
`pathlib.Path.is_file` to the POSIX `PermissionError`/EACCES shape, and
`test_extra_libraries_profile_windows_shape_clean_error` monkeypatches
`pathlib.Path.is_file` to the Windows `OSError`/`WinError 1920` shape --
each scoped to its own profile path only (real unprivileged `os.symlink`
needs Developer Mode/admin on Windows, so none of the three can use a
real symlink loop directly). The third test is the one that actually
pins this round's fix: reverting the `except` clause to
`(RuntimeError, PermissionError)` leaves the first two green and turns
only the third red, which is exactly how the Windows gap shipped unseen
in the first place.

Initially scoped out, then folded in: `scripts/alp_orchestrate/orchestrator.py`'s
`_resolve_app_path()` (`cores.<id>.app:`) has the identical unguarded
`.resolve()` on a different user-supplied field. It was filed separately
as #1987 to keep #1961's review surface narrow, and is now fixed on this
same branch once the `profile:` shape had been reviewed -- see
`changelog.d/1987.md`. Both `_resolve_app_path()`'s `.resolve()` and
`_zephyr_app_dir()`'s two `.is_file()` calls carry the guard.

Round-17 review found the reachable half `profile:`'s fix did not cover:
`scripts/alp_orchestrate/loader.py`'s `_load_yaml` -- the function that
loads the `--input` board.yaml itself, every `load_board_yaml` call's
very first file access, before any per-field validation runs -- had the
identical unguarded `path.is_file()`, with no `try` at all. Proven with
the same real WSL-made symlink loop used above, driven through the real
CLI (`python -m alp_orchestrate --input <loop> --emit build-plan`) on
Windows CPython 3.11.3: `.is_file()` raised the same `OSError`
(`WinError 1920`) unhandled. `_load_yaml` now wraps `path.is_file()` in
`except (OSError, RuntimeError)`, same tuple and same rationale as
`validate.py`'s guard, raising `OrchestratorError` instead. Verified by
re-driving the real CLI against real symlink loops on both Windows and
WSL for both entry points (`--input` and `profile:`); all four now exit
1 with a clean one-line message, none crash.

`tests/scripts/test_orchestrate_loader.py` adds two tests against this
path: `test_load_board_yaml_input_permission_denied_clean_error` (POSIX
`PermissionError`/EACCES) and
`test_load_board_yaml_input_windows_symlink_loop_clean_error` (the real
Windows `OSError`/`WinError 1920` shape); mutation-proven red against
the pre-fix `_load_yaml`. Also fixes `test_orchestrate_libraries.py`'s
`test_extra_libraries_profile_windows_shape_clean_error`, whose
`OSError(22, "...")` construction only ever sets `.errno` -- `winerror`
stays `None` regardless of the first positional value -- so it matched
the real WSL/WinError-1920 shape by errno alone, not by winerror; now
sets `.winerror = 1920` explicitly to reproduce it faithfully.

`_load_json` (loader.py's sibling loader, used for the SoC spec JSON)
and the SKU-preset/SoC-path/board-preset existence checks a few lines
away in the same file carry the identical unguarded `.is_file()` shape,
but are reached only through metadata-root-relative, schema-bounded
strings (`som.sku`, `silicon:`, `preset:`), not a raw filesystem path a
caller supplies directly like `--input`/`profile:` -- left alone here,
same "narrower review surface" reasoning as `_resolve_app_path()`
above, not folded into this fix.

### Fixed — three Yocto `poll()` sites checked only `POLLIN`, so a torn-down fd hot-spun an RX thread instead of terminating (#1962)

`src/backends/can/yocto_drv.c`, `src/backends/rpc/yocto_drv.c` and
`src/yocto/peripheral_gpio.c` each `poll()` a socket/endpoint/line fd with an
**infinite** timeout and then guarded only on `revents & POLLIN`. When the
underlying fd is torn down or becomes invalid, `poll()` returns a POSITIVE
`rc` with `POLLERR`/`POLLNVAL`/`POLLHUP` set in `revents` — not `-1` — so the
existing `rc < 0` guard never sees it, the `POLLIN` guard just `continue`s,
and the very next `poll()` call returns immediately again: the RX/dispatcher
thread burns a full core forever, with no deadline to ever stop it (strictly
worse than the bounded MQTT case fixed under #1938).
`src/yocto/peripheral_uart.c:447` ("POLLERR | POLLNVAL") already got this
right; the three sites below now follow the same shape:

* `src/backends/can/yocto_drv.c:335` ("POLLERR | POLLHUP | POLLNVAL") —
  `_rx_loop()` now breaks (the same terminal action its existing `rc < 0`
  branch already takes) instead of `continue`-ing back into another
  immediate poll().
* `src/backends/rpc/yocto_drv.c:413` ("POLLERR | POLLHUP | POLLNVAL") —
  `rpc_rx_main()` now reports `ALP_RPC_LINK_LOST` (the same call its
  `rc < 0` and read()-EOF branches already make) and breaks.
* `src/yocto/peripheral_gpio.c:383` ("POLLERR | POLLHUP | POLLNVAL") — the
  shared `irq_dispatcher()`'s own wake_fd going bad is as fatal to the whole
  dispatcher as its `rc < 0` branch, so it takes the same exit path.
* `src/yocto/peripheral_gpio.c:413` ("POLLERR | POLLHUP | POLLNVAL") — a
  single pin's `line_fd` going bad (its gpiochip hot-removed, say) disables
  just that slot instead — treating one bad pin as fatal to the shared
  dispatcher would silently kill IRQ delivery for every other, unrelated
  pin too.

No new shared helper: the three sites take three different terminal actions
(thread-break, link-notify, per-slot-disable-vs-whole-dispatcher-exit), so a
one-line `revents & (POLLERR|POLLHUP|POLLNVAL)` mask read inline at each site
stays clearer than a new header for a single boolean check.

Host-provable without hardware: `tests/yocto/can_yocto_self_close.c`,
`tests/yocto/rpc_yocto_self_close.c` and
`tests/yocto/peripheral_gpio_self_close.c` each drive the real production
loop over a closed socket fd / closed pipe read-end (`POLLNVAL` is
deterministic on a closed fd number no other fd was allocated over yet), and
were run against the pre-fix code first: `wait_until()` /
`wait_until_irq_disabled()` time out and (for CAN/RPC) the RX thread never
joins, hanging the test binary until an external timeout kills it. Against
the fix, all three return within the bound every time.

**Owed on silicon** (`src/backends/**` and `src/yocto/**` are bench-held per
#1937; the AEN bench is down, #1883, 0-of-10 boots): observe, on a real
board, per file, that a torn-down transport — a SocketCAN interface removed
under a live `CAN_RAW` socket, an RPMSG endpoint torn down by a remoteproc
reset, a `/dev/gpiochipN` line fd invalidated by a hot-unplugged GPIO
expander — makes the corresponding RX thread / dispatcher slot terminate
promptly instead of hot-spinning a core. This change is author-only until
that bench pass runs.

### Fixed — the issue-citation gate's historical-marker word list under-flagged real blocker phrasings (#1963)

`scripts/check_issue_citations.py`'s `_HISTORICAL_RE` matched a marker word
(`via`, `closed`, `fixed`, `resolved`, ...) anywhere in the clause around a
`#NNNN` citation, so a genuinely still-blocking claim that merely named what
would eventually land it read as historical and was silently skipped.
Probed: 4 of 11 realistic phrasings did this --- "Still partial: DMA path not
yet **fixed** (#1234)", "Blocked on #1234 **until** the pad-routing rework
**lands**", "**Waiting on** #1234 to be **resolved** before this can go
complete", "Open: #1234 **must be done** before the driver is complete".
Each reads unambiguously as a live blocker to a human and each used to be
skipped because a marker verb sat somewhere after the citation.

New `_FUTURITY_RE` (`not yet`, `until`, `waiting on`, `must be`) overrides
`_HISTORICAL_RE` back to a live blocker when one of those four
negation/futurity cues is BOUND to the marker match -- adjacent to it, with
no coordinating conjunction sitting between them (`_CONJUNCTION_RE`) -- the
marker alone no longer wins outright. Checked against the real tree's 15
harvested driver-status citations: none contain any of these cues, so the
tightening flags zero currently-passing citations; the four fixtures above
are synthetic regression tests
(`tests/scripts/test_check_issue_citations.py`), not drawn from the tree.

An earlier version of this fix checked for the cue anywhere in the clause
(co-occurrence, not binding), which over-flagged: caught in review before
it shipped, reproduced 6 for 6 against `metadata/chips/dp83825.yaml`'s
real "... this manifest itself landed via #1241 ..." prose plus five
constructed variants of the same shape -- a marker attached to one citation
and a futurity cue attached to an unrelated LATER subject, joined only by
", and"/", but"/etc., wrongly flipped the citation to a live blocker. Fixed
by requiring the cue and the marker match it overrides to be free of an
intervening coordinating conjunction (see `_is_historical`); all four
fixtures above and all 6 false-positive reproductions were re-checked
against the fixed version.

Still a word-list heuristic, not comprehension, and still biased to
under-flag by design: a blocker phrased with a marker word and none of these
four cues (bare "not fixed", no "yet"), or with a cue reachable only through
a coordinating conjunction, still slips through unflagged. That residual
gap is the accepted cost of never flipping a historical citation into a
false positive -- see the module docstring's HISTORICAL section for the
full trade-off.

**Round-21 follow-up: a conjunction is not English's only pivot.** The
binding rule above treated only a coordinating conjunction (`and`, `but`,
`or`, ...) as separating a futurity cue from the marker it would override.
A parenthetical, a colon and an em/en dash open a new sub-thought just as
plainly, inside the same `.`/`;`-delimited clause. Measured against the
conjunction-only rule, two shapes still flipped a plainly historical
citation to a live blocker:

    "register access closed via #730 (the register map must be
     re-derived from the datasheet)."     -> BLOCKER, want historical
    "landed via #1241: the C driver must be reworked."
                                          -> BLOCKER, want historical

while the `, and` / `, but` / `;` shapes the conjunction rule already
covered stayed correct. `_SUBTHOUGHT_RE` (`(`, `:`, `--`, en/em dash) now
counts as a separator alongside `_CONJUNCTION_RE`.

Measured, not asserted -- 14 phrasings, 0 misclassified after the change
(4 blocker phrasings from this issue, 3 clean historical, 7 marker/cue
splits across every separator). The whole tree is unchanged at rc=0,
15 of 15 citations historical, 0 evaluated, so neither shape occurs in the
tree today; this closes the hole before prose reaches it rather than after.

Mutation-proven: dropping `_SUBTHOUGHT_RE` from the binding check fails
exactly the three new tests --
`test_futurity_cue_after_a_parenthetical_does_not_override`,
`..._after_a_colon_...`, `..._after_an_em_dash_...` -- and leaves the other
27 green (`3 failed, 27 passed`).

### Documented — the AEN A32 Yocto path (`meta-alif-ensemble`) does not build; docs no longer instruct a broken clone (#1967)

`meta-alp-sdk/README.md` and `meta-alp-sdk/conf/layer.conf` told users to clone Alif's
`meta-alif-ensemble` BSP at branch `scarthgap`. Verified 2026-09-05: the public repo has exactly
one branch, `devkit-ex-b0` — `scarthgap` does not exist, so the documented `git clone -b
scarthgap ...` failed outright.

Both files, plus a parenthetical aside in `docs/bring-up-aen.md`, now say plainly that the AEN A32
Yocto path is **broken today** and name why: no `scarthgap` branch (#1967), the one real branch
carries no `conf/machine/devkit-e8.conf` the carrier MACHINE `require`s (#1968), and the layer is
Yocto-series-incompatible with this repo's Scarthgap baseline regardless (#1971) — a corrected
branch name alone would not make the path usable. The `meta-alp-sdk/README.md` build-steps block
is kept (clearly marked BROKEN) only so it documents the failure mode rather than being deleted
and silently rediscovered. None of this touches the M55/Zephyr side of AEN801/AEN701, which builds
today on upstream Zephyr's `ensemble_e8_dk` board.

**#1968 and #1971 are not closed by this change** — they describe defects in the upstream
`meta-alif-ensemble` layer and this repo's `e1m-aen801-a32.conf` / `e1m-aen701-a32.conf`, which PR
#264 is rebuilding on a real base. This entry only stops the docs from lying about the current
state.

### Fixed — the AEN A32 machine confs stopped asserting a `meta-alif-ensemble` BSP branch that does not exist (#1968, #1971)

`e1m-aen801-a32.conf` carried an active, uncommented `require
conf/machine/devkit-e8.conf # meta-alif-ensemble @scarthgap`. Neither the
file nor the branch exists: a fresh clone of
`github.com/alifsemi/meta-alif-ensemble` (verified 2026-09-05) has exactly
one branch, `devkit-ex-b0`, whose `conf/machine/` carries only
`appkit-e7.conf`, `devkit-e5.conf`, `devkit-e7.conf` — no `devkit-e8.conf`
anywhere public (#1968). The `require` is now commented out, following the
sibling `e1m-aen701-a32.conf`'s existing honest pattern for the same
situation.

Both files' headers repeated the same false narrative — that
`meta-alif-ensemble` has a `scarthgap` branch matching this repo's Yocto
series. It does not, and even granting the missing file existed, the one
real branch is structurally incompatible with Scarthgap: its
`conf/layer.conf` declares `LAYERSERIES_COMPAT_meta-alif-ensemble =
"warrior zeus"` (Yocto 3.0, 2019) against `meta-alp-sdk`'s Scarthgap
(5.0.11) baseline (#1971). Both headers now say plainly that
`e1m-aen801-a32` and `e1m-aen701-a32` are non-buildable placeholders today,
cite #1968 and #1971 for the two independent reasons, and note that
whether Alif's login-gated support portal carries a Scarthgap-compatible
layer is unconfirmed. `meta-alp-sdk/README.md` and `docs/bring-up-aen.md`
already carried this corrected account (PR #2006); the two machine confs
were the only remaining spot still asserting the old, false one.

No functional change: `scripts/alp_orchestrate/orchestrator.py`'s
`YOCTO_MACHINE_UNBUILDABLE` denylist already refused both MACHINEs before
this fix and is untouched here. Neither MACHINE builds after this change
either — that needs a Scarthgap-compatible BSP that does not exist yet.

### Fixed — `bring-up-aen.md` called OSPI0-unpopulated a batch-wide fact; it's SKU-scoped and false for E1M-AEN803 (#1973)

`docs/bring-up-aen.md` carried a blockquote headed "This batch: the SoM's OSPI
memories are NOT populated," asserting as a present-tense property of "this
batch" that the OSPI0 NOR and HyperRAM are un-stuffed and that boot and app
storage run from on-die MRAM only. That was true of the **E1M-AEN801** SKU on
the earlier 2026-06-15 bench batch, but the maintainer confirmed on 2026-09-05
that the **E1M-AEN803** SKU now on the bench ("ospi memories are there — this
is a new Batch") fits both external memories, and the doc never said so. A
back-reference later in the same file, in the §5.1 OPTIGA note, repeated the
blanket framing ("like the un-stuffed OSPI memories") and its own header
("This bench batch (2026-06-15)") mixed a batch date into what is actually a
SKU-scoped fact.

Both are now scoped to the SKU rather than to an unqualified "this batch": on
E1M-AEN801 both `ospi_memories.ospi0.assembled` and `hyperram.assembled` are
`false` (`metadata/e1m_modules/E1M-AEN801.yaml`), so MRAM-only stands for that
SKU; on E1M-AEN803 both are `true` (`metadata/e1m_modules/E1M-AEN803.yaml`) —
the `IS25WX256-JHLE` NOR on CS1 and the `S80KS5122GABHM02` HyperRAM on CS0.
The OPTIGA note is corrected the other way: OPTIGA is `assembled: false` on
**both** SKUs (`metadata/e1m_modules/E1M-AEN801.yaml:123`,
`metadata/e1m_modules/E1M-AEN803.yaml:129`), so unlike OSPI0
that absence is not SKU-differentiated, and the paragraph no longer implies
otherwise by naming one bench date.

The chip-select question the original issue left open ("confirm before
documenting it") was previously stated backwards in this same doc (NOR on
CS0, HyperRAM on CS1) — a probe wired from that wording would have aimed a
NOR opcode at CS0 and could have misread a live NOR as dead. It is now
measured: on the **AEN803** bench module serial `2026W36-0002`, a JEDEC ID
read on OSPI0 CS1 drains `9d 5b 19 10` (ISSI, IS25WX256) at a 20 MHz test
rate (alp-sdk#2041), matching the R2 netlist (U10 -> OSPI0_SS1). `ser` is a
bitmask, not an index — `0x00000002` selects CS1. The same read at the
driver's 100 MHz DT-derived default comes back `4e ad 8c 88` with
`RISR=0x00000001` — a sampling error, not silence — so clock headroom above
20 MHz is still open; two points is not a sweep. The CS0 read in the same
session used a NOR opcode against what should be the HyperRAM and drained all
zero bytes; that is not a probe of the HyperRAM and this fragment claims
nothing about its behaviour.

The reason nothing can boot or XIP from either OSPI0 device yet is
`zephyr/drivers/flash/flash_ospi_alif.c` having no pinctrl support at all
(`grep -ci pinctrl` on that file returns `0`) — no consumer can apply OSPI0's
pad configuration. `examples/aen/aen-ospi-regcheck`'s overlay pinctrl is a
symptom of that driver gap, not the cause: its pads silently never take
effect regardless of which board's pad set it names. The doc's "target MRAM,
not OSPI" instruction for MCUboot/storage partitions is kept, re-scoped from
a population claim to this driver-readiness one, until the OSPI0 pinctrl work
tracked in alp-sdk#2041 lands. [Corrected post-#2041: that work has since
landed and the pinctrl gap described in this paragraph is closed --
`flash_ospi_alif.c` applies `PINCTRL_STATE_DEFAULT` in `ospi_alif_init()`,
bench-verified on two E1M-AEN803 modules. The "target MRAM, not OSPI"
instruction still stands, re-scoped again in `docs/bring-up-aen.md` onto the
reason that outlived it: the driver implements no `flash_driver_api`
(alp-sdk#915), so there is no read/write/erase path for a partition.]

Not touched, on purpose: `aen-ospi-regcheck`'s own PASS banner
(`examples/aen/aen-ospi-regcheck/src/main.c:449` ("so its PASS says nothing about whether a NOR/HyperBus part answers")) still prints "live XiP
HW-blocked (no part populated this batch)," and its file header
(`examples/aen/aen-ospi-regcheck/src/main.c:62-64` ("a JEDEC ID read (opcode 0x9F")) still asserts "the bench
unit has NO OSPI memory fitted" — both now contradicted by the measurement
above. A parallel unit owns that file under alp-sdk#2041; this change only
flags the staleness from `docs/bring-up-aen.md`'s §0 rather than editing the
example directly. [Corrected post-#2041: that unit landed. Both the banner and
the file header were rewritten there, so neither stale claim survives in the
example today.]
`metadata/e1m_modules/E1M-AEN801.yaml`'s chip-select fields were already
corrected, in commit `eff266b6` (PR #1964), not in #2007 — #2007 never
touched `E1M-AEN801.yaml` and carries its own "netlist-inferred, never
probed on E3-E7" caveat that does not apply to AEN801's already-probed
values. #1969 (the HyperRAM capacity-metadata discrepancy) is CLOSED as of
2026-09-12; its residual `memory_map`/`mram_main.base` gap is tracked
separately as #2053. #1970's missing TF-A HyperRAM driver stays open. No A32
Linux boot has ever been demonstrated on any AEN module, on OSPI or
otherwise.

### Fixed — the E1M-EVK I2C map asserted three addresses that a bench sweep contradicts (#1974, #1975)

Read-only I2C censuses on **two** E1M-EVKs (carrying `E1M-AEN803` serials
`2026W36-0001` and `2026W36-0003`) found three of
`metadata/boards/e1m-evk.yaml`'s recorded addresses silent on **both**, with one
part answering somewhere else entirely:

* **Neither TCAL9538 GPIO expander answered.** `0x72` (U35 main) and `0x71`
  (U37 PCIe) were both clean `-EIO` NACKs, and so was the `0x20` TCA6408A
  alternative strap. Exactly one PCA9538-register-compatible expander replied,
  at **`0x73`** (`A1=1, A0=1`), at power-on defaults — `OUTPUT=0xFF`,
  `POL=0x00`, `CFG=0xFF`, `INPUT=0xFB` (bit 2 low, a live input). Since U37
  drives the PCIe slot RST/WAKE/CLKREQ lines and the I2C-mux SEL, this is the
  first thing to suspect when those misbehave.
* **One INA236 did not answer on each board — but not the same one.** On
  `2026W36-0001` it was `0x4A` (U30, +5V); on `2026W36-0003` it was `0x41`
  (U31, +1V8), while that board's `0x4A` answered and fingerprinted correctly.
  Every responding part gave `MFG_ID 0x5449` ("TI"). A third board,
  `2026W36-0002`, later answered on **all six** (2026-09-07), so a missing
  INA236 is per-unit and *not* a batch trait — an earlier reading of the first
  two boards called "five of six respond" batch-wide and that is disproven.
  "U30 unpopulated" explains neither absence. Power characterisation must check
  which rails actually answer on the board in hand.

**Resolved: U35 is at `0x73`, and U37 is not fitted on this revision.** The
maintainer's EVK I2C schedule gives `TCAL9538RSVR U35 = 1110011` = `0x73`
(`A1=1, A0=1`), matching both boards — so this file was wrong on the address
*and* on the strap it recorded (`A1=1, A0=0` → `0x72`). The schedule lists only
one TCAL9538, and the maintainer has confirmed this EVK revision, built for
Alif, does not need the second expander: **U37 is not assembled**. That is why
`0x71` never answered, and why `0x20` (the TCA6408A alternative, bench-confirmed
on an earlier revision) does not appear either.

U35's address is corrected. U37 is marked `assembled: false` rather than
deleted — the footprint is real and other revisions populate it — which needed
a new `assembled` key on `i2c_device_entry` in
`metadata/schemas/board-preset.schema.json`, mirroring the one SoM presets
already have. Note the limitation recorded there: `gen_board_header.py` does not
read the key, so it still emits the address macro for an unfitted part.

Three entries initially looked like schedule-vs-silicon conflicts and none of
them were. BMP581 U14 (schedule `0x46`, boards `0x47`) is `0x47`: SDO is
connected to VIO on this EVK, which is that strap. TAS2563 U27 and U28 (schedule
`0x4C`/`0x4F`, boards `0x4D`/`0x4E`) are `0x4D`/`0x4E`. All three schedule
entries were slips, confirmed by the maintainer; the addresses in this file were
already right and are unchanged. Recorded because anyone comparing the schedule
against this file will hit the same three and should find the answer here rather
than re-deriving it on a bench.

**One hypothesis was tested and failed.** `EVK_PIN_IO_EXP_RST`
(SPI0_CS1 pad, E1M `N1`, Alif `P3_6`) was driven HIGH (reset deasserted) and then
pulsed LOW 10 ms → HIGH, on both boards. The I2C2 ACK set was byte-identical
across all three phases on both units — nothing appeared, nothing vanished. So
this is **not** a "deassert `IO_EXP_RST` before using the expanders" firmware
requirement.

The addresses are **deliberately unchanged**, but the reason has narrowed. It is
no longer "one board's strap is not the contract" — 2 of 2 units agree, so this
looks like a design/documentation mismatch rather than a per-unit assembly
defect. They stay as designed because what `0x73` physically **is** remains
unknown, so there is nothing verified to change them to. Each entry records what
was observed, when, and the issue tracking it.

One earlier claim needed qualifying rather than deleting: the `0x20` entry said
`BENCH-CONFIRMED 2026-06-16: read back config=0xFF + a live input port`. That
still stands for the board it was taken on, but it is not a property of every
EVK — on the 2026-09-05 board `0x20` was silent and that exact signature
appeared at `0x73`.

Which physical part sits at `0x73` is deliberately left unresolved: telling U35
from U37 requires driving an output, and writing to an unidentified expander on
a bus that also carries the identity EEPROM can move PCIe reset or display
control lines.

One of the two unexplained responders is now explained. `0x48` is the TAS2563's
**global address** per the datasheet, so it ACKs on any board with an amp
fitted. The census evidence already fitted: `MFG_ID(0x3E)=0x1000` ruled out an
INA236, and `REVID(0x7D)=0x10` at `0x48` was byte-identical to both fitted amps
at `0x4D`/`0x4E`. It is recorded so a future I2C census does not re-report it as
an undocumented device.

`0x58` remains genuinely unidentified — it is in neither the schedule nor this
file, and a pointer-free read returns all `ff` (alp-sdk#1976).

### Fixed — three I2C addresses the shipped docs, examples and headers still got wrong (#1974, #1976, #1978)

A bench sweep of the E1M-EVK and the on-module E1M-AEN803 contradicted three
addresses that were still asserted across public headers, metadata, examples and
docs. Each is corrected everywhere it appeared, not only where it was first
noticed.

- **The main TCAL9538 I/O expander (U35) is at `0x73`, not `0x72`** — 2 of 2
  boards ACK at `0x73` and are silent at `0x72` (alp-sdk#1974). The
  `EVK_I2C_ADDR_TCAL9538_MAIN` macro was corrected earlier; this sweep fixes the
  copies that had drifted from it, including a copy-paste snippet in
  `include/alp/boards/alp_e1m_evk.h` that told the reader to call
  `tcal9538_init(&io_exp, i2c_bus, 0x72)` — an address that answers on neither
  board. The snippet now uses the macro so it cannot desynchronise again. The
  second expander U37 (`0x71`) is marked NOT ASSEMBLED on this revision.
  `metadata/chips/tcal9538.yaml` gains the missing `0x73` strap row; its `0x72`
  row is kept, because `0x72` remains a legal strap for A1=1/A0=0.
- **`0x48` on this bus is the TAS2563 global/broadcast address**, not an
  unidentified device (alp-sdk#1976). `docs/tutorials/02-i2c-scan.md`'s
  expected-output table had no `0x48` row at all, so a customer running the
  documented scan saw an ACK the docs never predicted.
- **The on-module TMP112 answers at `0x40`, not its declared `0x48`, on 2 of 2
  modules** (alp-sdk#1978) — a batch property of the 2026W36 build, not the
  per-unit solder defect the example, its overlay and `docs/soms/aen.md` all
  described. That framing sent readers to inspect a board that has nothing wrong
  with it. The devicetree deliberately still declares `tmp112@48`: at the time
  of this sweep, `0x40` looked like it could not be a legal TMP112 strap
  address at all, so whatever answered there had not been shown to be the
  TMP112, and re-addressing the node would have encoded a guess. **Later
  correction:** per TI SBOS473L p.44, the BOM's exact orderable MPN for U20,
  `TMP112DIDPWR`, is X2SON (DPW), 5 pins ONLY — no SOT563-6 orderable carries
  that MPN — and per SBOS473L Table 7-4 the X2SON-5 "Address Variant Only"
  row straps ADD0→GND to `0x40`, so `0x40` is the DESIGN address for the
  part this board specifies, and the responder's TMP112-shaped register
  fingerprint matches that design rather than merely being consistent with a
  legal strap. What remains open is only *as-built*: nobody has confirmed
  the fitted package marking on a physical module against a current
  netlist, and BOM is not as-built. Either way the consequence stands — the
  stock `CONFIG_TMP112` driver does not bind on these modules, since it
  looks for the declared `0x48`, which now contradicts the `0x40` design
