DSI panel #2204 wires up for `aen-dsi-display`, rather than inventing a new
panel bring-up.

`CMakeLists.txt` now appends the `e1m_evk_rk055hdmipi4ma0` shield before
`find_package(Zephyr)`, but only for this app's own AEN M55-HP board targets
(`examples/connectivity/iot-dashboard/CMakeLists.txt:46`
("list(APPEND SHIELD e1m_evk_rk055hdmipi4ma0)")) — a regex match on `BOARD`,
resolved from a `-DBOARD=` cache entry or `$ENV{BOARD}` for a plain build, or
read out of the sysbuild cache file for a `--sysbuild` build (the AEN flow's
documented default — see `docs/_aen-runbook-section.md` and
`scripts/bench/aen/README.md`), because sysbuild does not forward `BOARD` as
a `-D` cache entry to the image build at all; Zephyr only resolves it inside
`find_package(Zephyr)`, too late for this regex. Skipped
when the caller already set `SHIELD`, so a different panel can still be
substituted, and a no-op on `native_sim` and every other target. `board.yaml`
drops the `st7789` chip entry it no longer needs — the panel isn't declared
there at all, since it has no `metadata/chips/*.yaml` manifest of its own and
arrives as a Zephyr shield instead
(`examples/connectivity/iot-dashboard/board.yaml:61`
("The DSI panel (RK055HDMIPI4MA0, Himax HX8394) has no")) — and every stale
ST7789/SPI-display comment in `prj.conf`, `native_sim.conf`, the
`native_sim` board overlay, and `src/main.c`'s bring-up diagram is corrected
to describe the DSI chain instead. The `spi` and `gpio` peripheral entries
`board.yaml` still declares are unchanged in substance: both were already the
CC3501E bridge's (SPI transport, WIFI_EN/nRESET control), not the display's.

`testcase.yaml`'s AEN scenario now names both AEN SKUs the bench farm
carries, matching how `pr-twister-aen.yml` shards by SKU
(`examples/connectivity/iot-dashboard/testcase.yaml:40-41`
("alp_e1m_aen801_m55_hp/ae822fa0e5597ls0/rtss_hp")), `build_only: true`
throughout, and carries its own `CONFIG_ALP_SDK_ALLOW_TEST_ENTROPY=y`
(#2192 — no Ensemble entropy driver exists yet, so the weak-RNG refusal in
`zephyr/CMakeLists.txt` applies here the same way it does to
`mqtt-telemetry`) on the scenario rather than in `prj.conf`, so a copy
scaffolded by `tan init --from-example` for real hardware still meets the
refusal. `pr-twister-aen.yml` adds `examples/connectivity/iot-dashboard` to
both `paths:` filter blocks, adds `zephyr/boards/shields/**`, `zephyr/drivers/display/**` and
`zephyr/drivers/mipi_dsi/**` (the shield and the CDC200 / DesignWare DSI
drivers it compiles into this app, none previously covered by this gate), and
adds the
example as the third `--testsuite-root` line in this job's (now
seven-root) list
(`.github/workflows/pr-twister-aen.yml:600`
("alp-sdk/examples/connectivity/iot-dashboard")) — besides `examples/aen`,
one of only two roots (with `camera-mjpeg-stream`, added by #2265) that
contributes a scenario to *both* SKU matrix legs, since mqtt-telemetry and
iot-fleet-ota remain AEN801-only.

Verified locally (Zephyr v4.4.1 with `zephyr/patches.yml` applied, Zephyr SDK
1.0.1 `arm-zephyr-eabi-gcc` 14.3.0, picolibc; plain twister for both SKU legs
plus one `--sysbuild` configure-and-link): `iot-dashboard` links for both
`alp_e1m_aen801_m55_hp/ae822fa0e5597ls0/rtss_hp` and
`alp_e1m_aen803_m55_hp/ae822fa0e5597ls0/rtss_hp` with the shield applied and
`CONFIG_ALP_SDK_CHIP_ST7789` gone from the generated config; `mqtt-telemetry`
and `iot-fleet-ota` still link for AEN801 unchanged.

**Review found this shipped no AEN board overlay at all (#2242).**
`board.yaml` declares `spi` + `gpio` for the CC3501E bridge
(`cc3501e_bridge_bringup()`, `src/cc3501e_bridge.c`, bus_id
`CC3501E_BRIDGE_SPI_BUS_ID` = 1, `alp_pins` WIFI_EN/NRST), but the shield
added above wires only the display chain — it does nothing for SPI1 pinmux
or the LP-GPIO control nets. Without a board overlay, `alp_spi_open(1)` and
the `alp_pins` array had no DT node to resolve on either AEN target: the
app compiled, but could never reach the CC3501E, on real hardware or in
CI's `build_only` scenario (the DTS just lacked the node — nothing caught
it because `check_example_board_overlay_parity.py` checks for a `boards/`
overlay only where one is declared, and none was). Two new overlays fix
this — the CC3501E bridge subset of `alp-console`'s bench-validated
wiring, no I2C2/RGB-LED (this app has no sensor-manifest bus of its own
here):
`examples/connectivity/iot-dashboard/boards/alp_e1m_aen801_m55_hp_ae822fa0e5597ls0_rtss_hp.overlay:69`
("cc3501e_spi: spi@48104000 {") and
`examples/connectivity/iot-dashboard/boards/alp_e1m_aen803_m55_hp_ae822fa0e5597ls0_rtss_hp.overlay:119`
("alp_pins: alp-pins {"). This also turns on real coverage from
`check_example_board_overlay_parity.py` (#2101, and its `#1009` class
check -- a `board.yaml`-declared core with no matching overlay) and
`check_example_board_overlay_content_parity.py` (#2198) for this
example's AEN801/AEN803 pair, neither of which had anything to check
before these files existed.

**Second blocker, found by the orchestrator's own review of this change's
first commit (73a6f2752), not the PR review: the C-side pad-mux poke was
M55-HE only.** `aen_lp_pads_enable_output()` -- the raw LP-GPIO pad-config
store that actually powers WIFI_EN/nRESET -- was guarded
`#if defined(CONFIG_SOC_AE822FA0E5597LS0_RTSS_HE)` only
(`examples/aen/aen-cc3501e-bringup/src/cc3501e_bridge.c:10`
("#if defined(CONFIG_SOC_AE822FA0E5597LS0_RTSS_HE) || defined(CONFIG_SOC_AE822FA0E5597LS0_RTSS_HP)")
shows the fixed guard). The HP boards select
`CONFIG_SOC_AE822FA0E5597LS0_RTSS_HP`, so even with the DT wiring above
present, the function compiled to an empty stub on every HP target and
WIFI_EN never powered the CC3501E -- a second, independent way the same
bridge was unreachable on HP. `ALIF_LPGPIO_PADCTRL_BASE` (0x42007000) is
not an M55-HE-local address: the shared upstream `pin-controller@1a603000`
node (`ensemble_common.dtsi`, included by both cores' SoC dtsi) declares
this exact window as its second `reg` range, and
`alp_e1m_aen801_m55_hp-pinctrl.dtsi` already muxes a different LP-GPIO pad
(P15_0, RTC_ALARM) from the M55-HP pinctrl driver through it, so widening
the guard to both cores is a straight compile-time fix, not a new
behaviour. This is the canonical copy; the fix propagates byte-identically
to every non-divergent copy `scripts/check_cc3501e_bridge_copies.py`
locks (15 copies including `iot-dashboard`'s own), and the equivalent
guard was applied by hand to the divergent `alp-console` copy, keeping its
other divergence. **This guard widening changes every HP build of every
AEN example that uses the bridge, not just iot-dashboard** -- it was
undetectable before because no example had an HP board overlay to build
against until this change added one. `mqtt-telemetry` and
`iot-fleet-ota` target `alp_e1m_aen801_m55_hp` too but still ship no
`boards/` overlay at all, so their `cc3501e_bridge_bringup()` still
returns `ALP_ERR_NOT_PRESENT_ON_THIS_SOC` on HP regardless of this guard
fix -- tracked in #2363, not fixed by this change.

Verified: both HP targets link with `west build`; `zephyr.dts` in each
build tree shows `spi@48104000` `status = "okay"` with
`pinctrl-0 = <&pinctrl_spi1>` and the `alp-spi1` alias resolved, sourced
from the new overlay rather than left undeclared; and disassembly of the
built `cc3501e_bridge.c.obj` for the AEN801 HP target shows
`aen_lp_pads_enable_output()` inlined into `cc3501e_bridge_bringup()` with
the real pad-config stores present (`movs r2, #35 @ 0x23` /
`str r2, [r3, #20]`), not an empty stub. None of this is bench-proven on
HP -- it proves the DT node and the pad-config store are both compiled
in and reachable, not that the CC3501E answers on real M55-HP silicon.

**Not proven, and not silently left implicit.** This is a `build_only`
compile check, nothing more:

- No silicon has run this image. There is no pixel-on-glass confirmation for
  this app's use of the RK055HDMIPI4MA0/HX8394 chain, and the display chain
  itself depends on #2204 (the shield), which as of this change is a draft PR
  whose own bench evidence is an M55-HE run, not M55-HP.
- The new CC3501E bridge overlays are HP twins of the bench-proven M55-HE
  wiring (`alp-console`, `aen-cc3501e-bringup`) — the SPI1 IRQ and the
  whole HP bridge path are unbenched, same BENCH-TBD caveat the M55-HE
  overlays already carry. Same for the widened pad-mux guard above: it
  makes the M55-HE poke run on M55-HP too, but only the M55-HE poke is
  confirmed on silicon.
- The build still only compiles because of the #2192 weak-RNG acknowledgement.
  That flag is bench-only; a production build on real hardware needs a real
  entropy source, which does not exist for AEN yet.
- The dashboard's own UI layout is unchanged at 240×320 and is not adapted to
  the RK055's 720×1280 panel — it draws in the panel's top-left corner.

### Fixed — `bench_jlink_run()`'s netns loopback bring-up failed silently instead of refusing (#2174)

`scripts/bench/aen/bench-env.sh:856` ("ip link set lo up 2>/dev/null || true")
tolerated a failed loopback bring-up inside the fresh network namespace
`bench_jlink_run()` masks every J-Link probe under. The header comment on
this same mitigation already documented the failure mode it exists for -- a
new netns starts with loopback DOWN and the J-Link DLL segfaults against it
-- but a netns where `lo` never actually came up (permission, a race, ...)
fell through to JLinkExe unverified.

The line now verifies the bring-up instead of trusting it.
`scripts/bench/aen/bench-env.sh:874` ("lostate=$(ip -o link show lo 2>/dev/null)")
reads the UP flag word `ip -o link show lo` prints, not
`/sys/class/net/lo/flags`: that sysfs file measured stale under an `unshare
--net` namespace with no explicit sysfs remount -- unchanged before and
after `ip link set lo up` -- while `ip`, going over netlink, always reports
the live namespace's real state. A still-down loopback now refuses, with
exit 9,
`scripts/bench/aen/bench-env.sh:876-877` ("bench_jlink_run: loopback did not come up in the fresh netns") --
the same isolation-did-not-take family the three neighbouring checks in this same subshell already use
(target-node-vanished, mask-took, exactly-one-J-Link-visible) -- reused
deliberately, not a new code. That family's raw exit never reaches a
caller's own process exit code: every call site wraps
`bench_jlink_run`/`jlink_run` with `|| true` and translates any failure via
`bench_jlink_assert_connected`'s missing-transcript check into its own exit
7, so this does not collide with `ram-run.sh`'s unrelated, internally
assigned exit 9 ("session 2's `mem8` itself failed").

**Review finding:** the verification itself needs its own guard.
`lostate=$(ip -o link show lo 2>/dev/null)` alone, under the subshell's
`set -e`, aborts the WHOLE subshell with a bare, unexplained `rc=127` the
moment `ip` is missing from the netns -- the command substitution
assignment's own failure trips `set -e` before the "did not come up"
message ever gets a chance to print. `command -v ip` is now checked FIRST,
explicitly:
`scripts/bench/aen/bench-env.sh:870` ("command -v ip >/dev/null 2>&1 || {")
refuses with
`scripts/bench/aen/bench-env.sh:871` ("bench_jlink_run: ip not found in the fresh netns"),
exit 9 again, the same family, before ever reaching the command
substitution that would otherwise abort silently.

Unit tests extract this exact check text out of the real script -- from its
own `set -e` onward, so the extracted copy exercises the SAME errexit
semantics the production subshell does -- and run it for real inside a
genuine fresh `unshare --net` namespace:
`tests/scripts/test_bench_jlink_run.py:393`
("def test_lo_up_lets_the_session_proceed(tmp_path: Path) -> None:"),
`tests/scripts/test_bench_jlink_run.py:403`
("def test_lo_staying_down_refuses_instead_of_silently_continuing(tmp_path: Path) -> None:"),
and `tests/scripts/test_bench_jlink_run.py:418`
("def test_lo_check_missing_ip_refuses_instead_of_a_bare_set_dash_e_abort(tmp_path: Path) -> None:").
Mutation-proven twice: reverting the UP-flag check makes the second test
fail (the session proceeds instead of refusing), and separately removing
the `command -v ip` guard makes the third test fail (a bare exit 127 with
no message, instead of exit 9 with one).

**This does not explain either observed crash class.** A 97-iteration soak
recorded two distinct shapes: a SIGSEGV (`rc=139`) and a glibc heap abort
(`rc=134`, `double free or corruption (top)`) inside the J-Link DLL itself --
heap corruption is a different mechanism from a null/invalid pointer against
a down loopback, and this change does not claim to fix either. It removes
one silent failure the evidence says is worth removing on its own merits,
independent of whether it ever caused a crash.

Closes #2174's narrowed in-tree scope. The identical failure-tolerant line
in `board-farm/bin/jlink-run.sh` is a separate repository this change cannot
reach, and any root-cause hunt for the heap-corruption crash stays out of
this issue.

### Added — `--fix` re-derives a drifted `path:line` citation from its anchor (#2175)

Merging `dev` into a branch shifts the files its `changelog.d/` fragments cite, so every
citation into a moved file drifts at once. Two failures follow, and only one of them
announces itself:

- A fragment **both sides edited conflicts, and neither side is right after the merge**.
  Measured across the AEN branches, the same citations were branch+6 and dev+9..+39 — the
  correct post-merge line was neither, so `--ours` and `--theirs` each produce a tree this
  gate reds, and a human resolving by picking a side picks a wrong answer that looks
  entirely reasonable.
- A fragment **only one side edited merges cleanly and goes silently stale** — no conflict,
  no marker, wrong line numbers. `git merge-tree` reporting `CLEAN` is not evidence that a
  branch's citations survived the merge.

`python3 scripts/check_changelog_citations.py --fix` re-derives the line number by locating
the anchor text in the cited file, then rewrites the citation in place
(`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:861` ("def _fix_one(frag: Path, text: str) -> tuple[str, list[str], list[str], int]:")).
The anchor is the only part of a citation that survives a code move, so it is the only thing
the fixer keys on.

The checker is unchanged. Without the flag its exit code and stdout are bit-for-bit what they
were — it is a required CI gate and owns the default — and the one default-path difference is on
stderr: the failure message now names `--fix` (below). `--fix` falls through to the checker
afterwards, so the exit code is always this gate's own verdict on the tree the fixer just wrote
(`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:1498` ("if args.fix:")). Fixer and checker share one
file and one parser deliberately: a fixer with its own notion of what a citation *is* would
drift from the gate and then confidently "repair" fragments into a tree the gate rejects.

What it refuses to do matters more than the rewrite, because a fixer that guesses is worse
than no fixer at all:

- **Never an un-anchored citation.** There is nothing to verify against, so re-pointing one
  would be guessing; it is counted and left alone. This is the half no fixer can repair, and
  the argument for making anchors mandatory rather than optional.
- **Never inside a fenced block** — that is where a fragment documents the anchor *syntax*
  with a deliberately made-up citation, as this gate's own release note does. Detection runs
  on the blanked copy from `_strip_fenced_blocks`, whose spaces preserve every offset, so
  the rewrite still addresses the real file
  (`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:888` ("stripped = _strip_fenced_blocks(text)")).
- **Never released history.** `changelog.d/` and `[Unreleased]` describe the current tree
  and are fixable; a released section describes a tree that no longer exists, and rewriting
  it would falsify what shipped. The released tail is split off and carried through
  unchanged (`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:1065` ("def _run_fix(fragments: list[Path]) -> None:")).
  Unchanged as LF text, not literally byte for byte — the read translates universal newlines
  and the write passes `newline=""` — which this repo pins to LF on every platform anyway.
- **Never the first match on an ambiguous anchor.** Drift is small and consistent, so the
  intended occurrence is the one nearest the originally cited line. First-match silently
  retargets the note to an unrelated occurrence, which is the exact failure this gate exists
  to catch. An exact tie goes to the **later** line, because the drift measured here is
  consistently positive — merging `dev` inserts code above a fragment's citations and pushes
  them down. Every ambiguous resolution is reported with its candidate lines and the one
  chosen (`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:996` ("new_start = min(hits, key=lambda h: (abs(h - start), -h))")).
- **Never an anchor it cannot find.** The anchored code is gone rather than moved, so it is
  reported for a human instead of re-pointed at a plausible-looking line.
- **Never a range that would run past the end of the file.** Clamping the preserved width to
  the last line is the refusal that looks most harmless and is the most dangerous: `:1-10`
  re-anchored on line 19 of a 20-line file becomes `:19-20`, a two-line range where the note
  claimed ten, and the re-check then *passes* it because the anchor is inside. A green
  citation asserting something nobody wrote is this gate's own failure mode manufactured by
  its own fixer, so it is refused and reported like the two above.

A citation that still resolves is left alone, and a range keeps its width: `4372-4376`
re-anchored at 4378 becomes `4378-4382`. The known limit of that carry-over: a wide citation
re-anchored on a one-line anchor emits an equally wide range over whatever now follows it,
and the checker only requires the anchor to be somewhere *inside* the range, so the tail of
a re-derived range is not itself verified. The width is kept anyway — it is part of what the
note claimed — and verifying it would take an anchor per line.

When the gate goes red it now names `--fix` in the failure message, which is the only place
the fixer can reach the person who is about to re-resolve those citations by hand.

Run against this tree, `--fix` rewrites nothing, touches no file, and leaves all seven
released-history warnings exactly where they are — which is the behaviour working.

### Fixed — the citation gate checks `CHANGELOG.md` even when `changelog.d/` is empty (#2178)

`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py` returned **0 without looking at `CHANGELOG.md` at
all** whenever `changelog.d/` held no fragments. It said so on stdout — "This is not a
pass; it means the directory is empty" — but an honest message and an exit code of 0 are
not the same thing, and every caller reads the exit code.

An empty fragment directory is not a quiet tree. It is the **release cut**:
`scripts/assemble_changelog.py:228` (`path.unlink()`) deletes every fragment once it has folded
them into `CHANGELOG.md`'s `[Unreleased]`, so the one moment `changelog.d/` is empty is
the moment several hundred citations have just landed in a location they have never been
checked in. The gate grades `[Unreleased]` exactly like a fragment — and skipped it
precisely there.

The early return is now reserved for the genuinely-nothing case, no fragments **and** no
`CHANGELOG.md` (`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:1515`
("if not fragments and not CHANGELOG.is_file():")). The `CHANGELOG.md` half runs either
way, and keeps its split: `[Unreleased]` describes the current tree and is graded as
**errors**; released history describes trees that no longer exist, so its broken citations
stay **warnings** — visible, never silently passed, never blocking. Collapsing that split
would make the gate unlandable without rewriting shipped release notes to suit today's
tree, which is the opposite of what a changelog is for.

This also closes an asymmetry #2175 left behind: `--fix` falls through to the checker so
its exit code is the gate's own verdict (`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:1498`
("if args.fix:")), which meant a release-cut tree with an unrepairable citation answered
`1` with the flag and `0` without it. Which verdict you got depended on how you asked.
Both now answer `1`.

Run against unmodified `dev` the change is inert: with 316 fragments present the widened
condition is unreachable, and the gate's output is byte-identical to what it was. The
behaviour only differs on the tree nothing was checking
(`tests/scripts/test_check_changelog_citations.py:602`
("def test_empty_changelog_d_still_grades_a_broken_unreleased_citation(")).

That tree was not hypothetical. Running the actual release cut against today's `dev` —
`scripts/assemble_changelog.py` then `scripts/check_changelog_citations.py` — went red
with 5 broken citations, all one class: `[Unreleased]` prose citing a `changelog.d/**`
fragment that the fold itself had just deleted
(`scripts/assemble_changelog.py:228` ("path.unlink()")). `--fix` correctly refused all
five, because no anchor can resurrect a path that no longer exists. This is unresolvable
by construction, not a broken citation — the same shape `_FOREIGN_PREFIXES` already
covers for a citation into another repository
(`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:431`
("_FOREIGN_PREFIXES = (")) — so a
`changelog.d/**` citation made FROM `CHANGELOG.md` itself is classified the same way, but
only when the file it names is genuinely gone: the skip is gated on `not (REPO /
rel).is_file()`, not on the citing document alone. Keying it on the source alone was itself
over-broad — a `changelog.d/**` citation whose target has **not yet** been folded away (a
hand-edited `[Unreleased]` entry citing a fragment that still exists) was being SKIPPED
too, the exact grading this fragment's own gate exists to keep, silently lost the same way
#1387's citation was. It is now graded normally, same as any other citation. The same
citation made FROM INSIDE A FRAGMENT is unaffected either way and keeps grading exactly as
before, because fragments legitimately cross-reference each other before the fold ever
runs. That target-aware branch, applied identically in `_check_one` and `_fix_one`, is
what keeps the release-cut tree green without also swallowing a citation whose target
survived.

### Fixed — an I2S interrupt the half-duplex `dir` gate cannot service left `i2s_dw_isr()` returning without changing anything, so the NVIC tail-chained straight back in (#2179)

**Defensive hardening, and the diagnosis is NOT confirmed on silicon.** Read
this entry as four independently-correct fixes, not as "the #2179 HardFault is
fixed". What is **measured**: `alp_i2s_start(RX)` on `i2s3` left the M55-HE
spinning in `i2s_dw_isr()` / `_isr_wrapper` on E1M-AEN803 serial 2026W36-0002
(Alif Ensemble E8) in 6 of 6 runs — `CFSR (0xE000ED28) = 0x00000000`,
`BFAR (0xE000ED38) = 0x00000000`, `CycleCnt` advancing, thread mode starved, no
fault taken, PCs decoded against the exact ELF that ran. Also measured: the
block is **not** in the SYSRESETREQ reset domain — `CER` (`0x4901700C`) and
`TER` (`0x4901702C`) both persisted at `0x00000001` across a J-Link `loadbin`'s
implicit SYSRESETREQ, and a RESETPIN reset (`RSetType 2` / `r` / `RSetType 0`)
cleared both to `0x00000000`. What is **inferred**: that an orphaned TXFE is
what the core was spinning on. A follow-up bench campaign passed 8/8 and never
reproduced the fault, so no `ISR`/`IMR`/`IPSR` capture exists to confirm it, and
none of the four changes below is claimed to fix the observed hang. Each is
worth making on its own terms; issue #2179 stays open for the capture that
settles it.

**The shape of the defect.** `i2s_dw_isr()` gates both data branches on
`dev_data->dir`, a SINGLE field this half-duplex driver keeps for both streams
(`I2S_DIR_BOTH` is `-ENOSYS`). A source that is asserted **and unmasked** but
whose branch the `dir` gate skips made that function read `ISR`, match no
branch, change **nothing**, and return. These sources are level-held, so the
interrupt is still asserted on return and the NVIC re-enters immediately. It is
the only path in this driver that never terminates: every path that actually
reaches `i2s_rx_irq_handler()` self-terminates within ~2 blocks against the
backend's 2-block slab (`src/backends/i2s/zephyr_drv.c`), so even an RXDA flood
clears itself.

TXFE while `dir == I2S_DIR_RX` is the reachable case. TXFE is asserted by an
**empty** TX FIFO — the resting state — whereas RXDA needs data to arrive; and
`i2s_enable_rx_interrupt()` clears only `RXDAM|RXFOM`
(`zephyr/drivers/i2s/i2s_dw.h:753-760` ("i2s_enable_rx_interrupt")), so `TXFEM`
left unmasked by an earlier TX phase survived into the next RX stream. That
asymmetry is why RX-after-TX is the exposed ordering and TX-after-RX is not.

**Four sites, all in `zephyr/drivers/i2s/i2s_dw.c`.**

- **`i2s_dw_isr()` — the root-cause guard.** It now computes `ISR & ~IMR` on
  entry (`ISR` and `IMR` share a bit layout, and `IMR` is mask-to-disable, so
  that is exactly the set of sources holding the line up), each branch clears
  the bit it services, and anything left at the bottom is **masked**
  (`zephyr/drivers/i2s/i2s_dw.c:933` ("unserviced = int_status & ~i2s_get_interrupt_mask(i2s);")).
  Masking is the one action guaranteed to change the interrupt condition, so
  the function can no longer return without having changed it. Note that adding
  a clear inside `i2s_tx_irq_handler()`/`i2s_rx_irq_handler()` does **not**
  close this — on the unserviced path the handler is never called at all. The
  mask is not lost: `i2s_enable_tx_interrupt()`/`i2s_enable_rx_interrupt()`
  unmask again on that direction's next `tx_stream_start()`/`rx_stream_start()`.
  A source that IS serviced is never masked, so both working single-direction
  paths behave exactly as before.
- **`rx_stream_start()` / `tx_stream_start()` — the same defect at its source.**
  Each already disabled the OTHER direction's channel on every start but left
  that direction's interrupts unmasked; disabling the TX channel does not
  deassert TXFE, since an empty FIFO is exactly what asserts it. Both now mask
  the opposite direction's `IMR` bits alongside the channel disable
  (`zephyr/drivers/i2s/i2s_dw.c:1288` ("mask TX's interrupts alongside the TX channel")
  and `zephyr/drivers/i2s/i2s_dw.c:1413` ("mask RX's interrupts alongside the RX channel")).
  No behaviour change for a TX stream that is still meant to run: `dir` has
  already been repointed to `I2S_DIR_RX` by the `i2s_dw_configure(I2S_DIR_RX)`
  that precedes any RX start, so `i2s_tx_irq_handler()` was unreachable from
  there on regardless — see this file's header for that known full-duplex gap,
  which this change makes explicit rather than widening.
- **`i2s_dw_configure()` assigned `dev_data->dir` before validating it.** It was
  the first statement in the function, so a call that then failed — `-ENOSYS`
  for `I2S_DIR_BOTH`, `-EINVAL` for an unknown direction, `-EINVAL` for an
  invalid stream state — still repointed the only field `i2s_dw_isr()` consults,
  permanently, while changing nothing else. `I2S_DIR_BOTH` is the worst of the
  three: it leaves `dir` matching **neither** ISR branch, so every subsequent
  I2S interrupt is unserviced. The assignment now happens only once the call is
  committed to (re)configuring a stream
  (`zephyr/drivers/i2s/i2s_dw.c:397` ("dev_data->dir = dir;")).
- **`i2s_dw_initialize()` armed the NVIC before masking.** `i2s->irq_config()`
  (`IRQ_CONNECT` + `irq_enable`) ran two statements *before* the mask writes,
  with `dev_data->dir` fresh from BSS as `0` (== `I2S_DIR_RX`) and no stream
  configured at all. Since the block survives SYSRESETREQ (measured above), a
  fresh image inherits the previous one's `IER`/`IMR`/`IRER`/`ITER`/`RER`/`TER`.
  `IER`/`IRER`/`ITER`/`RER`/`TER` are now quiesced and every interrupt masked
  **before** `irq_config()`
  (`zephyr/drivers/i2s/i2s_dw.c:1051` ("quiesce the block and mask every interrupt")),
  and the two `k_sem_init()` calls move above it for the same reason (both ISR
  handlers `k_sem_give()` those semaphores). `CER` is deliberately **not**
  cleared: `i2s_enable_controller()` still sets `CER.CLKEN`, just a few
  statements later, so #2149's and #2150's shared invariant — "`CER.CLKEN`
  reads 1 from `i2s_dw_initialize()` onward" — is unchanged.

**Not a change to the half-duplex contract.** `I2S_DIR_BOTH` still returns
`-ENOSYS`, `dev_data->dir` is still a single field, and the two full-duplex gaps
#2150 phase 1 recorded in this file's header are unchanged in substance — the
first is now worded to include the interrupt masking as well as the channel
disable. TX-only and RX-only streaming behave exactly as before.

**Tests.** `tests/unit/i2s_dw_underrun` — the suite that compiles
`zephyr/drivers/i2s/i2s_dw.c` directly into its own translation unit against a
RAM-backed `struct I2S_Type` — gains seven cases and now drives `i2s_dw_isr()`
and `i2s_dw_initialize()` by name rather than one layer below them:
`test_isr_txfe_with_dir_rx_masks_txfe`, `test_isr_rxda_with_dir_tx_masks_rxda`,
`test_isr_rxda_with_dir_rx_is_serviced_not_masked` (the no-regression half: a
guard that simply masked everything asserted would pass the first two while
killing a working RX stream on its first interrupt),
`test_rx_start_masks_tx_interrupt`, `test_tx_start_masks_rx_interrupt`,
`test_failed_configure_leaves_dir_unchanged`, and
`test_initialize_quiesces_before_arming_irq` — the last reading the register
state captured **inside** a fake `irq_config()` callback, since the instant the
NVIC is armed is the only point at which the ordering is observable. `ISR` is
declared `__IM` (`volatile const`), so presenting an asserted source casts the
qualifier away through `uintptr_t` rather than a bare `(uint32_t *)`: this suite
is the first to compile the driver on a 64-bit host
(`native_sim/native/64`), where that distinction matters. The fake
`clock_control` device also gained a `struct device_state`, since
`i2s_dw_initialize()`'s `device_is_ready()` dereferences `dev->state`
unconditionally.

**Mutation table** — each site reverted individually, suite re-run, site
restored:

| site reverted | expected RED | observed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `i2s_dw_isr()` unserviced-source mask | `test_isr_txfe_with_dir_rx_masks_txfe`, `test_isr_rxda_with_dir_tx_masks_rxda` | as expected |
| `rx_stream_start()` `i2s_disable_tx_interrupt()` | `test_rx_start_masks_tx_interrupt` | as expected |
| `tx_stream_start()` `i2s_disable_rx_interrupt()` | `test_tx_start_masks_rx_interrupt` | as expected |
| `dev_data->dir` assignment moved back to the top of `i2s_dw_configure()` | `test_failed_configure_leaves_dir_unchanged` | as expected |
| `i2s_dw_initialize()` ordering restored (`irq_config()` before the masks) | `test_initialize_quiesces_before_arming_irq` | as expected |

**Bench check still owed**, and the capture that would settle the diagnosis, on
an AEN EVK bench unit with the core halted after a reproduction: `IPSR` and NVIC
`IABR4` (`0xE000E310`) bit 16 to identify the instance (`i2s3` is
`interrupts = <144 3>`, so `IPSR` `160` / `0xA0`), then `IMR` (`0x49017038`'s
neighbour `0x4901703C`) and `ISR` (`0x49017038`) to compute `ISR & ~IMR`, then
`TER` (`0x4901702C`), `RER` (`0x49017028`), `IRER` (`0x49017004`), `ITER`
(`0x49017008`). `ISR & ~IMR` bit 4 (TXFE) set with `dir != 1` confirms the
mechanism above. **Keep any J-Link memory window off `0x49017020`-`0x49017044`
while gathering that evidence**: `ROR`/`TOR` are clear-on-read (reading them
*is* the overrun clear), `LRBR`/`RRBR` and `RXDMA` each pop the RX FIFO on read,
and `0x49017020`/`0x49017024` are `LTHR`/`RTHR` on write — writing them pushes
TX data and deasserts TXFE, erasing the fault.

**Separate finding, not addressed here.** Both in-tree `i2s3` overlays declare
**TX-only pinmux** — `PIN_P9_3__I2S3_SDO_A`, `PIN_P9_4__I2S3_SCLK_A`,
`PIN_P9_5__I2S3_WS_A`, with SDI (`P9_2`) explicitly not declared. Any RX probe
reusing either unchanged has no SDI pad muxed at all, which matters
independently of this hang.

### Added — E8 custom MPU table now supports `zephyr,flash = &sram0` (#2180)

`zephyr/soc-bridge/alif/mpu_regions_e8.c` rejected any build whose code was
linked into SRAM0 (`BUILD_ASSERT`: flash base had to be the ITCM or MRAM
slot-0 base), so SRAM0-linked images could not be built for bench
experiments such as warm re-entry. When `zephyr,flash` resolves to `sram0`
the table now adds an `SRAM0` region (base and size from the `sram0` node,
executable, read-only, cacheable normal memory -- the same attributes as the
`ITCM` entry). Data must then live in DTCM (`zephyr,sram = &dtcm`). The
region is compiled out in every other configuration: the ITCM build's
`zephyr.bin` is byte-identical (`cmp`) to one built from `origin/dev`, and MRAM
builds are untouched.

Verified by building `aen-sdhc-probe` for
`alp_e1m_aen803_m55_he/ae822fa0e5597ls0/rtss_he` with `-Werror` in the ITCM
variant and an SRAM0-code variant (code `LOAD` at `0x02000000`). Not yet run
on silicon.

Refs #2180; the warm re-entry measurement is still to do.

### Added — aen-sdhc-probe captures the registers sdhc_dwc reset() should restore (#2181)

`sdhc_dwc_reset()` re-applying the DWC SDHC controller's configuration was
unmeasured on real silicon: no before/after capture existed for the
registers `sdhc_dwc_set_def_config()` programs at init. #2122 already made
`sdhc_dwc_reset()` re-call `sdhc_dwc_set_def_config()` after its
`SW_RST_ALL`, unconditionally, so RESTORED is the expected reading of
today's code; this is verification of #2122's fix against silicon, not a
demonstrated bug.

Changes:
- `examples/aen/aen-sdhc-probe/src/sdhc_reset_capture.h` — new
  `struct sdhc_reset_regs` (the seven registers the issue names), a pure,
  host-testable `sdhc_reset_regs_equal()`, and
  `sdhc_reset_regs_matches_def_config()` — the primary check, since
  `sdhc_dwc_init()` already calls `sdhc_dwc_reset()` at `POST_KERNEL`
  before `main()` runs, so a capture taken at `main()` entry is itself
  post-`set_def_config()`, not pre-reset; comparing it to the post-probe
  capture alone could never catch a silently no-op `set_def_config()`.
- `examples/aen/aen-sdhc-probe/src/main.c` — new PROBE 3, only compiled on
  a board where `sdhc0` is enabled: captures the register set at `main()`
  entry (boot state), calls `sdhc_hw_reset()`, captures again, and checks
  the after-capture against `set_def_config()`'s fixed values (RESTORED /
  NOT RESTORED) as the primary verdict, with the before/after comparison
  (MATCH/MISMATCH) as a secondary check. Produces the evidence for a later
  bench run; this change does not itself run on silicon.
- `tests/unit/sdhc_reset_regs_compare/` — native_sim unit test pinning
  both `sdhc_reset_regs_equal()` and `sdhc_reset_regs_matches_def_config()`
  without hardware.

Still open: the actual before/after register values on real silicon. If NOT
RESTORED is confirmed there, that would be a #2122 regression worth its own
issue, not a gap in `sdhc_dwc_reset()`'s current source.

### Fixed — the TAS2563 fault-IRQ unmask (#2165/#2140) now has a production caller and a bench discriminator (#2182)

At #2165's head `tas2563_configure_fault_pin()`'s `INT_MASK0` unmask had no
production caller anywhere in the tree -- only its own definition and a
ZTest against the fake existed -- so the read-modify-write it performs had
never actually run against silicon. Closing that needed splitting the
function, adding a caller, and building a probe that could tell a correct
read-modify-write apart from a blind write landing on the same byte.

`tas2563_configure_fault_pin()` is now a thin wrapper around a new
`tas2563_arm_fault_irq(tas2563_t *ctx, bool chip_internal_pullup)`
(`include/alp/chips/tas2563.h:801` ("tas2563_arm_fault_irq(tas2563_t *ctx, bool chip_internal_pullup);"),
implemented at `chips/tas2563/tas2563.c:626` ("alp_status_t tas2563_arm_fault_irq(tas2563_t *ctx, bool chip_internal_pullup)")):
the chip-only half -- page select, `MISC_CFG1.IRQZ_PU`, `INT & CLK
CFG.IRQZ_PIN_CFG` and the `INT_MASK0[2]` clear
(`chips/tas2563/tas2563.c:647` ("return reg_update(ctx, TAS2563_REG_INT_MASK0, TAS2563_INT_MASK0_TDM_CLOCK, 0u);")),
with no GPIO touched and `ctx->irq_n` left unbound. `tas2563_configure_fault_pin()`
(`chips/tas2563/tas2563.c:651` ("tas2563_configure_fault_pin(tas2563_t *ctx, alp_gpio_t *irq_n, bool chip_internal_pullup)"))
now only configures the host pin, calls the new function, and binds
`ctx->irq_n` -- unchanged behaviour for every existing caller. This exists
for boards where the fault pin is not reachable via `alp_gpio` and the
caller owns it directly; on a shared IRQZ net the unmask is per chip, so
every amp sharing the net needs its own call. Three new ZTests cover the
split (`tests/zephyr/chips/src/test_audio.c:757` ("ZTEST(alp_chips, test_tas2563_arm_fault_irq_rejects_uninitialised)"),
`:767` ("ZTEST(alp_chips, test_tas2563_arm_fault_irq_unmasks_tdm_clock_error)"),
`:791` ("ZTEST(alp_chips, test_tas2563_arm_fault_irq_leaves_irq_n_unbound)")); the
existing `configure_fault_pin` tests are unchanged and still pass.

`examples/aen/aen-evk-demo`'s TAS2563 phase ("Phase 11") is now that
production caller: right after `tas2563_configure_i2s()`, every
initialised amp gets `tas2563_arm_fault_irq(&amps[i], false)`
(`examples/aen/aen-evk-demo/src/main.c:4459` ("alp_status_t arm_rc = tas2563_arm_fault_irq(&amps[i], false);")),
`false` because the 0x4D/0x4E pair share IRQZ on P5_0 behind the R124
external pull-up
(`metadata/boards/e1m-evk.yaml:345` ("R124 a fitted 10 kOhm pull-up")),
with the rc printed per amp. The phase's step-list header comment
(`examples/aen/aen-evk-demo/src/main.c:3721` ("*   6. Arm each amp's fault IRQ -- tas2563_arm_fault_irq() on every"))
gains that step and renumbers every step after it. This is now the only
production caller of either function in the tree.

A new compile-time-gated bench build, `ALP_AEN_EVK_DEMO_PROBE_FAULT_PIN`
(`examples/aen/aen-evk-demo/CMakeLists.txt:27` ("set(ALP_AEN_EVK_DEMO_PROBE_FAULT_PIN OFF CACHE BOOL")),
OFF by default and mirroring `firmware-update-log`'s
`ALP_AEN_UPDATE_LOG_FIREWALL_PROBE` gate, replaces the plain call above
with a seeded read-modify-write discriminator
(`examples/aen/aen-evk-demo/src/main.c:3942` ("static void probe_fault_pin_seeded_rmw(tas2563_t                *amp,")):
`INT_MASK0`'s POR (`FCh`) and the post-arm value (`F8h`) differ only in
bit 2, so a blind write is indistinguishable from a correct RMW unless the
register is seeded first -- seeding to `FFh` makes a correct RMW land on
`FBh` and a blind write land on `F8h`. Seeding is safe because
`tas2563_init()` still has both amps in software shutdown at this point.
The register is then restored to its POR value and re-armed, and the
restore is only trusted once a readback confirms it. Every seed/restore
sub-step is attempted regardless of the previous one's return code, and
the restore always runs even when the seed step itself could not be
verified: this bus has been observed failing open (ACKing every address
and echoing the register address back as read data), so a write can land
even when its own readback says otherwise -- bailing out early would skip
the restore and leave `INT_MASK0` at whatever the seed write left it. An
amp whose restore cannot be verified is excluded both from the stimulus
below and from the (currently unreachable with playback off)
`tas2563_resume()` path
(`examples/aen/aen-evk-demo/src/main.c:4642` ("if (!amp_fault_pin_restore_ok[i]) {")).

When the probe's restore verifies -- and only then, and only once this
amp's own `TAS2563_AMP_LEVEL_MIN` write (phase step 5), I2S configure
(step 6) and the shared `AMP_FAULT` pin's own pinctrl/gpio configure
(step 3) have all also returned success -- the same build runs a
deliberate TDM-clock-fault stimulus
(`examples/aen/aen-evk-demo/src/main.c:4039` ("static void probe_fault_pin_stimulus(tas2563_t                *amp,")):
the inverse of #2146's rule, switching an amp `ACTIVE` with no I2S clock
started at all, on purpose, to prove the unmasked fault reaches both
`tas2563_read_faults()` and the `AMP_FAULT` pin. The pin is polled up to
three times (+10/+50/+200 ms), breaking on the first asserted reading
rather than always waiting out all three delays, and every raw pin read
(idle, poll, after-clear) is routed through the same `amp_fault_pin_verdict()`
helper the rest of the phase uses, so an invalid read (a negative errno,
not 0 or 1) counts as a failure rather than silently comparing false.
If `INT_LTCH3` bit 3 (`DC_DETECT`) latches instead, the stimulus does NOT
call `tas2563_clear_faults()` -- the latch is left standing as evidence --
switches the amp to `SHUTDOWN` (retried once if the first attempt does not
return `ALP_OK`), and sets a phase-wide abort flag: no later amp in the
same run gets the stimulus (its own seeded-RMW probe still runs, since
that half never leaves software shutdown), and the phase fails via
`ctx->note` once teardown and idle-restore have still run unconditionally.
Every `SHUTDOWN` the stimulus issues is now captured and retried once,
never a bare `(void)`, and a `SHUTDOWN` that still does not return
`ALP_OK` after the retry is itself an abort condition. Each amp prints one
greppable summary line,
`"[evkdemo] FAULTPIN amp=0x.. seed=0x.. rmw=0x.. restore=0x.. stim_pin=.. ltch=0x........ verdict=PASS|FAIL"`
(`examples/aen/aen-evk-demo/src/main.c:4449` ("FAULTPIN amp=0x%02x seed=0x%02x rmw=0x%02x restore=0x%02x")),
and the phase's own return value now reflects that verdict: any amp whose
probe or stimulus did not PASS fails the phase, the same as an unarmed
`tas2563_arm_fault_irq()` now fails the phase in the default (non-probe)
build. `PAGE`/`INT_MASK0` are re-declared locally in the demo at their raw
register addresses (SLASET3D §7.5.2 p.65 / §7.5.28 p.77) rather than
exposed as a new driver accessor -- this stays a one-shot bench
discriminator, not a second app-reachable way to poke the chip. A new
`testcase.yaml` scenario
(`examples/aen/aen-evk-demo/testcase.yaml:118` ("alp_sdk.examples.aen.evk_demo.probe_fault_pin.aen:"))
builds the flag ON so a regression in this block does not go unbuilt by
CI, mirroring `firmware-update-log`'s own `..._PROBE` scenario; both
remain `build_only`, since the probe's verdict only means something on
the bench.

**Verification: measured on silicon.** E1M-AEN803 serial 2026W36-0002,
`examples/aen/aen-evk-demo` built with `ALP_AEN_EVK_DEMO_PROBE_FAULT_PIN=ON`
for the M55-HE and RAM-run with playback off, amps at
`TAS2563_AMP_LEVEL_MIN`, no I2S started. Both amps, first run:

```
FAULTPIN amp=0x4d seed=0xff rmw=0xfb restore=0xf8 stim_pin=0 ltch=0x80000004 verdict=PASS
FAULTPIN amp=0x4e seed=0xff rmw=0xfb restore=0xf8 stim_pin=0 ltch=0x80000004 verdict=PASS
```

`rmw=0xfb` from a `0xff` seed proves `tas2563_arm_fault_irq()` performs a
read-modify-write (a blind write would read back `0xf8`). The pin read
not-asserted at idle, asserted by the first +10 ms poll once the amp went
`ACTIVE` with no clock, and released after `SHUTDOWN` + clear; the latch
word carried `TAS2563_FAULT_TDM_CLOCK` (`0x00000004`) and, on the first
activation after `tas2563_init()`, `TAS2563_FAULT_DEVICE_POWER_DOWN`
(`0x80000000`, the init-time shutdown; a second run that cleared the
latch first read `ltch=0x00000004`). `DC_DETECT` never latched.

The premise part 3(b) of the issue questioned -- `INT_MASK` gates the pin,
not the latch -- was measured directly in a one-off variant of the same
run that applied the identical stimulus BEFORE arming, with `INT_MASK0` at
its POR value:

```
MASKED amp=0x4d mask0=0xfc act=0 pin_raw=1 ltch=0x80000004 shut=0
MASKED amp=0x4e mask0=0xfc act=0 pin_raw=1 ltch=0x80000004 shut=0
```

With the TDM clock fault masked, `INT_LTCH0[2]` still latched while the
pin stayed high; unmasked, the same stimulus pulled it low. That settles
the contradiction in `changelog.d/2140.md` in favour of the latch: the
earlier "the flag read `0x00000000`" sentence there is withdrawn (see that
fragment), and the `0x80510004` word the issue cites as the original "masked
events still latch" reading (both amps, `INT_MASK0` at POR) decodes as `TAS2563_FAULT_TDM_CLOCK | TAS2563_FAULT_DEVICE_POWER_UP |
TAS2563_FAULT_PLL_LOCK | TAS2563_FAULT_BOOST_CLOCK |
TAS2563_FAULT_DEVICE_POWER_DOWN` -- power-sequencing events plus a TDM
clock fault latched while masked, consistent with the measurement above.
Part 3(a) (#2165's PR body naming a non-existent
`examples/aen/aen-i2s-tas2563-probe` and disclaiming the register-`0x11`
accessor it in fact shipped) concerns a merged PR's description, not the
tree; it is corrected by a comment on #2165.

Separately, #2182's bench notes also ask this fix to enforce "digital
volume <= 128" as a speaker-safety guard. That cannot be done from inside
the driver -- there is no digital-volume accessor on `tas2563_t`, only the
demo's own `alp_audio_out_set_volume()` on the I2S side -- and it is moot
here regardless: the TDM-clock-fault stimulus above never starts I2S or
queues any audio data, so no digital volume is ever in play during it. The
lever this stimulus does depend on is `TAS2563_AMP_LEVEL_MIN` (phase step
5), the amp's own analog-gain floor -- set on every initialised amp AFTER
`tas2563_init()` (step 4) parks it in software shutdown, and now checked
per amp (`amp_level_min_ok[i]`) before the stimulus is allowed to run on
that amp at all, rather than assumed.

### Fixed — a double-delimited changelog anchor silently downgraded to range-checked-only instead of failing (#2184)

`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py`'s `_ANCHOR` regex could not parse an
anchor written with **both** delimiters at once — `` (`"text"`) `` or
`` ("`text`") ``. The opening character class consumes one delimiter, and the
capture group then refuses the very next character because it is the OTHER
delimiter, so the whole match fails at position zero. The citation fell
through to the plain "no anchor" path and was graded as an ordinary
un-anchored, range-checked-only citation — silently, with no error, no skip,
and no line in the summary distinguishing it from a citation that was never
anchored to begin with. `--fix` inherited the same blind spot for the same
reason, so it could not repair what it could not see either.

That silent downgrade, not the malformed syntax itself, is this gate's third
blind spot found by hand rather than by the gate (after bare unbackticked
`path:NNN` and the empty-`changelog.d/` early return, #2178/#2185) — and it
is the worst of the three, because a double-delimited anchor *reads* as
anchored and text-verified to the next person, while the gate silently
treated it as though it carried no anchor at all.

Fixed by detecting the clash directly rather than requiring a symmetric
close: `_MALFORMED_ANCHOR` matches two delimiter characters back to back
right after the opening paren
(`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:706`
(`malformed = _MALFORMED_ANCHOR.match(rest)`)), which is what actually breaks
`_ANCHOR` regardless of how the anchor text is shaped further in — the two
real instances on `dev` were not the tidy textbook shape either
(`` (`"i2s": 10`) `` closes on a bare backtick, and one anchor's own text
contained further backticks, which `_ANCHOR`'s capture class forbids on its
own). Both `_check_one` and `_fix_one` now report this as a hard ERROR
naming the two clashing delimiter characters, never a silent pass and never
folded into the ordinary "un-anchored" count `_fix_one` uses for a citation
that genuinely carries no anchor at all — a double-delimited anchor is
entirely fixable by its author right here, unlike a foreign-repo path or a
folded fragment, so it does not get the SKIP treatment those get either.

Known limitation left in place, not fixed here: `_MALFORMED_ANCHOR` only
catches a delimiter as the very first character after the opening paren, so
a "shortened, delimiter-free" anchor that still contains a delimiter later
in the span — `` (`ab"cd`) ``, `` (`: 1`) ``, `` (` "text") ``,
`` (`i2s"`) `` — is not this class at all. `_ANCHOR`'s own capture-refusal
class trips on it first instead, so it fails to match, falls through to "no
anchor", and degrades to range-checked-only exactly as silently as the
double-delimiter case this fix closes, with no error and no line in the
summary distinguishing it. Widening the detector past offset 0 is
deliberately out of scope here and is being filed separately.

Four live instances were found on `dev` this way, not the three expected —
`changelog.d/1171.md`, `changelog.d/2138.md`, `changelog.d/2139.md` and
`changelog.d/2149.md` (the last already carried a single-delimiter fix on
the unmerged #2190 branch, but `dev` itself still had the double-delimited
form). All four are repointed to a single delimiter in this change; the
anchored count over the whole tree rises by exactly 4 and the range-checked
count falls by the same 4.

Also carries the two nits deferred from the #2185 review of this same file:
`_fix_one`'s docstring now lists `_CHANGELOG_D_PREFIX` alongside `_CITATION`,
`_ANCHOR` and `_strip_fenced_blocks` as machinery it shares with `_check_one`
— it was the one condition duplicated by hand into both halves and the
docstring didn't say so — and the mutation-testing comment above `main()`'s
`--fix` placement now says the suite was 33 (its current size), not the
stale 29 left over from before #2185.

### Fixed — a changelog citation that looked anchored could go unverified, and a new one could skip its anchor entirely (#2186)

`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py` text-verifies a citation only when its
anchor parses; every other citation is range-checked (the line exists, the text
is never compared). On `dev` before this change the gate printed
`750 citation(s) resolved across 327 fragment(s) + CHANGELOG.md (396 anchored
and text-verified, 354 range-checked only, 14 skipped)` — a pass that asserted
nothing about the text of almost half the citations in the repo. Three holes
fed that bucket, and each is closed here.

**A new citation must be anchored.** A citation on a line added relative to a
base now fails the gate unless it carries a parsed, text-verified anchor
(`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:1223` ("def _added_lines(base: str)")).
"Added" is `git diff --unified=0 $(git merge-base BASE HEAD) -- changelog.d/`
against the working tree, so staged and unstaged edits count, and every line of
an untracked fragment counts — a fragment is graded while it is being written.
Diffing from the merge base rather than from BASE keeps lines BASE gained after
the branch point, or that a merge of BASE brought in, from being charged to the
branch. BASE is `DIFF_BASE`, default `origin/dev`
(`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:1166` ("def _resolve_base()")). With no
base available the rule degrades loudly: an explicit `DIFF_BASE` that does not
resolve exits 2, and an unset one with no `origin/dev` prints a WARN and a
`new-citation rule: NOT APPLIED` line naming why. Every passing run now prints
what it graded and how many citations the rule saw on added lines. The diff is
read with `core.quotePath=false` and a path's trailing TAB stripped, and any
`+++` header that is neither `b/<path>` nor `/dev/null` exits 2: before that, a
committed fragment named with a space or a non-ASCII character parsed as "no
path", and its lines silently escaped the rule. Existing un-anchored citations
are grandfathered — nothing can anchor one without guessing — and CHANGELOG.md
is exempt, because the release-cut fold moves hundreds of grandfathered
citations into `[Unreleased]` at once and moving a citation is not writing
one. A foreign-repo citation is still only SKIPPED. CI turns the rule on for a
PR into `dev` with `DIFF_BASE=HEAD^1`
(`.github/workflows/pr-metadata-validate.yml:652` ("github.base_ref == 'dev' && 'HEAD^1'")),
the first parent of the PR's merge commit, which the checkout now fetches with
`.github/workflows/pr-metadata-validate.yml:246` ("Depth 2 fetches its parents"). Not on a
PR into `main`: `HEAD^1` is `main` there, and every line of every fragment
`dev` has not folded yet would count as new (272 errors measured), so the gate
warns that the rule did not run. A `workflow_dispatch` of `dev` runs it
vacuously, since `origin/dev` is HEAD.

**A near-miss anchor is a hard error, on every citation.** Two shapes read as
anchored to a human and anchored nothing. The paren opened before the
citation, `` (`path:NNN`, "text") ``, puts the quote inside the citation's own
parenthetical, where `_ANCHOR` never looks
(`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:419` ("_PAREN_BEFORE = re.compile(")):
this is the shape `changelog.d/2195.md` used for 5 of its 8 citations, two of
them 187 and 10 lines off and green throughout. The other is `(` plus a
delimiter right after the citation that `_ANCHOR` then declined — text under 4
or over 120 characters, unterminated, or holding a delimiter past its first
character, such as `` (`: 1`) `` or `` (`i2s"`) ``
(`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:406` ("_ANCHOR_OPEN = re.compile(")).
The detector in #2184 caught only a delimiter at offset 0, and its error text
said so; that caveat is gone because the hole is. Every near-miss error shows
the correct form; the paren-before one fills it in with the author's own quote
when that quote does not open with a backtick, and the other uses a
placeholder. `--fix` reports a near miss as needing a human rather than
counting it un-anchored. Old citations are included because a near miss is an
author who tried to anchor, and grandfathering them kept known-wrong lines
green: `dev` held 9 in the first shape and 0 in the second, and 4 of the 9
cited the wrong line —
`changelog.d/1988.md` pointed at lines 1261, 1321 and 1123 of
`scripts/gen_zephyr_board.py` (each 39 lines short, now 1300, 1360 and 1162)
and at line 232 of `metadata/e1m_modules/aen/on-module-links.yaml` (now 235).
All 9 are repaired: the quote moved after the citation, then `--fix`
re-derived the four drifted ones from it. `changelog.d/2076.md` and
`changelog.d/2140.md` needed only the syntax; `changelog.d/1958.md` quoted a
before-and-after edit rather than an anchor, so its quotes moved out of the
parenthetical and the citation got a real anchor. A range's anchor has to quote
its FIRST line, because `--fix` restarts the range at the line the anchor is
found on (#2177), so `changelog.d/1516.md` now quotes line 14 of its `:14-15`
and `changelog.d/1916.md` cites only the `:285` it quotes; `changelog.d/README.md`
now states that rule. An anchor whose quote is broken across a markdown line
now says so instead of claiming the code moved.

**`--against-merge` grades what will land.** CI already grades the merge
result: `pr-metadata-validate.yml` runs on `pull_request` and its
`.github/workflows/pr-metadata-validate.yml:242` ("uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1")
pins no `ref:`, so it checks out `refs/pull/N/merge`. The gap was local, where
a green run on the branch tip said nothing about citations into files `dev`
had since moved. The new mode builds BASE merged into HEAD with
`git merge-tree --write-tree`, never the three-argument form, and grades that
tree straight from the object store, touching no file, index or ref
(`scripts/check_changelog_citations.py:1248` ("def _merge_tree(base: str, base_ref: str) -> str:")).
Its dirty-tree check runs `git --no-optional-locks status`, since a plain
`git status` rewrites the index. It grades committed HEAD only and warns when
the working tree is dirty; a HEAD that does not merge cleanly exits 1 naming
the conflicted files; a base that is already an ancestor of HEAD is reported
as grading HEAD's own tree, not a merge; and it refuses `--fix`, because the
merge is not in the working tree. `scripts/test-all.sh` runs it as its own
`changelog-citations-merge` stage with `origin/dev` passed explicitly, since
`DIFF_BASE` is shared with the clang-format stage
(`scripts/test-all.sh:1260` ("DIFF_BASE=origin/dev python3 scripts/check_changelog_citations.py --against-merge")).
A host without `git merge-tree --write-tree` (git before 2.38: Ubuntu 22.04
ships 2.34, Apple's git is 2.37) or without `origin/dev` gets a `[GAP]` SKIP
naming the reason instead of a failed stage, and the pytest cases that need
it skip there too. Still open: `pr-metadata-validate.yml` has no
`merge_group` trigger, so the merge CI grades is the one computed at the PR's
last push, and a `dev` that moves afterwards is caught only by a re-run.

The two deferred nits from the issue had already landed with #2194. The
mutation count in `main()`'s `--fix` placement comment was re-measured against
the grown suite: moving the `--fix` block below the early return still leaves
all 64 tests passing. The 22 new tests
(`tests/scripts/test_check_changelog_citations.py:1088` ("def test_against_merge_grades_the_merge_not_the_tip("))
were mutation-proven: 21 separate mutations of the new code each turn at least
one of them red.

### Fixed — a Flow D ATOC query that could not run no longer points the operator at `--replace-atoc` (#2187)

`bench_flowd_atoc_guard()` routes to the real resident-ATOC query whenever
`SE_UART` is exported — whether or not the variable names a device that can
actually answer. A **stale or wrong** `SE_UART` therefore took the query path,
the query failed, and the shared `bench_atoc_replace_guard()` aborted (exit 5)
with a remedy naming **`--replace-atoc`**: the "I checked and still want to
replace it" override, recommended for a check that demonstrably never ran.
`--atoc-unqueryable` is ignored on that path by design, and `unset SE_UART` —
the actual fix — was named nowhere in the output.

This was always fail-closed: nothing was written, and that is unchanged. The
defect is what the refusal *teaches*: `scripts/bench/aen/flash-jlink.sh:39-40`
(`will pass this on every single Flow D`) names the habit that must never
form, and #2029/#2027 kept the two flags distinct for exactly that reason. This path re-conflated them from the
other direction: the no-check state demanded the checked-and-override flag.

**The refusal is unchanged; only the remedy it prints is flow-aware.** The
unverified branch now selects its closing lines on `$BENCH_ATOC_FLOW` at
`scripts/bench/aen/bench-env.sh:1536`
(`= D ]; then`, the readable tail of
`if [ "${BENCH_ATOC_FLOW:-A}" = D ]; then` — that leading `"` is where
`_ANCHOR` stops, so only the tail can serve as this line's anchor), which
`bench_flowd_atoc_guard()` sets for the duration of its call at
`scripts/bench/aen/bench-env.sh:1641` (`local BENCH_ATOC_FLOW=D`):

- **Flow A** is unchanged and still reads
  `scripts/bench/aen/bench-env.sh:1559`
  (`Confirm by hand what is resident, then re-run with --replace-atoc`).
  There `SE_UART` *is* the transport, so a human confirming by hand and
  overriding is the only way past.
- **Flow D** is instead told to fix or unset `SE_UART` — preferring `LG_PLACE`
  over a raw `/dev/ttyUSBn` path, which `bench-env.sh` already warns is
  enumeration-ordered and has been measured swapped on this bench
  (#2032/#2064) — and is told explicitly not to reach for the override, at
  `scripts/bench/aen/bench-env.sh:1549`
  (`NOT --replace-atoc: that flag asserts you checked what is resident, and`).
  Flow D never needs a serial device, so a set-but-unanswering `SE_UART` is
  almost always a stale value rather than a board problem.

`local` scoping means the selector restores whatever an outer frame held, so a
Flow A guard called later in the same shell is unaffected. That is now a
committed test rather than a one-off check: three cases were added to
`tests/scripts/test_bench_jlink_connect_guard.py` — Flow D's remedy naming
`unset SE_UART`, `--atoc-unqueryable` and `LG_PLACE` and *not* `--replace-atoc`
(`tests/scripts/test_bench_jlink_connect_guard.py:1496`
(`test_flowd_unverified_query_does_not_recommend_replace_atoc`)); Flow A's
wording unchanged, which is what a fix that made the new text unconditional
would break
(`tests/scripts/test_bench_jlink_connect_guard.py:1528`
(`test_flow_a_unverified_query_still_recommends_replace_atoc`)); and both
guards driven in sequence in ONE shell, each asserted on its own transcript
(`tests/scripts/test_bench_jlink_connect_guard.py:1595`
(`test_flowd_flow_selector_does_not_leak_into_a_later_flow_a_guard`)).

That third one is why the `local` is there. Drop it and `BENCH_ATOC_FLOW`
leaks, so every later Flow A guard in the same shell — `flash-run.sh` and
`flash-run-dualcore.sh` both call one — starts advising `unset SE_UART` on a
board whose SE-UART is the only way to write it. All three were
mutation-proven: forcing the Flow A branch, forcing the Flow D branch, and
removing the `local` each turn the expected test red and no other.

`scripts/bench/aen/README.md`'s `flash-jlink.sh` row now records what an
exported-but-unusable `$SE_UART` prints, since that is what changed.

**Option (a) from the issue was deliberately not taken.** Honouring
`--atoc-unqueryable` whenever the query fails would let a broken cable or a
wrong device path on a slot that *does* have an SE-UART wired
silently downgrade into a blind write — strictly worse than the current
behaviour, and the #2025 failure mode. Distinguishing "no SE-UART on this slot"
from "SE-UART wired but currently broken" needs a signal the guard does not
have. This is option (b): the safety property is untouched, and only the
misleading advice is fixed.

### Note on the citations this change shifted

Inserting into `bench_atoc_replace_guard()` moved `changelog.d/2027.md`'s three
citations into the same file, and the two halves behaved exactly as #2186
predicts, which is worth recording while it is fresh:

- Its two **anchored** citations went red and were re-derived with
  `scripts/check_changelog_citations.py --fix`, as the gate instructs.
- `--fix` then resolved one of them **wrongly**, and said so: the anchor
  `bench_atoc_replace_guard` occurs eight times in the file, so the tool
  reported `AMBIGUOUS` and chose the nearest match, a comment line, over the
  call site the fragment's own parenthetical quotes. Corrected by hand to
  `scripts/bench/aen/bench-env.sh:1584` (`bench_atoc_replace_guard`). That bare
  name is all the anchor this line can carry, and it is the weakness itself:
  `_ANCHOR` stops at the first `"`, so a quoted code snippet truncates to its
  first token — the #2184 shape.
- Its third citation, an **un-anchored** range naming the function's extent,
  drifted silently from `1230-1289` to `1256-1336` and the gate stayed green,
  because an un-anchored citation is range-checked only and both ranges are
  valid. Found by reading, not by the gate. Corrected too.

Neither correction is load-bearing for this fix; they are recorded because
#2186 is open on precisely this and one more measured instance is useful to it.

Refs #2027. Refs #2029. Refs #2025. Refs #2032. Refs #2064. Refs #2186. Refs #2184.

### Fixed — `flash-all-flowd.sh` can flash a serial-less bench again, and a refused batch now explains itself (#2189)

`scripts/bench/aen/flash-all-flowd.sh` invoked the Flow D writer with
positional arguments only, forwarding neither `--atoc-unqueryable` nor
`--replace-atoc`. Since #2029 made `--atoc-unqueryable` mandatory when the
resident ATOC cannot be queried, **every entry in the batch aborted with exit
8 on a bench slot with no `SE_UART` exported, and the batch flashed nothing at
all** — and on a slot with no SE-UART wired at all, where Flow D is the only
load path, that left the batch runner entirely non-functional. `#2027`/`#2080`
re-armed the query path for slots that do export `SE_UART`, which is why this
went unnoticed there.

The regression dates from `ff2f316d` (#2029, merged 2026-09-07);
`flash-all-flowd.sh` was itself edited afterwards by `d1ac97d` (#2032/#2064)
without its call site being updated.

**The flag is opt-in, not hardcoded.** A new whole-argv scan at
`scripts/bench/aen/flash-all-flowd.sh:51-59`
(`--atoc-unqueryable) ATOC_UNQUERYABLE=(--atoc-unqueryable) ;;`) collects it
and forwards it verbatim at
`scripts/bench/aen/flash-all-flowd.sh:126`
(`flash-jlink.sh` invocation). Hardcoding it at the call site would have made
the batch replace the ATOC blindly on every run with the acknowledgement
recorded nowhere — the #2025 hazard, re-entered through the batch runner — so
the property #2029 and #2027 both protect is preserved: the operator says
"I cannot check" once, deliberately. `--replace-atoc` is deliberately **not**
forwarded; `scripts/bench/aen/flash-jlink.sh:39-42`
(`will pass this on every single Flow D`) states why the two flags must never
be merged or aliased.

The parser is the same whole-argv `for` shape `flash-jlink.sh` already uses for
this flag rather than `flash-run.sh`'s `while`/`shift` loop, because this
script's positionals are a variable-length app list: a parser that stops
honouring flags at the first non-option token would silently ignore
`flash-all-flowd.sh aen-wdt-feed --atoc-unqueryable`, and silently ignoring
this flag is the bug being fixed. Verified both orderings are honoured and that
the flag never lands in the app list.

**Exit 8 now has its own summary arm**, at
`scripts/bench/aen/flash-all-flowd.sh:184-190`
(`FLASH-REFUSED (no resident-ATOC check available)`), where before it fell to
the catch-all `FLASH-ERROR (exit $frc)` — the one Flow D exit code the summary
map did not explain.

Unlike every other arm, this one **breaks the batch** instead of continuing.
That is a deliberate departure from the script's "a failed app is logged and
the batch continues" design, and it is scoped to this single code: exit 8 is a
run-level configuration refusal decided before any probe or target access, so
it cannot differ between apps and every remaining entry would abort
identically. Continuing produced a `BATCH SUMMARY` that was 100% failure with
no board ever written and no line naming the cause. Entries already processed
keep their real verdicts and the `BATCH SUMMARY` still prints. Every other
exit code keeps the per-app resilience unchanged.

**Regression coverage**, in a new
`tests/scripts/test_bench_flash_all_flowd.py`, which drives the real batch
runner against a stub `flash-jlink.sh` that records its own argv and exits
with a scripted status — no probe, no module, no SETOOLS install. It pins
both orderings of the flag
(`tests/scripts/test_bench_flash_all_flowd.py:205`
(`test_atoc_unqueryable_after_the_app_list_is_still_honoured`)), that it
reaches every child rather than only the first, that it never lands in the
app list, that it is absent when nobody asked for it
(`tests/scripts/test_bench_flash_all_flowd.py:248`
(`test_the_flag_is_opt_in_and_never_hardcoded`)), that `--replace-atoc` is
not forwarded, and the whole exit-8 contract — the `FLASH-REFUSED` label, the
early stop, the earlier entries keeping their own verdicts, and the
`BATCH SUMMARY` still printing
(`tests/scripts/test_bench_flash_all_flowd.py:285`
(`test_exit_8_is_labelled_stops_the_batch_and_still_summarises`)). One test
pins the *other* direction too: a per-app failure must still continue the
batch, so a later "simplification" cannot turn one bad verify into a dead
run.

Every assertion was mutation-proven against the fixed script: dropping the
forwarding, hardcoding the flag, swapping the whole-argv scan for
`flash-run.sh`'s `while`/`shift` loop, deleting the exit-8 arm, turning its
`break` into a `continue`, relabelling it back to the catch-all, and
forwarding `--replace-atoc` each turn the expected test red and no other.

`scripts/bench/aen/README.md`'s batch-runner row documented the pre-change
contract — no flag in the signature, exit 8 unexplained, the serial-less
batch described as unusable — and is updated in the same change: the
signature, the opt-in acknowledgement semantics, the `FLASH-REFUSED` label
and early stop, and the summary contract.

Refs #2029. Refs #2027. Refs #2025. Refs #2032.

### Added — AEN boards seed their CSPRNG from the Secure-Enclave TRNG by default (#2192)

AEN had no Zephyr entropy driver, so the mbedTLS PSA core fell back to
`TEST_RANDOM_GENERATOR`, and #2193's refusal made every TLS build opt in
to that weak RNG explicitly. A new `alif,se-trng` entropy driver
(`zephyr/drivers/entropy/entropy_alif_se.c`, `CONFIG_ENTROPY_ALIF_SE`)
fixes this. It is thin glue over hal_alif's public
`se_service_get_rnd_num()`, chunked to the SE's 256-byte per-request
limit, with no ISR variant. `ensemble_e8_peripherals.dtsi` carries a
disabled `se_trng` node next to `se_service`.

`ensemble_e8_peripherals.dtsi` enables the SE-service channel
(`se_service`, `seservice0r/s`) and `se_trng`, and chooses
`zephyr,entropy = &se_trng`. Every AEN board therefore gets
`CONFIG_CSPRNG_ENABLED=y` on real hardware entropy. The weak-RNG opt-ins
are gone from the `mqtt-telemetry`, `iot-fleet-ota` and `aen-se-crypto`
AEN scenarios; the native_sim scenarios keep theirs. `aen-se-crypto`
gained a `zephyr,entropy` step: two 300-byte draws, which cross the chunk
limit, plus `sys_csrand_get()`.

**Caveat (#1700):** the first CSPRNG draw is now an SE `GET_RND` request.
On a module with a mismatched SERAM/services pair, that is the reported
trigger for the M55-HP dropping to 76.8 MHz. ADR 0030 makes such a pairing
unsupported, and a matched v110 pair was re-tested clean: the CGU
oscillator and PLL registers were unchanged across the request. An app
that must avoid SE traffic can disable `&se_trng` and choose its own
`zephyr,entropy`.

Bench-verified on E1M-AEN803 2026W36-0009 (M55-HE, Flow C RAM-run), 2 of
2 `RESULT PASS`:
- `zephyr,entropy (se_trng): get=0/0 differ=1 csrand=0 OK`;
- no `Using a test - not safe - entropy source` warning at boot;
- the CSPRNG output differed across boots (`dfcf56a3…` vs `36884390…`),
  which a test generator would repeat.

The same build for the M55-HP
(`alp_e1m_aen803_m55_hp/ae822fa0e5597ls0/rtss_hp`), using the same
`seservice0r/s` pair, also passed:
`zephyr,entropy (se_trng): get=0/0 differ=1 csrand=0 OK`. The
`0x40040000`/`0x40050000` mailboxes are core-local, so each core reaches
the SE through its own copy.

A board-default build of `aen-se-crypto` passed again, `aen-gpio-bench`
(no entropy consumer) still passes with the SE channel linked, and
`mqtt-telemetry` on the M55-HP boots without the test-entropy warning.

### Added — `check_cross_platform.py` flags implicit text-encoding calls under `scripts/**`/`tests/**` (#2195)

Python resolves the default text encoding from the platform locale — UTF-8 on
our Linux/Mac hosts, cp1252 on the `windows-latest` CI runner — so a
`Path.read_text()`/`open()`/`subprocess.run(..., text=True)` call with no
explicit `encoding=` works on every host the author tested on and raises
`UnicodeDecodeError` the moment non-ASCII content reaches Windows. Not
hypothetical: this is what turned PR #2194's curly-quote fixtures into a red
Windows leg while `bash scripts/test-all.sh` (Linux-only) stayed green
throughout.

`scripts/check_cross_platform.py:20`
("IMPLICIT-ENCODING -- a Python text-IO call with no explicit") gains a sixth
finding category, alongside `LINUX-ONLY-IDIOM` and `BASH-ONLY-SHEBANG`. It
flags, when no `encoding=` keyword is present: `Path.read_text()`/
`Path.write_text()`; bare `open()` or `Path.open()` in text mode; and
`subprocess.run`/`check_output`/`Popen` with `text=True` or
`universal_newlines=True`. Binary-mode IO and any call already passing
`encoding=` (including `encoding=locale.getpreferredencoding()`) are correct
and never flagged.

The check is AST-driven — `scripts/check_cross_platform.py:582`
("def scan_python_encoding") — not regex-driven like the existing five
`LINUX-ONLY-IDIOM` patterns: the flagged calls routinely spread their keyword
arguments across several lines, and "does this Call node have an `encoding=`
keyword anywhere" is exactly what `ast.parse` answers for free. It's scoped
to `scripts/**` and `tests/**` — `scripts/check_cross_platform.py:238`
("PY_SCAN_ROOTS") — the SDK's own tooling and test surface; an explicit
`--path` still scans any `.py` file regardless of that default-walk scope.
(#2197 later widened this scope to include `examples/` too -- see
`changelog.d/2197-retire-encoding-baseline.md`.)

`tests/scripts/conftest.py:105` (`encoding=`) — this rule's known
live site, `subprocess.run([exe, "--version"], capture_output=True,
text=True, check=True)` with no `encoding=` — fixed in the same change so
the rule ships clean; it was the only implicit-encoding call left in the
`pytest tests/scripts/` surface.

A wider repo sweep with the new rule found 478 further implicit-encoding
sites across 139 files (overwhelmingly `write_text`/`subprocess.run` calls in
test fixtures under `tests/scripts/`); those are deliberately left for a
follow-up rather than folded into this change, so this fragment ships the
rule + its two mandated fixes (`tests/scripts/conftest.py`, and this rule's
own test-harness `_run` helper), not a sprawling mechanical diff.

Those 478 sites are not left unenforced, though:
`scripts/check_cross_platform.py`
(`IMPLICIT_ENCODING_BASELINE` frozenset — removed when #2197 finished the
drain) grandfathers them
by file — a **file-level**, not site-level, allowlist deliberately shaped
after the existing `INTENTIONALLY_DISCUSSES_OS_PATHS` allowlist rather than a
line-numbered one, because a line-numbered baseline rots on the next
unrelated edit to a listed file and this repo has been bitten by exactly
that kind of silent drift before. The tradeoff is real and was spelled out in
a comment at `scripts/check_cross_platform.py`
(`What this is: the day` — removed when #2197 finished the drain): touching a
baselined file did not force a fix of
its other pre-existing findings, and a genuinely new implicit-encoding call
added to a baselined file was still only a warning —
`scripts/check_cross_platform.py` (`baselined: bool = False` — removed when
#2197 finished the drain) — printed,
not silenced, but not `--fail-on-warning`-failing either:
`scripts/check_cross_platform.py` (`not f.baselined` — removed when #2197
finished the drain). New files, and
every file not on the list, were gated from day one. The baseline was
temporary and only shrank; draining it was tracked in #2197 and is now done —
see `changelog.d/2197-retire-encoding-baseline.md`.

`tests/scripts/test_check_cross_platform.py`'s
`test_linter_fail_on_warning_against_real_repo_passes` then asserted the thing
that was actually true post-baseline — zero findings *outside*
`IMPLICIT_ENCODING_BASELINE` against the live tree — instead of the
then-false "zero findings" it asserted before this fragment; three new cases
covered the baseline mechanism itself (a baselined file doesn't fail, a
non-baselined file does, a brand-new finding in an already-baselined file
still prints as a warning without failing). All of that baseline-specific
coverage was retired along with the baseline itself in #2197's final drain —
see `changelog.d/2197-retire-encoding-baseline.md`.

Review follow-ups, folded into this change. The baseline comment claimed a
compensating control that does not exist — per-file counts "still visible via
the summary line" — when `_print_summary` printed one aggregate
`478 IMPLICIT-ENCODING finding(s) in IMPLICIT_ENCODING_BASELINE files` and no
per-file breakdown anywhere. The comment then stated that aggregate reality
(`scripts/check_cross_platform.py`, "accepted cost of file-level granularity,
and it is NOT" — removed with the rest of the baseline comment when #2197
finished the drain). Replacing the
imaginary control was a real one, free from data
`test_linter_fail_on_warning_against_real_repo_passes` already computed — a
shrink-only size pin at `tests/scripts/test_check_cross_platform.py`
("len(linter.IMPLICIT_ENCODING_BASELINE) <=" — the pin was removed when
#2197 finished the drain; the test itself survives as a plain zero-findings
check) plus a stale-entry check at `tests/scripts/test_check_cross_platform.py`
("stale = set(linter.IMPLICIT_ENCODING_BASELINE)" — likewise removed) — so
the set could only
shrink and could not keep a file that no longer produced a finding. Three stale
claims were corrected alongside it.
`.github/workflows/cross-platform-zephyr.yml` ("Not silent, though:" — that
wording was replaced when #2197 finished the drain)
promised "0 findings as of this change" for a step that then printed 478
baselined warnings and still exited 0.
`docs/cross-platform-setup.md:690` ("The lint itself is") described its 6.2
lint step as printing warnings about Linux-only idioms in docs, when the run
then printed 478 `IMPLICIT-ENCODING` lines about Python files under `scripts/`
and `tests/`; the same paragraph also called the lint "soft", which was
already wrong *before* this branch — CI flipped it to `--fail-on-warning` in
#1032 A5 — so the expected output and the soft-lint claim are both fixed.
And the gate's one-line description at `metadata/quality-tasks-v1.json:313`
("cross-platform hazards") no longer says only "Linux-only idioms in
customer-facing surfaces", which never covered this category: `scripts/` and
`tests/` are not customer-facing and an encoding default is not a Linux-only
idiom. That one line is generated into `metadata/catalog.json:3437`
("cross-platform hazards") from the module docstring's first paragraph by
`gen_catalog.py`, so the docstring, the regenerated catalog, and the registry
moved together.

The same stale claim survived in the decision record itself, at
`docs/adr/0012-cross-platform-developer-host.md:213`
("both halves of that sentence are now"), which still described the
fail-on-warning flip as "a future cleanup task, scoped separately". The
original decision text is left standing — an ADR records what was decided at
the time — and a dated amendment now records that the flip landed in #1032 A5,
that this change added the `IMPLICIT-ENCODING` category on top of it, and that
the category deliberately scans `scripts/` and `tests/`, which are not the
customer-facing surfaces the ADR originally scoped the check to.

Adding `encoding="utf-8"` to this rule's own test harness, to make it pass its
own check, broke five CLI tests on `windows-latest` only — the exact failure
class the rule exists to catch, introduced by following the rule's advice
halfway. `encoding=` sets only how the *parent* decodes. The child Python
still writes its locale encoding, cp1252 on Windows, and the linter's output
carries a `§` that cp1252 writes as the single byte `0xa7`, which is not valid
UTF-8. The decode failed inside `subprocess`'s reader thread, the exception
was swallowed, and `stdout` came back `None`
(`TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`). Before this
change both ends used the locale default and agreed, which is why `dev`
passed. The harness now makes the child write UTF-8 as well, at
`tests/scripts/test_check_cross_platform.py:74` ("env={**os.environ"). Forcing
`PYTHONIOENCODING=cp1252` on a Linux run reproduces all five failures before
the fix and passes after it. The rule's own advice for `subprocess` calls now
says the same thing, at `scripts/check_cross_platform.py:688`
("sure the child WRITES UTF-8"), so draining #2197 does not repeat this at
every call site that spawns a Python child.

### Fixed — i2s3's pinctrl group declared TX only, leaving SDI (P9_2) unmuxed even though it is the one U46 leg wired correctly (#2196)

Both in-tree `i2s3` board overlays for the E1M-AEN801 (`ae822fa0e5597ls0`,
RTSS-HE) muxed only SDO/SCLK/WS and left `P9_2` (`I2S3_SDI_A`) undeclared.
`P9_2` is the one leg of U46 (a 74LVC157 2:1 mux) that is wired in the
*correct* direction — it feeds the amps' SDOUT/IV-sense back to the SoC —
